The poll of polls did not include a new Talbot-Mills corporate poll, which had National down two points and out of Government unless it did a deal with Opportunity.

Act’s leader David Seymour last week confirmed his party could work with Opportunity, provided they gave up their land tax and universal basic income policies.

The tax package was defended by leader Qiulae Wong on TVNZ’s Q+A on Sunday, after she admitted the party had not modelled its impact on “wealth flight”. Kiwis returning to New Zealand could also be left worse off but should look at the “bigger picture”, Wong said.

Parties continue to release new policy proposals, with Act proposing to remove “good employer” requirements from the public service and Opportunity pledging to clean up political lobbying and cap donations.

Ted Charlton has a rare medical condition. He’s died seven times

New Zealand Herald August 16, 2026

A rare disorder has caused Dannevirke man Ted Charlton to die seven times.

By Kate Green of RNZ

When Ted Charlton was wheeled into the Palmerston North emergency department in 2023, it was actually the seventh time he had died.

The 58-year-old has a rare temperature and thirst disorder, meaning if he gets too hot or too cold, his body starts to shut down.

And living rurally, just outside of Dannevirke, time is usually of the essence.

“Within five minutes I can be in a catastrophic condition,” he told RNZ,“ Charlton said.

Each time, he was resuscitated. On one occasion, while swimming lengths at the local pool, a friend emerged from the water to find Ted floating face-down in the next lane.

Luckily, this friend was an ambulance officer, who “fished me out, read my bracelet, started on the routine and then they got the ambo”.

“A doctor who was going to work at the medical centre in Dannevirke happened to be driving past and saw an ambulance. He shot in and he took over – and he was a Navy doctor.”

Then there was the time he fell into a coma after driving over a patch of slippery road and careening into a river.

The car “turned into the Titanic”, he said. “Thank goodness for wind-down windows.”

He made it to the bank, but his body temperature dropped and he ended up in hospital again.

Even on a day-to-day basis, he said he had to pay close attention to what his body needed so it didn’t overheat or grow too cold.

“I just have to look at absolutely everything in the sense of what I’m wearing, my environment, and mitigate that from happening.”

His most recent brush with death had no discernible cause.

“I got up that Sunday morning and I just couldn’t get warm. And in the end, driving to the hospital, we drove in the car and it was 500m from the hospital that my wife looked over and saw me. And the heater was on full bore. I had two bomber jackets on. And she said I just started to collapse.”

He was dead for two minutes before being revived by hospital doctors.

The condition had likely affected him his whole life, but it hadn’t caused major problems in his younger years. He remembered feeling hot or cold, but he’d fix that by taking off a jumper like anyone else.

He was issued with a medic alert bracelet in 1992, and he credits it for a lot, saying it almost certainly sped up the provision of life-saving care when he was unable to speak for himself – especially with such a rare condition.

A medic alert bracelet costs less than $100.

“There’s so many people that they’ll go and insure their $80,000 BMW, but won’t spend a little bit more on themselves. It’s like you can replace the BMW, mate. You can’t replace you.”

Charlton took his health seriously, but he could appreciate a well-placed joke.

“Dad has a bit of a laugh about it because I love cats and he says, ‘You’ve got to be careful, you’ve only got two [lives] left’.”

It had certainly made him look at life differently – and given him an appreciation of how lucky he was.

“I look back at my life and I think, ‘well, I certainly had quite a few close scrapes that most people wouldn’t have come out of’,” he said.

Was he worried he was running out of lives and luck?

“Depends whether we’re cats or not, Kate.”

Rotorua Museum closure: Council spends more than $300k a year to store $21.5m art collection

New Zealand Herald August 16, 2026

Former Rotorua Museum curator Paul Tapsell in front of Ngāti Whakaue chief Pūkaki at the museum storage site in 2024. Photo / Laura Smith

Rotorua Lakes Council is spending more than $319,000 a year to store, insure and maintain a $21 million-plus art collection – much of which the public hasn’t seen since Rotorua Museum closed in 2016.

The council holds 2878 works of art, including 1526 donated pieces, and stores 348 works owned by other parties.

The council-owned collection is estimated to be worth $13.66m, including $6.9m of gifted works. The privately owned works held by council have a combined estimated value of $7.9m.

Figures supplied to Local Democracy Reporting show the council spends about $288,627 a year on storage, $25,343 on insurance and $5000 on maintenance and conservation.

The collection has not been publicly displayed at the museum since it closed for earthquake strengthening and restoration work in 2016.

Council community experience manager Alex Wilson said opportunities to display more of the collection elsewhere had been explored but were not progressed for financial reasons.

“The cost of the security and environmental control standards that are required was prohibitive,” she said.

Wilson said decisions about the future management, display and investment in the collection could be considered as part of the next Long-Term Plan process.

She said the council had not commissioned a standalone review of its art collection.

Mayor Tania Tapsell said the museum’s reopening would provide an opportunity to display more of the collection.

The museum building work should be completed next month, reopening in mid-to-late 2028.

“In September, the museum building will be fixed, and work will start on our world-class exhibition,” Tapsell said.

“The exciting part now begins as we complete the design and confirm which taonga and artwork will be on display.”

Tapsell said she wanted more of the collection to be accessible.

“What I hope is that these incredible pieces get to be displayed publicly, even if during temporary and changing exhibitions,” she said.

She also acknowledged museums could not display their entire collection. She said any decisions to remove works from the collection – a process known as deaccessioning n–eeded to be made carefully, particularly where items had cultural, historical or local significance.

“I believe there is a very real need to protect historic and cultural artefacts, especially with local connection,” she said.

“Keeping artwork in storage is a debate that has started across the country, and I’m committed to reviewing how we can best protect our art and history while ensuring a return on this investment for locals.”

Tapsell said that return could be social or financial.

The council could not reveal who owned the works held on loan, citing confidentiality.

Almost all scaffolding has been removed from the museum, with construction work expected to finish next month.

However, the museum faces another major hurdle before it can reopen: a $7m-$8m shortfall in its exhibition budget.

Fundraising is underway, including the Friends of Rotorua Museum’s 1000 Friends campaign, which has raised $94,000 towards a $1m target.

An Off-Broadway concert fundraiser is later this month.

Tapsell said she would welcome opportunities to display works before 2028 if suitable venues could be found.

“I’d love for locals and visitors to see nationally and internationally significant artwork in Rotorua and not just the big cities,” she said.

Mathew Nash is a Local Democracy Reporting journalist based at the Rotorua Daily Post. He has previously written for SunLive, been a regular contributor to RNZ and was a football reporter in the UK for eight years.

Snow has closed the Desert Rd as a bitterly cold air mass drives up from the south.

The closure of State Highway 1 from Rangipo to Waiōuru – in place since 9pm – has added a detour of at least 40 minutes to the journey, according to the NZ Transport Agency’s website.

The cold southerly is bringing a frigid and frosty start to the working week, with Mount Cook Village recording a low of -7.3C.

By 6.30am this morning, all New Zealand towns and cities hovered around single-digit temperatures, with the Coromandel’s Waikawau Bay the warmest with a high of 9C.

The shivery start follows a wintry weekend that brought wet weather and snow to parts of both islands, with warnings in place across several major roads.

Much of that wet weather was set to clear overnight, but showers will linger along eastern regions.

MetService meteorologist Alanna Burrows told the Herald much of the country would wake to “fine and frosty” conditions today.

“It’s going to be chilly,” Burrows said.

“For Mt Cook, we’ve got a forecast of -9C, then it’s like 2C for Kaikōura, so it’s going to be a chilly morning.”

Taupō was forecast to fall to 0C, Hamilton and Rotorua to 4C, while Auckland and Wellington were both expected to start the day at around 6C.

Burrows said the bitterly cold air was being drawn from around 60 degrees south, near the Southern Ocean.

“It starts to change perhaps on Friday, but for most of the week, we’ve got a southerly flow drawing up those cold temperatures with frost expected overnight,” she said.

That southerly flow would also push showers on to eastern parts of the country.

Despite fine spells elsewhere, Burrows said daytime temperatures would remain low.

“It actually looks like most of the max temperatures are in the low teens for most places.”

Auckland was forecast to reach just 12C, after any isolated showers clear before dawn.

Wellington faced a cooler high of just 9C, with cloudy periods and occasional showers expected to clear later this afternoon.

Christchurch was forecast to reach 11C, with showers mainly around Banks Peninsula “clearing to fine” this morning and morning frosts also possible in sheltered places, Burrows said.

The week ahead is otherwise looking relatively settled, with high pressure in the Tasman Sea helping keep conditions mostly dry.

Eastern areas and the far south are most likely to see showers through to Thursday, before the flow turns more westerly on Friday.

Burrows said Thursday currently looked like the pick of the week.

“Those showers in the east are kind of easing off through Thursday and we also have some stronger southerly winds and they’ll be easing off on Thursday as well.

“So, lighter winds and drier weather. I think that’s probably the best day.”

Letters: Rod Liddle’s satire needed no label; dog owners and the law; and happy tax

New Zealand Herald August 16, 2026

Dog owners who fear prosecution may be more responsible, a reader says. Photo / Michael Craig

Letter of the week - Liddle less yackety-yack

I agree with David Cohen (Herald Aug 14). Satirical exposure of gaps between ideal and real is a much-needed art form.

Cousins only in the New Zealand sense, Rod Liddle and I at least share origins: that “debatable land” between Scotland and England. Renowned for its reivers (or pirates), it was the better-sounding name for thieves and brigands who enjoyed a similar reputation for independence, irreverent wit, and what the Scots still call spunk.

Whatever, as a satirist Rod had these gifts and more. Rod was not required to label his Spectator columns satire. As anyone who’s lived in the United Kingdom knows, all egos are fair game and taking yourself seriously not seen as part of a liberal society.

Hyperbole, generalisations, insinuations and even clever insults are part of the cost of satirists’ uncomfortable insights. Exponents don’t last long under authoritarians, of course, yet are needed to alert us when their self-righteous, my-way-or-the-highway views are in danger of taking hold.

Steve Liddle, Napier.

Dog owner laws

When will the lawmakers of New Zealand deal properly with the owners of dogs that are maiming and killing humans?

Clearly the owners should be prosecuted and jailed?

The fear of this action taken by the jurisdiction would surely protect us from the scourge of outrageous dog owner behaviour. Why does it take so long to remedy?

The SPCA should spend its funds on educating humans, not euthanising animals. That’s the gate out of which the dog has bolted.

Jan Elliott, Ōrātia.

High tax, high happiness

Saturday’s letters showed this great desire of some in New Zealand to have no debt. Finance Minister Nicola Willis agrees and is out of kilter with countries doing well.

In the letters to the editor, George worries about grandchildren inheriting this debt when that is a spurious argument only applicable to business and home economy, not countries.

The happiest and most successful countries tax high and see debt as necessary for infrastructure like hospitals and education.

Our grandchildren want to be happy, well-educated and healthy, like the Nordics.

As our homelessness increases, Finland no longer has homelessness. It tops the happiness index.

The high-taxed Nordic countries are at the top and the low-tax regimes such as the United States and UK are around the bottom 20s.

We are 11 and descending fast as our government cuts health and infrastructure. Willis wants to balance the budget and create more misery. The US, Europe and the UK have enormous rising debt, ours is tiny in comparison. Why is Willis so determined not to make us happy?

Frankie Letford, Hamilton.

Alcohol analysis

DB Breweries posted a $33.8 million loss for financial year 2025/26, (Herald, Aug 15).

It would be of major public interest to see an analysis giving reasons for this decline.

Is it due to a fall in volumes or a rise in price? or possibly a change in consumer preferences with other alcoholic drinks being substituted for beer?

Could it be because of a rise in the consumption of very drinkable low or no alcohol “near beers”? Or have drinkers recently discovered that alcohol is a toxin that destroys both livers and kidneys ... and is an endangerment to a long and healthy life?

Whatever the reason, we can be very happy with the trend.

Larry Mitchell, Rothesay Bay.

Bishop’s ‘antics’

The antics of Chris Bishop, and no doubt at least one or two others, remind me of the character Sergeant Shultz in the TV satire Hogan’s Heroes with his legendary phrase, “I know nothing”. Members of the public, in general, are not that stupid.

Paul Beck, West Harbour.

Political memory

Political memory is very short. Christopher Luxon became leader of the Nats shortly after becoming an MP mainly because he was not tainted with the leadership changes of Bridges, Collins and others in a short time.

He had no “baggage”. He had come from a corporate background where what he said his staff did.

In politics, every MP follows their preferences first and party policy second. He had no time to learn how to herd sheep. He has managed the coalition Government remarkably well.

Now is not the time to change – no good for the Nats, Luxon or any incomer. Time to focus on all that this Government has achieved and will do better in next term.

Derek Paterson, Sunnyhills.

Challenging the numbers

Reading Bruce Cotterill’s article (Herald, Aug 15) makes me wonder if he has actually fact-checked all the figures he is quoting.

All the figures regarding health education, law and order and exports are the ones propagated by the right, are all speculative and well worthy of challenging.

Hamish Walsh, Devonport.

Wildfires kill two in Greece and torch Belgian nature reserve

The Guardian Sun, 16 Aug 2026 21:27:03 GMT

Couple die in Salamis, while multinational forces and local farmers tackle Belgium’s biggest fire in a century near Liège

An elderly couple died in fires on the Greek island of Salamis on Sunday and a fire ravaged Belgium’s largest nature reserve, in the latest wave of European wildfires.

The couple died outside their home in the Peristeria beach area of Salamis, Greece’s coastguard said. More than 500 people were ordered to evacuate.

In Spain, a soldier died on Sunday while helping efforts to extinguish a large wildfire in Aragon, authorities said. The fire in the north-eastern region has raged for a week and threatened a 1,000-year-old monastery.

In Belgium, a wildfire that broke out on Friday in the High Fens, a large nature reserve popular with hikers, had ravaged about 3,000 hectares (7,400 acres) of land and was encroaching on the border with Germany by early Sunday morning.

About 600 people in the municipalities of Waimes and Bütgenbach, in Liège province, were told on Saturday to evacuate from their homes, and tourists were also advised to leave, as winds shifted and smoke spread.

Of those who followed the order, about 20 spent the night in a sports hall, while others sought refuge with family and friends.

Hervé Jamar, the governor of Liège, said more than 250 firefighters and emergency staff were involved in the operation, including firefighters from Germany.

Farmers have also been helping to battle the blaze, using their tractors to pull in water from Lake Robertville.

Air support, provided by two water-bombing aircraft from Sweden and four helicopters – two from Belgium and two from the Netherlands – is crucial owing to the nature reserve’s complex and fragile terrain, which is made up of dense forest, peat bogs and raised wooden boardwalks where heavy firefighting vehicles risk sinking.

Access to Lake Bütgenbach was prohibited on Sunday to allow the aircraft to refill.

Authorities described the conditions as still challenging, although two fire fronts towards Jalhay and Monschau were now under control, said Belgium’s interior minister, Bernard Quintin, after visiting the crisis centre in Vottem on Sunday afternoon.

“On this third day of fighting the fires, all resources remain mobilised on the ground,” he wrote on X, and he thanked all those involved. “We can also count on the solidarity of our European partners … Thank you to everyone who mobilised to fight the fires. United, we are stronger.”

The fire, described by officials as the largest in Belgium’s modern history, began in an area that in 1911 was badly affected by massive wildfires during a drought.

Human-caused climate breakdown is supercharging extreme weather around the world, driving more frequent and deadlier disasters from heatwaves to floods to wildfires. Much of Europe is experiencing a new period of intense heat, creating conditions conducive to wildfire outbreaks.

On Friday a fire engulfed ⁠homes in a Croatian holiday resort, killing one person, injuring 40 and forcing 1,200 to evacuate, officials said, as the EU warned that pockets of “very extreme” wildfire conditions stretched across the continent.

Hundreds more people were evacuated from villages in western Germany and south-west France, while stranded holidaymakers were picked up from beaches threatened by flames in Greece and the army rescued historical relics in Spain.

Amy Hunt’s ‘dream comes true’ with fourth European Championships gold

The Guardian Sun, 16 Aug 2026 21:09:15 GMT

British sprinter first to win four titles at single event

Dina Asher-Smith hits record 11 European medals total

If there was any remaining doubt that this has been Amy Hunt’s European Championships, it was dispelled over 10 seconds of controlled fury as the newest British sporting superstar completed an unprecedented quadruple.

When the baton was slapped into her hand on the anchor leg of the mixed 4x100m relay, the British athlete was a fraction behind Gina Lückenkemper of Germany. But then Hunt became the hunter.

In no time at all those legs began to whirr, her vast stride started to widen, and she found her wings. Within in a blink of an eye she had chased down Lückenkemper – and ran into the history books.

As Hunt crossed the line, she outstretched her arms and held four fingers to the camera. And just like that Hunt had completed the quadruple.

“It’s just a dream come true – I’ll remember this week for the rest of my life,” she said after becoming the first athlete in the 92-year history of the European Championships to win four gold medals in a single event.

Britain’s time was a European record 39.97 seconds, with Germany taking silver in 40.11 and Spain winning bronze.

To run seven races in seven days is difficult enough. To win all seven takes not only talent and guts but a hefty dose of chutzpah.

But while Hunt certainly has main-character energy she quickly wanted to ensure that her teammates Jeremiah Azu, Dina Asher-Smith and Zharnel Hughes were hailed as well.

“To do it all together is incredible, especially because that was the first time we kind of did that changeover about an hour ago in warm-up,” said Hunt. “And look how smooth it was. Such professionals.

“It was a bit like when you’re queueing for a rollercoaster and you’re a little bit nervous and you’re seeing the drops, and then when you get off you want to do it again. So it was that adrenaline kick certainly. I loved the event.”

But Hunt wasn’t the only history maker on the night as Asher-Smith made it a record 11 European medals in total – surpassing Polish sprinter Irena Szewinska.

It was the first time the mixed 4x100m relay has taken place at these championships, which brought its own challenges. For while the British team had the strongest team on paper, and alternating the men and women increased the jeopardy. No wonder the Netherlands and Italy were disqualified.

“I’m gonna be completely frank with you, I was absolutely terrified,” said Asher-Smith. “When the gun was going, I was like ‘Dina, please relax relax, it’s only going to go well if you relax’. And when I gave that baton to Zharnel, I was so happy, I can’t lie. That’s exactly how I feel. Very unfiltered. I was just like ‘get this out of my hand – bye’.”

That message was shared by Hunt. “We don’t get to do that very often, have something new in our sport,” she said. “It’s so rudimentary just running as fast as you can from A to B. So to do something brand new was amazing.”

Asher-Smith’s achievements were also acknowledged by Azu, who said it was a privilege to compete with her.

Reform accused of targeting the most vulnerable with £50bn benefit cut

The Guardian Sun, 16 Aug 2026 21:00:35 GMT

Robert Jenrick takes aim at disabled people and foreign nationals after saying UK guilty of ‘suicidal empathy’

Reform UK has been accused of excluding the most vulnerable from society and punishing non-Britons living in the UK as it prepared to outline £50bn of cuts to benefits for disabled people and foreign nationals.

Robert Jenrick, Reform’s finance spokesperson, will detail the plans for £20bn of cuts to disability benefits overall, as well as another £21bn from stopping foreign nationals – including EU citizens with settled status – claiming almost any benefits, among other cuts.

The party said the plans were aimed at reducing the welfare bill by a quarter, with personal independence payments (Pip) replaced by another cash benefit that would be restricted to only the “gravely ill and severely challenged”.

It said “lower level conditions” would get support overseen by councils and mayors.

In relation to foreign nationals, the plans extend proposals set out by Nigel Farage last year in which he claimed that banning migrants from claiming some benefits and scrapping indefinite leave to remain would save £234bn over several decades.

Jenrick’s policy paper goes further by stopping foreign-born households claiming universal credit, housing benefit, pension credit, jobseeker’s allowance, child benefit, free childcare, free school meals or disability benefits.

The paper says the change would save the taxpayer £21bn a year by the fifth year of the policy, and would also apply to those with EU settled status. However, foreign-born parents with British-born children would still be eligible for child benefit and free school meals.

Best for Britain, the pro-EU campaign group, said denying benefits to those with indefinite leave to remain would tear up Britain’s EU withdrawal agreement.

Tom Brufatto, the executive director of policy at the organisation, said: “Our polling shows that people do want to renegotiate our relationship with Europe, but by moving closer, not by damaging ties with vital allies and punishing our neighbours, colleagues and friends who have settled status here.”

Jenrick claimed paying benefits to non-British people was “plain immoral” – even though many would have paid into the tax system through working. He also wrote in the Telegraph over the weekend that the amount spent on disability benefits was “not generosity … it is suicidal empathy”.

However, Jenrick was accused by campaigners of making life harder for disabled people and of not understanding that it would not save money.

Rachael Maskell, the Labour MP who led the campaign against previous disability benefit cuts under Keir Starmer, said: “When Pip helps people go to work, play a role in our society and simply live, threatening to remove Pip demonstrates that Reform do not want disabled people to play a full role in our society.

“Instead, Labour is working with disabled people through the Timms review to optimise the impact of Pip to ensure both taxpayers and disabled people get real value out of the system.

“Instead of making it harder for disabled people, who already experience significant financial deprivation, they should spend time learning of the benefit it brings.”

Linda Burnip, the co-founder of Disabled People Against Cuts, said previous attempts to replace disability benefits with cheaper options had not been successful.

“Originally the Tories scrapped disability living allowance and replaced it with Pip, aiming to save 20% from the social security bill,” she said.

“However, this obviously has failed and the major problem with Reform’s crude plans to save money by denying payments to disabled people is that they fail to understand that a relatively small payment, which supports someone, could result in a massive saving overall from the public purse.

“It could, for example, mean someone with a mental health condition is able to remain living safely in the community rather than needing to spend weeks or even months in a hospital for which private firms often charge around £12,000 per person a week.”

Labour described the plans to cut disability benefits as “fantasy economics” that would “strip support” from disabled people and shift the costs of employing people with sickness or a disability on to employers through an insurance-based model.

Mothin Ali, the Green party deputy leader, said the “establishment parties are all trying to outdo each other when it comes to who can be the most xenophobic, who can punch down the hardest to the most vulnerable in our country, and who can cut the most support from disabled people”. He added: “It is cowardly to take from the most defenceless when we should be taxing the super-wealthy, including those who are in the privileged position of accepting £5m donations,” he added, referring to Farage, the leader of Reform UK.

Meanwhile, the Conservatives, who are trying to show they are taking a tough stance on welfare, said Reform’s announcement was “cobbled together” and claimed only the Tories had a “credible plan to save £23bn from welfare alongside our root and branch review of sickness benefits”.

Tim Seifert set up victory with 72 off 38 balls; Liam Dawson completed it with two balls remaining, a six to seal it.

The New Zealand opener turned Jos Buttler into a support act in a chase of 159, his scarily high backlift producing seven sixes and a 23-ball half-century. The 31-year-old launched far higher than any of the Rockets, their innings defined by useful cameos. Noor Ahmad sparkled with the ball for the Super Giants, taking three for 33, but this was Seifert’s night.

The Rockets, who were going for a double after their women’s side had triumphed earlier in the piece, did offer a serious scare at the close. Seifert departed with 22 balls remaining, 23 still required, and the Super Giants refused to cruise. Mohammad Amir removed Heinrich Klaasen and Michael Bracewell, and with three required off the last over, Dawson struck air with his first two balls. It would be third-time lucky, Ben Sanderson sent over deep midwicket to close a tournament that should have been won minutes earlier.

Lord’s was a psychedelic place before kick-off. Ella Eyre had the thankless task as musical guest while the two sides warmed up yards away, daytime fireworks in full flow. This was a second consecutive men’s final for the Rockets but they had just the one survivor from last year: Northamptonshire’s Sanderson. Their run to this point had been fuelled largely by the runs of Ben Duckett while the Super Giants had enjoyed the fruits of an England pace triumvirate: Josh Tongue, Sonny Baker and Gus Atkinson. With Buttler deciding to bowl, Duckett against the quicks – what felt like the key battle at the start of the day – was first up.

Duckett welcomed the fuller length from Atkinson and Baker, getting the scoop out for a couple of sixes, and was grateful for a drop on 23; the left-hander reverse-swept the ball to Tongue, his England and Nottinghamshire teammate, who erred at short third. Duckett, who slapped 141 against India on this ground in July, looked on for a big one, putting on 48 for the first wicket alongside Finn Allen.

Ahmad decided otherwise. The left-arm wrist-spinner struck with his first ball, getting Allen holed out at long-off, but the delivery to Duckett moments later would’ve belonged in a red-ball game. A fizzing wrong’un caught the inside-edge before finding Buttler’s gloves, Duckett gone for 31. Another Ahmad googly later in the innings accounted for Australia’s Tim David, whose difficult tournament – 90 runs from eight knocks for the £350,000 signing – ended with a first-ball edge to the sharp Buttler, leaving the Rockets on 91 for four after 59 deliveries.

In a match packed with seasoned internationals it was the uncapped Aneurin Donald who gave the Rockets their biggest lift. He didn’t let Ahmad bother him, sweeping hard for six, while a Baker short ball was hooked into the crowds, too. His 19-ball 38 included some miscommunication with Sam Billings, prompting the captain’s run out, but the Rockets could call upon a strong lower order for the finish.

Mitch Santner’s unbeaten 20 took him to a season’s batting average of 146. Lewis Gregory, who hit the winning runs when the Rockets won the tournament four years ago, was brutal with a 16-ball 32.

Djokovic’s medical malaise in Cincinnati exposes fraying edges of ageing great’s game

The Guardian Sun, 16 Aug 2026 19:00:33 GMT

First-round exit for 24-time grand slam winner made for a difficult watch but there is an emerging pattern of saving his best for the big occasion

Novak Djokovic walked from the ­stadium court in Cincinnati to the corridor reserved for post-match press interviews practically without breaking stride. The 39-year-old had been cruising up a set and well on his way to a seemingly comfortable victory when he began to feel the full force of the elements. Djokovic would devote much of his time during the final two sets to crouching on all fours between points, vomiting into towels and desperately struggling to perform.

Such was his disappointment with his ageing body failing him once again that Djokovic, who is usually one of the most loquacious on the tour, briskly answered four questions in about a minute before offering his thanks and striding to the locker room. He wanted nothing more than to get out of there.

There was once a time when an opening-round loss for Djokovic at the final Masters 1000 event would send alarm bells ringing, but ­perhaps the most interesting part of this defeat is how familiar such results have become. This year, his results in the paltry three non-slam events he has played were losses in his opening match at the Cincinnati and Italian Opens and a fourth-round defeat at Indian Wells. His last quarter-final at a Masters 1000 tournament came in October at the Shanghai Masters.

There have been numerous issues during those reverses, from injuries to other physical ailments or difficult preparation, but Djokovic’s motivation in these tournaments has clearly been a factor. He has spent his entire career finding a way to drag himself through impossible situations, even when things have been physically or mentally awry. Such ­recoveries require an immense amount of ­commitment, something he clearly does not have in these tournaments of less importance. Djokovic has long identified the grand slam tournaments and ­Olympics as his priorities at this point in his career, and his results have reflected those convictions. For the past year and a half, Djokovic has been the most consistent player at the grand slams beyond Carlos Alcaraz or Jannik Sinner. He has reliably found his way through nearly every other obstacle.

Perhaps the most striking part of Djokovic’s fleeting one-minute press conference came when he was asked whether he envisioned himself being back at Cincinnati. He issued a sober response: “I certainly hope so, but it looks more likely not, unfortunately. But let’s see what the future brings.”

The tennis world has spent the past few years trying to anticipate when Djokovic might retire, and his tendency to cast doubt on his future after tough defeats has often looked an indicator. In this case, it is totally reasonable that he never wishes to compete in the Ohio humidity again. Otherwise, as long as he remains competitive at the grand slams, it does seem like he is content with his current life. While he stresses the importance of not looking too far forward at his age, when everything can change quickly, he has also been clear about wanting to compete in one final Olympics in Los Angeles, where he will be the defending champion.

For those reasons, it does not feel that much has changed for him ahead of the US Open, the final grand slam tournament of the year. Time and again, he has shown that he will raise his game and find a way through to the latter rounds at the majors, even when he is barely competitive elsewhere. At his age, it is only a matter of time before he also loses his edge in the biggest events, but it remains to be seen when that shift will occur.

In some ways, the final stretch of Djokovic’s career has been quite a confusing time. He has never hesitated to recognise the superiority of Sinner and Alcaraz at this stage in their careers, but he also remains one of the top four players in the world in both his own mind and according to the rest of the field.

He has repeatedly stressed that he is not fixated by the prospect of winning a 25th grand slam title and that pursuit is not the primary motivation for his longevity, but his standards have been high for so long that he still cannot help but feel the same amount of immense disappointment when he fails to live up to them as if he was still No 1. He knows that his ­performances and level are rare for a player of his age, that he should be proud of what he is achieving in the latter stages of his career, but he still wants more.

The one certainty, though, is his enduring love for this sport. Despite how much his reality has changed compared with the years when he was the best player in the world and racking up titles from grand slams to 250s, he continues to show up, compete and find meaning and enjoyment in the success. Long may it continue.

Brazil’s Lula launches historic fourth term bid – but son of jailed Bolsonaro stands in his way

The Guardian Sun, 16 Aug 2026 18:44:41 GMT

President, 80, vows to keep far-right from power as Flávio Bolsonaro tells supporters he will ‘fight this system’

Brazil’s leftwing president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, has launched his campaign for a historic fourth term and vowed that as long as he lived he would not allow the “shameless” right to return to power.

Addressing a sea of supporters in São Bernardo do Campo, the industrial city where his political career began nearly half a century ago, the 80-year-old politician reminded voters of the chaos and violence that unfolded during the 2018-22 presidency of his far-right predecessor, Jair Bolsonaro, whose son Flávio Bolsonaro will face Lula in October’s presidential election.

Lula recalled how hundreds of thousands of citizens died during a Covid outbreak Jair Bolsonaro was accused of bungling with his anti-science policies. Gun ownership soared as laws were relaxed, allowing criminal groups to expand their arsenals. “They handed out … more than a million weapons,” Lula said, promising to dedicate a fourth term to improving education and healthcare as well as developing Brazil’s rare-earth deposits, the world’s second largest after China’s.

Lula also said he would improve security by targeting the rich organised crime bosses who lived in luxury apartments. “It’s easy to kill a crook in a favela. But the guy running the show lives in a penthouse … and we need to stop this,” Lula said. He also told his far-right rivals to “show some shame”.

Lula was speaking at the Vila Euclides football stadium, where his astonishing rise to the presidency began in 1979 when, as 33-year-old union leader, he spearheaded two historic strikes that helped end the military dictatorship. Those strikes made Lula a household name and in 2002, after three failed attempts, he won a landslide victory to become his country’s first working-class president.

During Lula’s first two-terms, from 2002 until 2010, he was credited with fighting hunger, dramatically expanding social welfare programmes and access to higher education, and improving Brazil’s global standing, although his administration was blighted by corruption scandals. His successor, Dilma Rousseff, became Brazil’s first female president but led the country into a severe economic recession before being controversially impeached in 2016.

In 2018, Lula was jailed for alleged corruption and he spent 580 days in prison before the supreme court quashed his conviction. Lula’s imprisonment allowed Bolsonaro to win that year’s election, ushering in four years of environmental destruction and international isolation.

In 2022 Lula won his third term, defeating Bolsonaro by a razor-thin margin and vowing to rescue the country from “one of the worst periods in Brazilian history”. “This nightmare is over,” Lula declared at his January 2023 inauguration. A week later, far-right radicals rampaged through the capital, Brasília, in a botched attempt to bring Bolsonaro back.

Bolsonaro was jailed in 2025 for 27 years for plotting that failed post-election power grab. Flávio Bolsonaro, a 45-year-old senator, launched his campaign on Sunday with an event on Rio’s Copacabana beach, previously the scene of huge rallies in support of his father. “I am going to be Brazil’s next president because I’m going to fight this system,” Bolsonaro, who wore a bullet-proof vest under a yellow Brazil shirt, told a crowd far smaller than those his father used to attract.

Polls suggest Lula holds a slender advantage over Bolsonaro, with 43% of intended votes to his rival’s 40% in a run-off which will take place on 25 October if, as expected, no candidate secures 50% of the vote in the 4 October first round.

André Pagliarini, the author of a book about Lula called A People’s President and the Fight for Brazil’s Future, said the showdown would be “the single most important electoral contest this year in the world”.

Pagliarini said he believed a Bolsonaro victory would be a significant boost for the pro-Trump “reactionary block” that has won elections across Latin America, from Argentina and Chile to Colombia, where the far-right lawyer Abelardo de la Espriella recently took office.

Donald Trump’s administration has repeatedly asserted its leadership over the region, launching deadly military operations against alleged “narco-terrorists” in the Caribbean Sea and Pacific, threatening to “take back” the Panama canal and, in January, abducting Venezuela’s dictator, Nicolás Maduro. Last week, the US state department published an incendiary video declaring that “American dominance in the western hemisphere will never be questioned again”.

​In recent months Trump has turned up the heat on Brazil, designating its two biggest organised crime groups, the Red Command and the PCC, as terrorist organisations. That has kindled fears of a US military intervention on Brazilian soil or interference in Brazil’s presidential election.

During a visit to a jungle training camp in Panama on Friday, Trump’s defence secretary, Pete Hegseth, said Washington planned to use the military to “ruthlessly” pursue Latin American drug traffickers, “just like [they did with] Isis and al-Qaida” during the “war on terror”.

The idea, Hegseth said, was to “do bad things to bad people – because for too long, bad people did bad things to good people inside the United States of America and across Central and South America”.

There was anger at the US outside Lula’s campaign launch on Sunday, where some activists handed out stickers that read: “Fuck Trump.”

Seixas Alves, a 33-year-old Lula supporter, said he worried the decision to classify Brazilian drug factions as terrorist groups could be used as a pretext for a US attack. “Just like they [did with] Saddam Hussein,” Alves added, referring to the Iraqi dictator’s supposed development of weapons of mass destruction.

In Rio, Flávio Bolsonaro praised Trump’s decision to target the Brazilian crime groups and said he was the only politician capable of “sitting down with the US”.

In Vila Euclides, Simone Tebet, a centrist Lula ally, urged voters to do everything they could to stop Brazil falling back into the hands of far-right politicians who wanted “to kill Brazilian democracy” and create “a country of hate”.

‘It’s been very tough’: hope of progress in gruelling battle against south Wales wildfire

The Guardian Sun, 16 Aug 2026 18:27:39 GMT

Efforts of emergency services and military in Blaenavon appear to be working but there are fears for the future

More than three weeks after it began burning and two days after the military deployed to the area, there is hope that the huge wildfire on the hillside above the Ebbw valley village of Blaenavon may finally be coming under control.

Emergency workers and soldiers described a gruelling battle against the deep-seated peat fire that has spread over 4,000 hectares (9,800 acres), putting lives, farmland and property at risk.

At least 13 other fires have blazed across the valleys this weekend, prompting South Wales fire and rescue service to ask for military support – the first UK military deployment to deal with wildfires since 2018.

Nationally, approximately 36 fires are still burning, 11 of which have been declared major incidents. Extreme heat and a lack of rain, supercharged by the climate crisis, have made this summer the busiest on record for wildfires in the UK, placing significant pressure on crews and resources.

Jamie Windsor, a group commander at Ebbw Vale station, said underground layers of peat beneath the orange and purple heather on the Blaenavon hillside had made the fire harder to put out.

“It burns very deep, the peat, and because it’s been so hot, it’s not cooling down at night. You think you’ve got a handle on it but it’s burning underground and it just pops up again somewhere else,” he said. “We’re got a lot of wildfire experience here in south Wales but I’ve never seen anything like it in 30 years.”

During the Guardian’s visit to the scene on Sunday, soldiers from the Queen’s Own Gurkha Logistic Regiment tirelessly dug firebreaks and turned over smoking soil to minimise the spread of fire. Small flames licked around the base of blackened trees a few metres away as they worked, while in another part of the woods several trees lit up quickly with no warning.

On the ridge of the hill, a civilian-contracted helicopter picked up water from a huge plastic pool fed by a local dam and circled again and again to dowse reigniting pockets of the smouldering hillside.

Smoke from the area has been visible as far away as Cardiff and Gloucestershire. Firefighters from services around the UK have come to help improvise how to get water to hard-to-reach places, using an old steel mill on the edge of town as a temporary headquarters. New thermal camera drones and specialised response vehicles designed by the South Wales fire service came online this summer.

“Just in time,” said Darren Cleaves, the group manager for the service, as he radioed a colleague at the perimeter of the fire to report what he could see on the drone screen. “The drone means we can be much more accurate with pinpointing where we need to go, and it keeps our teams safer.”

The combined efforts have worked, saving houses in Blaenavon a few hundred metres away. For weeks, residents on Llanover Close, a road on the village boundary, have watched a steady stream of fire engines, water tankers, tractors and other emergency vehicles and equipment go back and forth to the forestry track above their homes.

Cindy Rogers, 60, lives in the last house on the road where Blaenavon meets the hillside. A fire in 2004 that began on the top of the mountain almost reached her house, she said, pointing from her back garden to where the fire line is still visible.

“It’s a worry that this is going to get worse in the future with climate change, but I wouldn’t move unless I really had to,” she said. “All it takes is the wind to change direction and that’s it.”

By Sunday afternoon, the Blaenavon fire was showing signs it may be slowing, said Fin Monahan, the chief fire officer of South Wales fire and rescue.

“It’s been very tough, but I’m so proud of the professionalism of these teams and how hard they are working,” he said. “Morale is still high, everything is calm and controlled … It’s just the scale of what we’re dealing with is unprecedented. We normally get about 1,000 999 calls a week, and at the moment it’s 7,000.”

Arson had been a major contributor to this summer’s fires, Monahan said. “Not every investigation has been completed yet but we can already see it’s been a significant issue this year in south Wales. Fire safety education is another key area we focus on … Driving home last night, I saw smoke and I went and found a guy burning tires and other stuff in his garden, under a tree. I had to tell him to put it out.”

The cause of the Blaenavon fire is still unknown, but across the country arson arrests have been made in relation to this summer’s fires. On Saturday, four teenage boys from Porth in the Rhondda valley were detained on suspicion of arson and later released on bail.

In Stoke-on-Trent, a man and woman have been arrested in connection to a fire that destroyed four homes, and a man in King’s Norton and another in east London have been arrested on suspicion of arson to endanger life.

The UK has experienced multiple heatwaves this summer, as climate breakdown makes extreme heat, drought and wildfires more likely. The whole of Wales and almost three-quarters of England were declared officially in drought last month, and the Met Office said this week that the UK was on course for its hottest summer on record by average temperature.

The Blaenavon fire and many others across the country may only finally settle with cooler temperatures and rain, but the onset of autumn and more rainfall is not guaranteed to reverse the drought conditions, the Met Office said on Saturday.

In Blaenavon, flash flooding has plagued residents in recent years. A supercharged El Niño is now predicted to bring wet and stormy conditions to the UK this winter.

An 89-year-old resident of Llanover Close, who did not want to give his name, said he had lived on the street since it was built. “It’s the flooding that worries me. My basement flooded last winter,” he said. “Fire and flood … I never thought it would come to this.”

The Scottish Football Association has appointed the Belgian Sébastien Pocognoli as the successor to Steve Clarke as manager. The 39-year-old, who was sacked by Monaco in June, will become the country’s first non-Scottish manager since Berti Vogts, who was in charge from 2002 to 2004.

Clarke’s abrupt departure came after Scotland were knocked out of the World Cup at the group stage. He had signed a four-year contract extension immediately before the tournament. It quickly became clear the SFA would turn towards a foreign manager with the Danes Jon Dahl Tomasson and Kasper Hjulmand being linked with the position.

Pocognoli, a left-back who played for Brighton and West Brom, will probably be welcomed by Scotland fans seeking a fresh approach. Clarke was in position for a generally successful seven years, including appearances at three major tournaments, but was often criticised for a pragmatic style.

Craig Mulholland, the SFA’s chief football officer, said Pocognoli “will bring an aggressive, front-foot style of play that will excite supporters”.

After a period in youth coaching, Pocognoli enjoyed a successful time in charge of Union Saint-Gilloise in his homeland. Under Pocognoli, Union won their first title in 90 years in 2025. A move to Monaco followed, but Pocognoli lasted eight months and 38 games in France. The former Everton and Belgum winger Kevin Mirallas is expected to join him in the dugout.

Pocognoli said: “When I first heard of the interest, I was immediately excited about the opportunity. Scotland’s supporters are famous for their passion – most recently at the World Cup in the USA - and I have experienced it myself as a player for Belgium when we played in 2013.

“Along with my coaching staff, I will do everything I can to give them a team to be proud of and build on the success that has been achieved already by my predecessor.”

Tarling, the younger brother of the Netcompany Ineos professional Josh Tarling, was in collision with a non-race vehicle driving towards the peloton while he competed in the Portuguese race’s eighth stage. The 19-year-old’s death on Friday has led to a surge of anger, with the riders’ union, the Cyclistes Professionnels Associés (CPA), describing itself as “furious”.

“We are speechless and filled with anger after the news of Finlay Tarling’s death at the Tour of Portugal,” the CPA posted. “It is not right that a young athlete’s life should end this way, and we are furious that even today it is still not possible to prevent such serious accidents.”

The former French professional Jérôme Pineau was one of those to criticise the levels of security in place at the race, which he labelled “catastrophic”.

Pineau, who rode multiple Grand Tours between 2002 and 2015, described the lack of other incidents in the race as “a constant miracle” and added that “the finishes are not worthy of a race of this level”.

“It’s the result of the lack of resources to organise major cycling races which are becoming increasingly expensive,” Pineau said.

“All of this should primarily concern the authorities in charge,” he said, referencing the sport’s governing body, the UCI. “They must implement approval processes, and if security is not guaranteed, if the organisers are not capable of it, they should not be authorised to organise the event.”

Both the Volta a Portugal organisers and the UCI have been contacted for further comment.

The circumstances of Tarling’s death are now subject to a police investigation, but the Portuguese police stated that while “more evidence will be gathered,” it is thought unlikely that the driver will face criminal charges.

The Volta a Portugal does not benefit from full road closures, as is the case with Grand Tours such as the Tour de France, and instead uses a rolling road closure, effectively a “bubble” of security that encloses the race convoy, from front to back.

Carlos Catanario, of the Portugese police, told RTP that Tarling was racing to catch up on a downhill section, with the peloton ahead of him and split into three groups. The “broom” wagon, the van signifying the rear of the convoy and the end of the rolling road closure, was behind him.

Catanario said that the GNR (National Republican Guard) police escort “could not keep up with Tarling”. Further ahead, the driver involved had been stopped at the roadside for some time, to allow the race to pass.

After waiting, the driver is understood to have asked bystanders if he could join the road, and then drove on to the course, before the broom wagon had passed. “In that specific location, we know there were no officers present because it was not one of the locations prioritised in the assessment that had been carried out,” Catanario said.

“The vehicle was going in the opposite direction to the direction of the race. The cyclist [Tarling] cut across the curve on the left lane – as is natural, as [racing] cyclists do – and that is what caused the cyclist and the vehicle to collide.”

Tarling’s loss is the latest in a sport increasingly beleaguered by safety issues. As racing speeds increase and traffic intensifies, costs for event security rise, meaning race organisers are coming under increasing pressure to implement more effective measures.

“It’s becoming increasingly expensive to organise races, and some organisers are abandoning the safety principles that govern the entire cycling bubble,” Pineau said. “The Volta a Portugal is a second-tier race; they have to find race officials, staff to organise it, and funds for the police.”

Tarling’s team, NSN Development, withdrew from the race on Saturday, but the race otherwise completed its final stages over the weekend as planned. Riders observed a minute’s silence at the start of the ninth stage, the leader’s jersey worn by Alexis Guérin was changed from yellow to black and the peloton wore black armbands.

Tributes were paid and black armbands worn at other races including the Czech Tour and the Arctic Race of Norway.

On Sunday Tarling’s father, Michael, posted a message on social media. “This has been the hardest couple of days of our lives and it’s taken us a bit of time to be able to post this. Hearing how lovingly and fondly Fin was thought of has been a huge help to us. We simply can’t thank you all enough for the support we’ve had.

“I don’t know how we carry on from here, but we’ll figure it out with the support of all our family, friends, and community. Whilst our broken hearts will never be fixed, he was not only our son and brother but our best mate. Gentle, loving with the driest sense of humour, we will miss him terribly.”

The Guardian view on the changed world of job interviews: missing the human factor

The Guardian Sun, 16 Aug 2026 17:30:31 GMT

Andy Burnham’s doubts about Zoom interviews apply more widely to a hiring process being transformed by AI

Almost half of UK jobseekers have found themselves pitching to an AI bot, according to recent research, leading many to give up in frustration. As one despairing applicant lamented in the pages of the Guardian a few months ago: “The hiring process has become so mechanised, both figuratively and literally, that it’s hard to believe that the people who end up getting hired aren’t merely the best at gaming the system.” For young people especially, experiencing repeated rejection without interacting with a single human being is alienating as well as disappointing.

It was encouraging, therefore, to hear Andy Burnham voice concerns about online recruitment processes on a recent employment-focused podcast. Describing the jobseeking environment for young people as “harsh”, the prime minister criticised the widespread use of interviews on Zoom and Microsoft Teams, and questioned whether applicants could properly convey their personal qualities without a face-to-face meeting.

There is another side to the story, as Zoom executives were swift to point out. Online interviewing cuts out travel costs, for example, giving a chance to applicants who may not be able to fund long journeys and possible overnight stays. But Mr Burnham is right to identify a dangerous drift towards selection processes that undervalue the worth of conversations between people in the same room at the same time.

The increasingly used “one-way” video interview – in which applicants are given fixed periods of time to plan and deliver responses to prerecorded questions – seems to offer a particularly disorientating experience. Interviewees, in effect, speak into a void, unable to process feedback or interpret body language.

The sorting processes deployed in AI interviews have been rightly criticised for their opacity, and susceptibility to algorithmic bias. A lack of transparency in relation to the programming of recruitment software means that an unlevel playing field may be suspected but difficult to prove. The US Equal Employment Opportunity Commission settled an age discrimination case with a company that came to light only when a failed applicant reapplied, changing just her age, and miraculously passed through to the next round.

It could hardly be claimed that traditional recruitment processes were bias-free. Used in the right way, new technologies can play their part in opening up possibilities for applicants rather than simply screening them out with minimal explanation or feedback. But while it may be convenient for businesses to rely on tech to do the work, the struggle even to present one’s credentials to another human being is adding insult to injuries already inflicted by an exceptionally unforgiving labour market. A recent report from the Institute for Public Policy Research found that young people in England were increasingly “losing faith in their futures”.

The Information Commissioner’s Office has been tasked by parliament with producing a code of practice on AI and automated decision-making. In a recent report it found that when companies claimed that AI-generated hiring recommendations were subjected to human review, that was often only partially true, if at all. Applicants deserve better. The use of digital technologies is already changing the face of the entry-level jobs market. Interviewees should be protected from the downsides of their growing dominance in the recruitment process.

The Guardian view on London’s social housing: pumping billions into the economy every year

The Guardian Sun, 16 Aug 2026 17:25:31 GMT

The provision of homes needs to be thought of as a service, not a commodity to be traded. It is vital economic infrastructure, so let’s make it affordable for all

London’s city centre has long been a place where rich and poor live side by side, while so many other metropolitan equivalents – Paris, New York, San Francisco – remain the preserve of the rich. It maintains its mix today: in many inner London boroughs, between 20% and 40% of households live in social housing. A small but steady decline in social housing in these areas leaves many fearing that the city’s diversity is under threat.

What happens when cities become less socially mixed? The G15 group of housing associations, which provide social and affordable homes for about one in 10 Londoners, commissioned research recently on the economic contribution of those living in social housing. It found that they contributed £27.8bn to London’s economy in 2024, even after housing benefit was taken into account. Its methodology involved comparing the lives of people in social housing with those without a stable and affordable place to live. The conclusion was that stable and affordable housing reduces spend and demand on public services, promotes better physical and mental overall health, and results in a higher likelihood that tenants stay in work and contribute economically.

The idea that social housing is an economic investment is not new. England’s municipal housing was designed in recognition that a city could not function without healthy employees living nearby. Gordon Brown and Tony Blair revisited this idea in the early 2000s, arguing that England’s public services would deteriorate if hospital workers and police officers were pushed out of major urban centres. They framed social housing not as a charitable act, but as critical economic infrastructure.

The G15 report finds that key workers such as nurses and care and retail workers account for about 65% of London’s social housing population (compared with 40% of London’s population). Not so long ago, these same workers were clapped in the streets for keeping cities functioning during the Covid-19 pandemic; they were the reason that people could buy milk and elderly people remained cared for while others had to stay at home. But many such workers would not be able to afford to live in big cities without the help of social housing. Even moving to the outer bounds of the city would add thousands to their commuting bill, as well as hours to their working days, according to the research.

Viewed through that lens, housing that average-wage earners can afford becomes a vital asset for the country’s resilience. Social rents are proof that housing costs need not be a key driver of poverty – and yet our current building targets aren’t being pursued urgently enough to fix the problem. Housing charities say that 90,000 social homes a year are needed in England. No major party has plans for anything like that number.

Mr Blair shifted social housing from councils towards housing associations, and the coalition commercialised that model. Andy Burnham now appears to want to put councils back at the centre. In an interview with the London Review of Books in 2024, Mr Burnham said: “If you read Nye Bevan’s speeches, as I do, if you read his speech that was the postwar Housing Act, second reading, he talked about how housing needs to be thought of as a service, not a commodity to be traded and sold, a wealth creator. Everybody needs it, it’s an essential service. And it was interesting how he positioned it like the NHS. And so that’s the philosophy that we need.” Amen to that.

This is an issue that makes young professionals think twice about accepting posts in teaching and healthcare in the north Highlands.

At the other end of the scale, that distance from a major hospital led me and other colleagues who had lived and worked in Caithness for four decades to decide not to retire in the far north. Julie Adams Arbroath, Angus

My parents lived in Lynton in north Devon when my mother was pregnant in 1978, and she hoped to give birth in the local cottage hospital where my father was born. However, she was told that she would have to travel to Barnstaple. Now, 46 years later, women in north Devon are being told that they need to travel to Taunton or Exeter for “spontaneous” births. Or they can stay at home and hope for the best. It’s horrifying.

Cars may be radically different compared with the 1970s, but congestion on the local roads only gets worse. What next? Plymouth? Bristol? Working-age people are already being priced out by holiday lets and second homes, and now they can’t give birth safely either. Name and address supplied

Although it is good news that Yvette Cooper, our new health secretary, plans to reintroduce binding national maternity standards (6 August), I was dismayed to discover while on a visit to my old home town of Barnstaple, north Devon, that women will have to travel to Exeter, 40 miles away along narrow country roads, while in labour to deliver their babies. To anyone who knows north Devon this is sheer madness. Women might well end up having to have their babies by the roadside.

I had quick labours and one of my children had the cord around his neck. He would not have survived if we had not been safely in hospital. I hope Cooper can act quickly to address the chronic shortage of midwives in this country. Sarah SheilsYork

How surrogacy helped my sister and friends

The Guardian Sun, 16 Aug 2026 16:54:13 GMT

Hazel Davis responds to a letter about the regulation and ethics of surrogacy

I wish to respond to Lexi Ellingsworth’s letter (Regulation cannot eliminate surrogacy risks, 23 July). I gave birth to a baby for my friends in January. While the baby is living with its parents, my husband and I are the legal parents. We are waiting for our family court date in September to recognise the baby’s biological parents as legal parents.

My surrogacy story started when my sister suffered complications following the birth of her first child. After a second difficult birth, the doctors told her that it wouldn’t be safe for her to carry any more children. I became an auntie via surrogacy when my sister’s friend carried her third child. Now my niece is a determined five‑year-old, just as much a part of the family as her older siblings, and I see no evidence that her origins have any impact.

In 2023, some friends confided they had joined SurrogacyUK as they hoped to start a family, but needed some help. David had been my husband’s best friend since primary school, and my friend since university, and is now our daughter’s godfather.

They were very surprised when I offered to be their surrogate. I was aware of the risks, but I was surrounded by support. During the pregnancy, our friends recorded children’s stories. I played these through little speakers on my belly so the baby would recognise their parents’ voices from birth.

The legal challenges were highlighted when their baby became extremely unwell at only 11 days old. My husband and I – as legal parents – were glued to our phones in case the hospital needed us to consent to medical tests. His parents were at his bedside, ready to make those decisions. The law is not acting in the best interests of the children.

To those who wish to protect me by denying me the choice to use my body to help my friends, your concern is misguided. Susan Golombok, professor emerita of family research at the University of Cambridge, wrote in April that a 20-year study of UK surrogacy families had “found no evidence of widespread psychological harm to children, parents, or surrogates”.

Our friends’ baby will grow up knowing where they came from, how much they were wanted and how much they are loved. Hazel DavisTrustee, SurrogacyUK Foundation

Cameras would help catch perpetrators earlier and save children from harm, says Tulip Siddiq MP

For seven years, my youngest constituents were abused at Bright Horizons nursery in West Hampstead, London. Earlier this year, Vincent Chan was jailed for 18 years for his horrific crimes.

It is every parent’s worst nightmare to discover that their child has been subject to abuse. For this to have happened in a nursery, where parents trusted their children would be safe, is truly abhorrent. Tragically, many families will probably never know whether their child was a victim. The lack of evidence about what was happening in the nursery, in the rooms where Chan was in charge, means that some parents have been left only with questions.

A group of 200 locally affected parents have come together to call for mandatory CCTV in nurseries, as well as requiring Ofsted to review such footage in all inspections. Together we have met the previous education secretary and the previous early years minister, and gave evidence to an expert panel to assess the feasibility of mandatory CCTV in nurseries. With none of these ministers still in post, we must not lose momentum.

All the parents I have met are truly inspirational, given everything that they’ve been through, and are doing all they can to stand up for their little ones.

Alongside the parents of Genevieve Meehan in Manchester (Parents of baby girl killed at nursery fear unsafe sleeping ‘rife’ in sector across England, 9 August), and the Lullaby Trust, I am urging Andy Burnham, the new prime minister, to take heed of our campaign, to strengthen the safety and regulation of nurseries.

With 20,000 reports of serious childcare incidents in English nurseries in the past five years, we need mandatory CCTV to tackle this. While it may not be the magic bullet, in several cases across the county – from Bristol and Manchester to Twickenham in London – CCTV would have caught the perpetrators earlier and saved children from harm.

More broadly, parents are calling for an improved inspection and accountability framework of early years settings after concerns were repeatedly ignored by nursery staff and regulators. Babies and toddlers are the most vulnerable people in our society, and we must do all we can to protect them from harm. Tulip Siddiq MPLabour, Hampstead and Highgate

Symeon Brown’s argument that class is the elephant in the room in conversations about race (Interview, 9 August) is nowhere more visible than in classical music.

Celebrated black classical musicians held up as evidence of progress are very often solidly middle class: children of professionals who could afford the instruments, tuition, exam fees and travel that serious musical training demands. Their success is real, but is mainly evidence that class opens doors.

My son is white, working class, was on free school meals until he was 12, and still lives in one of England’s most deprived areas. He won a scholarship to a specialist music school and went on to a top conservatoire. His closest friend, a black working-class classical musician, followed an almost identical path. Both were judged too privileged for widening-participation support at master’s level because they had attended independent schools, ignoring their bursaries, or that their families could not fund exam entries, let alone two years of postgraduate fees and living costs. Todd Blanche declines to pledge independence from White House

The Guardian Sun, 16 Aug 2026 16:33:08 GMT

US attorney general says no one in his role ‘should ever’ make this vow amid concern over Trump steering DoJ

US attorney general Todd Blanche on Sunday declined to assure that the federal justice department he helms would always act independently of the White House and Donald Trump.

“No, I’m not going to pledge that,” he said when asked about the topic by NBC’s Meet the Press host, Kristen Welker. “And no attorney general should ever pledge that.”

Blanche also claimed Trump would never ask him to do something that crosses an ethical or legal line – after the president dismissed his predecessor, Pam Bondi, having become frustrated over insufficient action from the justice department against Trump’s political foes.

“The president will never ask me to do something unethical or legal or illegal,” Blanche told Welker. “He never has. He never will. And no, I have – I swore to the constitution of the United States, like every cabinet secretary has done, and like every attorney general before me has done.

“And so, this narrative that’s mostly pushed by the left and pushed by the media that the president’s going to pull me aside and ask me to do something illegal is completely a false narrative, not true, will not happen and hasn’t happened.”

In response to his demurring on the questions of always acting independently of the White House, Barb McQuade, a University of Michigan law professor, wrote on social media that Blanche’s stated position was “an appalling departure” from the justice department’s mission after the Watergate scandal that prompted Richard Nixon to resign from the presidency in 1974.

The justice department, “as we once knew it, is no more”, McQuade wrote. “Blanche has turned it into Trump’s private law firm. What a complete disgrace.”

Blanche’s comments to Welker on Sunday came days after he was only narrowly confirmed by the US Senate in a 50-49 vote to succeed Bondi, with all Democrats voting against him. He previously served as Trump’s criminal defense lawyer when a New York state jury convicted Trump between his two presidencies of 34 felony counts of falsifying business records in connection with payments to adult film star Stormy Daniels.

In April, Blanche said he would tell Trump, “I love you, sir,” if the president decided to fire him and nominate someone else to replace Bondi.

Blanche, meanwhile, in December defended moving Ghislaine Maxwell, the convicted child sexual trafficker and Jeffrey Epstein associate, to a minimum-security prison. And Blanche has also continued facing scrutiny over his handling of the so-called Epstein files and his treatment of those victimized by the sex-trafficking network built by Epstein.

While speaking with Welker on Sunday, Blanche also defended Trump’s pardoning of 1,500 supporters who were convicted of attacking the US Capitol toward the end of his first presidency in early 2021.

“I’m not opining or in any way saying what President Trump did was wrong,” Blanche said when asked about the pardons, which included more than 170 people who pleaded guilty to assaulting police officers. “That is the president’s right.”

Water companies in England and Wales explore ‘surge pricing’ during drought

The Guardian Sun, 16 Aug 2026 16:28:00 GMT

Suppliers could factor water scarcity into charges as part of Ofwat proposal to reduce consumption

Water companies could be allowed to raise bills for customers during periods of drought under proposals being considered by the sector’s regulator for England and Wales.

Suppliers would be permitted to factor “water scarcity” into bills as part of efforts to reduce consumption under Ofwat’s plans, which are being likened to surge pricing – the practice where private hire firms raise taxi fares at times of higher demand.

The proposals come just a few days after the prime minster, Andy Burnham, said he was angry with water companies and accused them of treating their customers like a “blank cheque” after more than a dozen firms were given the green light to raise water bills even higher.

It emerged last Thursday that five companies – Southern Water, Thames Water, Severn Trent, Wessex Water and South East Water – would be allowed to raise bills more than originally planned before the end of the decade to allow for billions of pounds of extra spending on repairs and infrastructure.

The surge pricing proposals, first reported by the Sunday Telegraph, come after the 30 July conclusion of Ofwat’s consultation on changing the rules relating to wholesale charging, with the regulator due to share its final decision shortly.

Public anger over the behaviour of water companies has soared in recent years as bills have continued to climb even while sewage has flowed into the nation’s waterways and firms have increased bosses’ pay and handed out millions of pounds in dividends to shareholders.

During an exceptionally hot and dry summer, leading to almost three-quarters of England and all of Wales being declared officially in drought, suppliers have also come under fire for failing to save water lost through leaky pipes, which campaigners say far outstrips the amount that could be saved through a nationwide hosepipe ban.

An Ofwat spokesperson said: “The efficient use of water is in the best interests of everyone, including businesses. The options we are progressing would support greater consideration of water scarcity and efficiency by water companies when setting their charges, and encourage more tariff innovation.”

Several water companies have been carrying out charging trials over the past few years aimed at making bills more affordable and, potentially, reducing demand.

South West Water, which supplies water to about 1.8 million customers across south-west England, including Cornwall and Devon, is trialling a “rising block tariff”, where about 500 household customers are charged a cheaper rate for using a lower amount (or “block”) of water and progressively higher prices for higher consumption.

The company said 90% of its customers would see lower bills on this trial, according to its assessments.

Anglian Water, which supplies 7 million customers across the east of England, the UK’s driest region, and South West Water are also trialling charging customers more for water used in the summer than in the winter months.

A government spokesperson said: “Water companies are trialling new charging structures which must, as promised, make bills fairer and more affordable while encouraging greater water efficiency.”

They added: “We have already ringfenced money earmarked for new infrastructure so it can only be spent on fixing the problems, and will go further by fundamentally reforming the water sector so that it works for the public, keeping bills as low as they can be.”

Andy White, a senior lead for social policy at the Consumer Council for Water (CCW), a government-sponsored body that represents customers’ interests, said water companies were right to explore new tariff structures that could help manage demand and give customers more control over their bills.

He said: “Any new approach must be fair and protect customers who are already struggling with rising water costs. None of the schemes currently being trialled are designed to generate additional revenue for water companies, and many are structured so that most customers will pay less overall.”

This might include eliminating standing charges or expanding discounts for customers who save water.”

Ukrainian drone attack on Russia kills at least six, says Moscow
