Kyiv launches what may be its largest attack wave of war, with fire breaking out at warehouse near Russian capital

Ukraine has launched one of its largest drone attacks since the start of the war, causing a fire at a distribution warehouse near Moscow and killing at least six people overnight, according to Russian authorities.

The defence ministry in Moscow said it had shot down 1,478 Ukrainian drones in the past 24 hours – the highest ever total claimed – in an escalating air war in which seven Ukrainians were also killed as Russia bombed 13 locations inside the country.

A huge fire engulfed a 250,000 sq metre building near Podolsk, 25 miles south of Moscow’s city centre, belonging to the Wildberries distribution company. The facility was disabled as a result, Ukraine’s military said.

Sergei Sobyanin, the mayor of Moscow, said 600 drones targeted the Moscow region overnight, of which 201 were destroyed. One person was reported killed in the region, while Ukraine said a second warehouse at nearby Domodedovo was also targeted.

The Russian news agency RIA Novosti reported that the figure was the largest daily total claimed by the defence ministry, exceeding a record that had been set only the day before, though the figure is probably exaggerated and could not be verified.

Experts said Russian numbers needed to be treated with caution but added that the scale of damage caused overnight nevertheless demonstrated how rapidly Ukraine had expanded its long-range attack capabilities in 2026.

Serhii Kuzan, the chair of the Ukrainian Security and Cooperation Center, a thinktank, said Russian authorities “deliberately inflate their figures” to make exaggerated claims about the effectiveness of their air defence.

But he said that “against the backdrop of increased production of Ukrainian long-range drones and missiles, both the number of strikes and the scale of Ukrainian weaponry’s deployment are on the rise” as the war continues.

Kuzan argued that it was “quite possible” it was the largest-scale attack on the Moscow region, and it was “at least on a par” with the May strikes on an oil refinery in the Kapotnya area near Moscow.

A rapid development of largely homegrown technologies, including the Flamingo cruise missile and the FP-1 long-range fixed-wing drone from Fire Point, have allowed Ukraine to bomb warehouses, oil refineries, ports and military facilities up to 1,500 miles from its border.

Ukraine can now almost match the deep-strike capability that Russia has had since the beginning of the war using large drones and cruise missiles, though it still does not possess the high-speed ballistic missiles fired frequently by Moscow.

At the same time, both sides’ air defences are stretched to the point of near exhaustion, leading to a rise in civilian casualties and worries that the impact of the conflict beyond the immediate frontlines will only increase into the winter.

Kuzan said: “With every successful strike, Russia’s economic and military capabilities are diminished, and the Kremlin faces a new dilemma: how to counter this in a war of attrition.”

In the past month, Kyiv has shifted focus to attacking facilities linked to Wildberries, used widely by businesses to support online retail. Ukraine says the warehouses are used by the military for logistics, though they also store stock sold by large and small Russian businesses.

Ukraine’s military said on Sunday it had disabled seven out of 10 of the company’s largest warehouses in an effort to hurt the Russian economy and affect ordinary citizens financially, in a strike conducted with FP-1 drones.

Five people were reported to have been killed in Russia’s southern Rostov region, which borders Ukraine, and the local governor said a further 150 incoming drones had been destroyed. Ukraine said it had targeted a factory that produced rocket fuel in Kamensk-Shakhtinsky, causing a fire there.

Russian drone and missile attacks killed two people in the central city of Kryvyi Rih, while a Spanish F-18 jet shot down what appeared to be a Russia drone that had crossed over the border into Romania.

The Spanish fighter was part of a Nato patrol mission and shot down the drone at about 5am after it crossed into Romanian airspace. “The drone appears to be Russian,” a Nato military spokesperson said.

Andrey Vorobyov, the governor of the Moscow region, said the assault on the region was “one of the most massive drone attacks in recent memory”. Video footage on social media showed a fast fire raging across the Wildberries warehouse complex.

Russian attacks on Ukraine also killed two in the Sumy border region and three others across the country. A ballistic missile attack on Kyiv shortly before 3am injured six and caused several fires in the capital.

A blaze caused by the attacks destroyed a large part of the Petrovka book market in the Obolonskyi district in Kyiv overnight, with some booksellers reporting they had lost their entire stock in the incident.

“There is nothing. Nobody has anything left,” said Natalya, a bookstore owner who was interviewed by Ukraine’s Hromadske website. “Everything burned down. I was selling foreign language [textbooks] for schoolchildren. We were waiting for September so that everyone would have textbooks … But what happened happened.”

Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, praised the work of the country’s emergency services and accused the Russians of attacking ordinary people. “Wherever the Russians can reach with their ballistic missiles, they strike civilian infrastructure,” he said in a social media post.

Zelenskyy said Russia had launched more than 1,550 attack drones, nearly 1,560 guided aerial bombs and 62 missiles at Ukrainian cities and communities over the past week, most of them ballistic missiles of various types.

Though Ukraine is effective at stopping slower-moving drones, it has little to no defence against high-speed ballistics, its stock of US-made Patriot interceptor missiles – the only weapons capable of knocking them out – having been run down.

Turbocharge special needs internships to help tackle UK youth jobs crisis, says Milburn

The Guardian Sun, 16 Aug 2026 16:00:30 GMT

Exclusive: Government review led by former minister to recommend huge expansion of onsite schemes for those who need support

Specialist internships designed to secure work for young people with special educational needs should be put on “turbocharge” to help tackle the growing youth jobs crisis, a government review is to propose.

Alan Milburn who is leading a review of young people and work, said supported internships should be scaled up to combat “devastating” joblessness rates for young people with a learning disability, autism or mental illness.

Nationally, as few as 5% of some groups of young people with special educational needs and disabilities (Send) move into permanent jobs. However, employment rates among those who complete supported internship schemes can be as high as 70%.

Nearly 1 million 16- to 24-year-olds in the UK are classified as Neet (not in employment, education or training), a 10-year high that Milburn – a former minister in the Tony Blair government – has said represents a moral crisis and is economically unsustainable.

In May, his first report warned that Britain risked a 25% rise in the number of Neets to 1.25 million by the early 2030s without urgent government action. Central to the recent growth of Neets is an increase in young people diagnosed at school with neurodevelopmental conditions or mental illness who do not make the transition into work, leaving them at high risk of becoming economically inactive.

Milburn said the UK had to move away from the idea that people with a diagnosis were unable to work. They can work, he said. “The question is: are the opportunities there and is the support there?

“Supported internships have got such an effective track record. With the best ones around 70% of the people on them end up in paid employment. In my view we have to turbocharge support – and at the moment the system is not set up to do that.”

Milburn dismissed “myths” about 18- to 24-year-olds being a “snowflake generation”, saying: “The problem isn’t shortage of effort on the part of young people. It’s a shortage of opportunities, jobs, support.”

He added: “There are two views about [the rise in youth ill health]. You can either say it’s fake or you can decide its real. It’s a real phenomenon. So we’ve got to deal with it and we have got to adjust our systems to deal with it.”

The Guardian recently reported that English primary schools could be required to identify children at risk of leaving education at 16 without finding a job as part of the Milburn review.

“The warning signs are there from a very early, early age,” he told the newspaper. “You know, frankly from preschool.

“So, definitely primary schools should be identifying children who are at risk of being Neet. And secondary schools and other services should be intercepting, intervening, supporting and helping those young people to get on a different path.”

The year-long internships provide tailored onsite work experience and job coaching for 16- to 24-year-olds with education, health and care plans (EHCPs) who face high barriers to the job market. Employers involved include the NHS, Asda and Amazon.

Callum Beeston, a 20-year-old from Doncaster who has autism, recently completed a supported internship at Amazon with job coach support from Aspirations Doncaster. This month he started a full-time job there as a warehouse operative, and has been praised for his work from his bosses.

Beeston said his family’s expectations of him finding work after he finished school were low and he was “unsure what to do next”. His grandmother used to say she would leave her will to him because she was worried he would never get work. “In the last 12 months I’ve become a very confident young fella,” he said.

Kim Patterson, the finance director at Aspirations Doncaster, said school-based ECHP support often “drops off a cliff” once students leave. Some autistic young people find it hard to manage job applications and interviews, and can struggle to adapt to work routines without specialist support.

In England there are just 4,500 supported internships. About 48% of supported interns found paid work, according to an official evaluation published this year by the Department for Education, although some internship providers report job success rates as high as 70%.

Milburn said capacity shortages meant there was no guarantee a young person with Send could access a supported internship in their local area. He believed that while the model worked it lacked the resources to be delivered at scale, and there was low awareness of the scheme among parents, employers and schools.

He was tight-lipped on how such an expansion might be paid for, with fears funding might be taken from young people’s disability benefits. His final recommendations are expected to be delivered to the government in the autumn.

Milburn said the system was geared too much towards paying health and disability benefits and not enough towards supporting young people to enter the job market.

“If you are a young person today and you apply and get a health and disability benefit, there’s a 50% chance that in 15 years’ time you will still be eligible. You’ll still be out of work. That is neither a good outcome, frankly, nor is it a progressive cause,” he said.

Can exercise really help improve my sex life?

The Guardian Sun, 16 Aug 2026 16:00:29 GMT

Here’s what experts say about how sex and exercise are linked, and whether the type, timing and intensity of movement matter

Here’s a reason to put your sneakers on: exercise can improve your sex life.

It’s not necessarily about changing how your body looks, or being strong enough to swing from the chandelier. Regular movement improves smaller, less visible bodily functions that increase your desire and capacity for sex – like the release of arousal-promoting hormones and enhanced circulation in the nether regions. Perhaps just as critically, it gets your mind in the right frame to do it.

While the links between physical activity and having great sex might seem obvious, they are not as linear as you might expect.

Here’s what you need to know.

Two of the main ways exercise can upgrade your sex life are that your body gets better at arousal and your mind less likely to interrupt it.

The physical impacts relate largely to circulation. Good blood flow underpins arousal: it promotes the function of fluid-secreting glands and sensation-conducting nerves in women, and facilitates erections in men.

Exercise also improves rest, which leads to increased energy levels. Certain types of activity can strengthen pelvic floor muscles, which boosts sexual satisfaction in both men and women, and positively affects the levels of hormones and neurotransmitters tied to sexual response.

Scientists measure sexual function in many different ways, including the subjective sense of desire and arousal, the presence of lubrication (in women) or erection (in men), the ability to achieve orgasm and overall satisfaction with one’s sex life. A recent review of multiple studies found that across those domains, women who engaged in various forms of exercise – including cardio, yoga and pelvic-floor work – scored significantly higher than women who did not. (These studies were randomized controlled trials, which differentiate between exercise effects and sex habits likely to already be present in people who exercise.) Other studies have found similarly positive effects in men, although their quality and the effects they have measured have been a little spottier.

The psychological effects relate to exercise’s tendency to improve mood, energy and body image. Both chronic stress and a busy, self-critical mind interfere with arousal, although that plays out differently for women and men, said Debby Herbenick, a psychologist and researcher who directs Indiana University’s Center for Sexual Health Promotion.

To be clear, exercise is not a magic fix for anxious thoughts about appearance and performance. But, Herbenick says, it can “decrease cognitive distractions and enhance arousal and orgasm”.

What type? When it comes to physical benefits for your sex life, aerobic exercise – the kind that makes you sweat and increases your heart rate – has the best evidence, in part because it is what has been studied the most.

But for the psychological benefits, it’s less important to focus on what the movement is than on how it makes you feel. Exercise that you do because it makes you feel healthy and fit is more likely to make you feel good about yourself. In turn, that positive self-image helps your brain minimize arousal killers such as stress and anxiety. It’s best for people to “choose the exercises that they enjoy rather than try to choose an exercise just to enhance arousal or orgasm”, said Herbenick.

Sign up to Well Actually

Practical advice, expert insights and answers to your questions about how to live a good life

after newsletter promotion

When? Workouts can act as an aphrodisiac for some women – but not straight away. Cindy Meston, a sex researcher and professor at the University of Texas at Austin, ran lab studies in the 1990s and 2000s aimed at understanding how the timing of exercise affected sexual function. She found women’s genital blood flow was actually suppressed right after vigorous exercise, then rose above baseline 15 to 30 minutes later, once hardworking muscles had stopped hogging the body’s blood supply.

Herbenick’s research has corroborated this finding, but structuring your sex life around your workouts “is not realistic for everyone”, she says.

What about intensity? Workout intensity seems to matter more than timing. In Herbenick’s research, low-intensity or low-repetition exercise had little effect on arousal or orgasm – but push too hard, and the exercise can backfire. Stick to the middle of the range; if it makes your entire body ache, it’s less likely to turn you on.

You don’t need to sweat the details to enjoy the sexual benefits of exercise. For most people, it’s enough to move regularly, with some effort, in a way that feels good and sustainable. Real life is messy, and exercise might mean swimming laps or walking the soccer fields while your kids are in the pool or at practice, said Herbenick.

Exercise has been proven to improve sexual function in women taking anti-depressants and those who have had hysterectomies. People who exercise for other health reasons may also earn sexy dividends. Diabetes and heart disease can impair the same blood vessels and nerves that arousal depends on, so exercise prescribed to manage those conditions often improves sexual function as a side effect.

If you’re an athlete training hard for something demanding, good communication with your partner is key, said Herbenick. Talk to your partner honestly about when you actually have the energy and comfort for sex, rather than assuming your body will cooperate on cue.

Ali came to me seeking help for disordered eating. The real issue was a relationship built on control

The Guardian Sun, 16 Aug 2026 15:00:29 GMT

She second-guessed herself and was eager to please. She ‘felt frozen’ when she believed she displeased someone

The modern mind is a column where experts discuss mental health issues they are seeing in their work

Ali* initially came to therapy for disordered eating. She was a young and diffident woman. She described recurrent cycles of restricted eating followed by attempts to exercise it away. We used cognitive behavioural therapy for eating disorders to unpick her “food rules” – the underlying beliefs which can drive eating disorders, such as “the less I eat the better” or “carbs are bad”.

As we worked on understanding and shifting her beliefs and behaviours around food, we noticed that most of her assumptions around eating, shape and weight coincided with the start of her relationship with her ex-partner. She told me he was a “gym junkie” and spent hours working out and encouraged her to do the same. “He got angry if I ate carbs,” she said, “and created a couples meal plan for us so I could shred and look hot when we were out together.”

Slowly, she spoke of other forms of control: encouraging her to dress in a “sexier” manner than she felt comfortable with, jealousy if he saw her talking to another man, watching her bank transactions to see where she was going, and insisting on going to all her social events so he could get to know her friends. “But he’d always start an argument, or would say he didn’t like them,” she told me. “And then I had to stop seeing them to prove my loyalty to him.” He used her fears about being an inexperienced sexual partner to coerce her into a range of sexual acts, telling her that what he wanted was “normal” and she was not being a good partner if she refused.

As she spoke to me, I saw the shift in her eyes when she realised the pattern which had slowly emerged over three years: coercive control.

After this realisation, her eating stabilised. Food was one of the initial mechanisms of control he used to start shaping her body and personality, and her difficulties with eating were a symptom of the trauma she had experienced.

Unlike physical violence, coercive control can be easy to miss as it is a pattern of repeated subtle behaviours and usually inflicted with the victim’s seeming agreement. At other times the coercion is more overt and can involve threats such as taking away children, or inflicting violence if sexual demands are not met. Regardless of the level of severity of this behaviour, the impacts can create psychological harm for victims.

Like many other victims of coercive control, Ali had very poor self-esteem and was racked with anxiety. She second-guessed herself and was overly deferential and eager to please, reporting she “felt frozen” when she believed she displeased someone. Her beliefs about herself and about relationships were distorted (“I have no radar”, “all relationships are unsafe”). These are all typical responses demonstrated by people who have experienced coercion or violence in intimate relationships.

Our work together encompassed a few stages. First, we worked together to understand what coercive control is, and used a simple ABC model derived from CBT to help Ali understand how certain statements or behaviours by her ex bypassed her instinctive radar and influenced her to give in to him by creating feelings of insecurity and anxiety. We looked at the way she experienced his approval as a potent reinforcer for compliance as it signalled that the danger of relational rupture or loss was over.

We named the distinction between her emotions/thoughts and reality, allowing her to separate from the belief that she was “not enough”. We also adapted cognitive processing therapy for PTSD techniques to help her understand and reframe her “stuck points” (eg the trauma of her distorted beliefs about how she failed herself through her “poor radar”). We also looked at the characteristics of healthy relationships, and helped her create a checklist for herself of the signs of healthy relationships so she could date with more confidence.

Together, we also worked on Ali’s anxiety. This predated her former partner though had considerably worsened after the relationship. We utilised a cognitive behavioural approach and looked at the beliefs which fuelled her anxiety (“my friends don’t like me because I withdrew from them while with my ex”) and how she responded to these beliefs, such as by refusing to go to gatherings or engaging in safety behaviours like drinking. We did some behavioural “experiments” to challenge her beliefs and to learn new ways of coping, and also brainstormed ways she could talk to her friends about the relationship with Ian. She was pleasantly surprised to find that her friends understood and were supportive of her once they knew the context.

Recovery was not a linear journey, but these small steps allowed Ali to stop blaming herself, to feel more confident in her body and to show up in the world just as she was, without focusing on pleasing a partner.

*all clients are fictional amalgams

In Australia, the Butterfly Foundation is at 1800 33 4673. In the UK, Beat can be contacted on 0808-801-0677. In the US, help is available at nationaleatingdisorders. org or by calling ANAD’s eating disorders hotline at 800-375-7767. Other international helplines can be found at Eating Disorder Hope

Dr Ahona Guha is a clinical and forensic psychologist, trauma expert and author from Melbourne. She is the author of Reclaim: Understanding Complex Trauma and Those Who Abuse, and Life Skills For a Broken World

Europe’s tallest Virgin Mary statue unveiled in small Polish village

The Guardian Sun, 16 Aug 2026 15:00:04 GMT

Hundreds watched the 56-metre monument’s consecration, including anti-communist leader Lech Wałęsa

An enormous statue of the Virgin Mary that is believed to be Europe’s tallest was inaugurated on Saturday in a small Polish village, in the presence of the anti-communist leader Lech Wałęsa.

Hundreds of people took part in the consecration of the monument, which towers 55.6 metres (182ft) over Konotopie in central Poland, a village of fewer than 150 people.

While helicopters scattered miniature red roses over the crowd, priests in white robes celebrated mass and the Mazowsze folk ensemble sang and danced to traditional Polish music.

The statue is taller – if less dramatically located – than the Christ the Redeemer statue in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil, which measures 38 metres including its pedestal. The Polish monument’s height includes a crown-shaped 15-metre pedestal.

It also surpasses another large-scale religious monument in Poland, the Christ the King statue in the western town of Świebodzin, which was revealed in 2010 and, with the mound it stands on, is 52.5 metres tall.

There is a taller statue of the Virgin Mary in the Philippines, which measures 98 metres. But the new one in Poland is believed to be the largest of its kind in Europe.

Wałęsa, who won the Nobel peace prize for his leadership of the Polish anti-communist resistance as the head of the Solidarity trade union and was later Poland’s president, had a front-row seat during the inauguration ceremony.

“This is the end of my path,” said Wałęsa, 82, suggesting the causes he had long championed, including democracy and the Catholic faith, were now completed. “I started with the Virgin Mary and I end with the Virgin Mary.”

During his Solidarity days, Wałęsa famously wore a Black Madonna pin and he has often credited his faith in God with giving him the strength to fight against communism.

Most Poles identify as Catholic. The church played a powerful role in public life after the fall of communism in 1989, benefiting from the prestige it earned through its support of the anti-communist opposition.

The country is the homeland of Saint John Paul II, who was pope from 1978 until his death in 2005. A huge statue of him – but much smaller than the one of Mary – was revealed more than a decade ago in the city of Częstochowa.

The influence of religion in public life has gradually declined in recent years, particularly among younger people and in urban areas. However, the Catholic church remains influential, especially in rural communities and among older generations.

Wiesław Mering, a Polish Roman Catholic prelate who attended the ceremony, said: “I cannot help but notice the weakening of the institution of the church, a withdrawal of specific social categories from Catholicism, and this hurts me. The history of Christianity has ups and downs, but this place is a reminder that Mary won’t give up on Poland.”

The statue was commissioned by Roman Karkosik, a wealthy Polish businessman, and his wife, Grażyna. The couple live in a small palace a few miles from Konotopie.

Roman Karkosik, an entrepreneur whose ventures included plastic bottle manufacturing in the 1990s, amassed a fortune through investments on the Warsaw stock exchange to become one of Poland’s wealthiest individuals.

The couple have said the monument is an expression of their gratitude to God. “The statue will be for all people,” Grażyna Karkosik said. “Each of us coming to see it will think more deeply about their own lives, not only about God.”

Local authorities hope the monument will become an important pilgrimage site and a tourist destination. The statue has a viewing platform built inside its pedestal.

Ariana Grande Eternal Sunshine tour review: pop illusion at its most effective – for good and bad

The Guardian Sun, 16 Aug 2026 14:20:50 GMT

The O2, LondonOn her last live dates before she steps back from the public eye, Grande holds her own – but it’s also impossible to avoid feeling concerned for her wellbeing

There’s a thrum of excitement in the air as an eight-minute countdown starts and Ariana Grande’s unmistakable silhouette appears on a giant backlit curtain on the stage of the O2. Is it actually her? Posing there for eight minutes before the show starts? It can’t be. But is it? It’s the first time we question what is and isn’t real at this Eternal Sunshine tour stop, a 10-night residency and a robust arena show that ultimately wants us to see one thing and experience another.

Collectively, we’ve been scolded for talking about it – the “endless, ongoing public scrutiny” of Ariana Grande’s body has pushed her to “[take] a step back from visibility” when this tour ends. It can’t be nice or fun to have your body examined and discussed for any reason but it is impossible to witness the 33-year-old’s frame on stage and not be gripped by genuine concern for her. Two songs in, a lump forms in my throat, which is not the intended effect of Positions, the zippy title track of her 2020 album. As the set around her is engulfed in digital flames, Grande sings about her infinite flexibility vis a vis relationship boundaries and sexual olympics and all I can think is: she looks like a little kid.

But you put it aside, of course. That’s how this all works: you’re powerless in the face of it, so you get on with enjoying the show, which is grand and sincere and slick, and full of songs that are so huge they rattle the rafters of the O2. There’s no pyro but who needs it when you have a voice as explosive as Ariana Grande’s? Her diva-era belters like Break Free and One Last Time are peaks amid the troughs of her newer, more subdued sounds. Dangerous Woman is punctuated by drums that sound like firecrackers as she drags the mic stand around the B-stage to belt the chorus directly to as many fans as possible. The songs from Petal, her eighth album released weeks ago, are largely packed into the final portion and forgo the juddering choreo of the rest of the show for something more gig-like. Pogoing through the live debut of Bad Thing and swishing her Victorian nightie around through a ferocious Petal, Grande cries: “It’s such a fucked situation.” Well, yes.

The energy of the show is buoyed by a gaggle of dancers who orbit around her, and you never feel Grande wane even as she struts up and down the runway on impossible stilettos. Her vocals are supple and astonishing, ad libs that scamper and swandive over songs – at the climax of Safety Net, she kneels at the edge of the stage casually emitting sounds that her peers would envy. When she speaks, her words run together like her thoughts are racing to get out of her mouth first: “I’msohappyfortheconnectionwe’veshared,” she says. “You’resuchabeautifulpresenceinmylife.”

Much of Grande’s music has been created in the face of painful adversity but it – and she, in this moment too – carries a lightness with it. She has a smile playing around her lips for most of Thank U, Next, which is a laundry list of romantic misadventures and regret, and a song that had the capacity to feel like a diary entry you cringe at years later. She throws her arms open to the crowd and flicks her long ponytail around with whip-like precision and all the sass of the woman who sees it and wants it and wants it and gets it.

Every so often that illusion of lightness breaks. She turns on the mid-stage and leans sort of forward as she sings Past Life, a move to communicate her earnest romantic pain, a plea for empathy. The angle she’s standing at and the lighting collude to knock the breath out of me for a second: I shouldn’t be able to see this person’s skeleton.

Those moments are deeply conflicting and in them I wish she had cancelled this run of dates rather than wait for them to wrap up. The show is a good testament to her 13-year pop career and worthy of being enjoyed, but that is hard to do when you feel that someone spectacular might be slipping through our fingers right in front of us. I really hope this tour does not go down in history for the wrong reasons: I hope it ends up a four-star aside in a long and rich life.

Cambridge University defends its mental health support for Jason Arday

The Guardian Sun, 16 Aug 2026 14:09:13 GMT

University says it continued to provide support after resignation of academic, who was found dead on Friday

The University of Cambridge has defended its mental health support for the academic Jason Arday.

The university said it had continued to provide Arday with extensive mental health support and security measures, including installing panic alarms and screening racist emails and post, after he resigned from his post as professor of sociology of education this month.

He quit after widespread press coverage of accusations of plagiarism and inconsistencies in statements about his career and achievements.

A University of Cambridge spokesperson said: “Our support continued in the face of intense public and media scrutiny and after his resignation. Our thoughts and deepest condolences are with Jason’s family and loved ones at this extremely difficult time.”

Arday, 41, was pronounced dead after emergency services were called to his home in Battersea, south London, on Friday.

When he was appointed professor of sociology of education at Cambridge at the age of 37 in 2023, he was the university’s youngest ever black professor.

A vigil in Arday’s memory organised by the campaign group Stand Up to Racism will be held on the steps of the National Gallery in Trafalgar Square, central London, at 6pm on Monday. The group’s co-convener Weyman Bennett said in a statement that Arday’s death was the “result of a racist witch-hunt”.

He added: “For more than a week, the rightwing press, politicians and the far right have hounded Jason with the most vicious racism. They are spreading the far-right lie that black people are only appointed because of the colour of our skin, rather than our ability.”

Arday was initially accused of plagiarising another academic’s work for his PhD thesis. He denied the accusations, and an investigation by Liverpool John Moores University this year upheld its decision to award him a PhD.

When allegations surfaced in the UK media in July, Cambridge said it had investigated the claims and found no wrongdoing, describing Arday as the victim of a “vile smear campaign to undermine his credibility”.

This month, the university announced it would open a fresh investigation after it said it received “new information” about Arday’s qualifications and career.

Other elements of Arday’s life story were increasingly questioned, including claims of prodigious money-raising for charity and feats of long-distance running. He was also challenged about whether he was nonverbal until the age of 11, as well as being illiterate until 18.

It is understood Cambridge has paused the investigation while Arday’s family are grieving, and will consider whether to reopen it in due course.

Academics and politicians have cast doubt on whether Cambridge took Arday’s vulnerability seriously when he was appointed to the ­senior public-facing role in 2023. At the time, the university had been facing criticism for its lack of diversity in senior roles.

Prof Simon Baron-Cohen, Arday’s friend and former colleague, told Times Radio he thought the university should proceed with the investigation. “We should see what we learn from it. This is the whole purpose of investigations,” he said.

He also questioned whether the media had failed in its duty of care towards Arday, as a vulnerable person with disabilities. He said Arday faced racist abuse and was used as a “lightning rod for a culture war on [diversity, equity and inclusion]”.

Simon Woolley, the principal of Homerton College, Cambridge, and Arday’s former mentor, has called for an investigation into the “vicious media onslaught”.

In a statement on Saturday, Prof Deborah Prentice, the vice-chancellor of Cambridge University, said her “thoughts and deepest condolences” were with Arday’s family, as well as with colleagues and students in the faculty of education and at Jesus College where he was a fellow.

“Supporting our community through this tragedy is the single most important priority for me and my leadership team right now. We will be reaching out to many of you directly, and we are committed to ensuring that no one feels they must face this alone,” she said.

A fundraiser launched by the Windrush campaigner Patrick Vernon on Saturday afternoon has raised more than £65,000 to contribute towards funeral and memorial costs and support for Arday’s family.

On the crowdfunder’s webpage, Vernon said: “I was one of the people who publicly supported Jason during the recent controversy because I was deeply concerned about the nature and intensity of the attacks directed towards him. I was also subject to media scrutiny for signing the letter of support and challenged in supporting Jason.”

Andy Burnham, the prime minister, described Arday’s death as a “tragedy on so many levels” and urged a “moment of reflection”.

In a statement issued via Simon & Schuster, which published Arday’s memoir, Great and Unfortunate Things, in the US this week, Arday’s family said they were “in shock to have lost this amazing father, partner, brother, uncle and son”.

They added: “Jason was subjected to a campaign of sustained abuse for more than three years since he accepted the role of professor at Cambridge University by those who would leave no stone unturned in their quest to undermine him. The campaign of misinformation was too much for Jason, who was a gentle man and who always wanted to see the best in everyone.”

The five-year plans that turned into lifetimes: Windrush elders’ stories ‘open door’ for young people

The Guardian Sun, 16 Aug 2026 14:00:28 GMT

Collecting first-hand accounts of older generation’s struggles is opportunity for Hackney’s children, says leader of pioneering project

There are faces young and old around a table in Hackney library as people share a meal of curry goat, rice and peas and sorrel cake. There are photos of the smiling faces of Windrush elders scattered around. They will soon become permanent fixtures of the Hackney Archives.

There is a feeling among the group that somebody is missing. Lessept Saunders, the founder of the Hackney Caribbean Elderly Organisation, died in April aged 107. He had been the second-oldest known living man in London and the oldest contributor to Stories of Windrush. Saunders was part of the Windrush generation, having arrived in London from Jamaica in 1944 after hearing stories about higher wages and hope from returning friends who had served in the second world war.

“Saunders had a five-year-plan, like many of the elders who came to the UK,” says Paul Anderson, the CEO of Voyage Youth, a social justice charity leading the archival project. “They would tell themselves ‘I’m only going to be here for five years and go back’ but many were not able to do that. The cost to travel back home was such a barrier that many just stayed.”

Stories of Windrush is one of the first projects in the UK to document first-hand accounts from Windrush elders collected entirely by young people. The accompanying book and photographs and its digital counterparts will have a permanent place in the Hackney Archives.

Zainab Awonoki was 15 when she first started working on the archive four years ago. “I never grew up with my grandparents so speaking to elders has been so eye-opening,” she says. Despite learning briefly about the Windrush generation in her Hackney secondary school, it was only through the archives that she learned about the struggles these elders had faced. “Hearing their stories first hand lets you see that they practically fought for us to actually stay here. It tells our elders that they’re not alone with their past and trauma.”

Research has found that giving young people access to archives can improve educational attainment and increase awareness of local decision-making. It seems to resonate with Diane Abbott, the MP for Hackney North and Stoke Newington, who wrote a foreword for the book. She wrote: “For all those who form part of the Windrush generation, and many who have been subject to scandalous impositions by state agencies, we must not forget their lives, their struggles, their achievements and their legacy are worth celebrating.”

Claudette Barned arrived in the 1960s from Jamaica at the age of nine and was immediately struck by the freezing temperatures in Clapton, east London. Today, the 74-year-old fans herself in the scorching heat, wearing a pink summer dress and recently having dyed her hair blue. “My mother passed away before I could ask her about history,” she says. “Talking to the young people means that when we die our stories are shared and when they’re old they can repeat the cycle.” Now retired, she has not forgotten the loneliness of her first few years in England. She socialises at elderly clubs with other Windrush elders and has passed on her Caribbean traditions to her grandson, who has nicknamed her “Reggae Grandma”.

Through the archives, Anderson hopes to address the youth unemployment crisis, starting with Hackney’s children who experience some of the highest rates of child poverty in England. He says: “For many, it opened a door they had not known was there: a route into the heritage sector, a reason to consider higher education, and a genuine change of pathway into a field where African and Caribbean communities remain significantly under-represented, despite so much of the history held within it being their own.”

after newsletter promotion

Yvonne Straughn was born in Barbados in 1941 as the only girl among five brothers. “I was rebellious,” she told the young archivists, recalling how she would refuse to do chores unless she was paid. At 85, her rebellious spirit seems to live on. As Anderson describes the legacy of the archives, she is quick to remind the elders that none of them will be around to see it.

Straughn’s tale is a classic Windrush story. In 1966 she arrived in England to work in a hospital, treating patients who were often hostile to the sight of a black nurse. Awonoki says it is a big responsibility to be entrusted with stories such as Straughn’s, particularly in the rollback of diversity initiatives. “You need their stories to realise this isn’t something new,” she says. “The older generation had a massive impact on life. They gave us the Equality Act and now we’re talking about getting rid of it?”

‘Absolutely manic’: hot weather puts unprecedented pressure on Greater Manchester police

The Guardian Sun, 16 Aug 2026 14:00:27 GMT

Force has seen busiest month in its history, with heatwaves putting added strain on criminal justice system

On England’s hottest day of the year so far, Ashton-under-Lyne in Greater Manchester was thronging with pedestrians, many clutching ice-creams or cold drinks as they passed through the town centre.

Officers from Greater Manchester police were also out in force, some in plainclothes, some stationed by a facial-recognition van, apprehending wanted suspects and stopping persons of interest. In total, officers made 54 arrests across the borough of Tameside as part of Operation Avro, GMP’s blitz on local crime which runs in a different district each month.

For the past two months, the demand on officers here has been greater than ever, and GMP received a record-breaking 152,000 contacts from the public in July – the highest number ever recorded by the force in a single month.

The World Cup is likely to have played a part, but the main driver, officers said, was the continued hot weather, which is putting an added strain not just on health services but also on the criminal justice system.

And GMP is not alone – according to data from the National Police Chiefs’ Council, which includes all the Home Office’s forces, British Transport Police and Police Scotland, emergency call volumes increased by about 11.5% year on year during July.

Digital contact with the public also increased. Online reports submitted through Single Online Home, the platform used by most police forces, increased by about 10% year on year.

The Met Office has confirmed that July was the hottest and the driest month on record, while heatwaves have continued into August. “These factors bring people outside, there’s an increase in alcohol consumption, an increase in people going into reservoirs, into water,” said Tameside’s neighbourhood chief inspector, James Grundy. “So that does increase the demand for police.”

Grundy said there had been an increase in calls on everything from off-road bike use to antisocial behaviour and people taking disposable barbecues to locations prone to wildfires.

“It is challenging,” Grundy said. “Obviously we have to attend incidents based on the threat, harm and risk, so we have to prioritise certain incidents over others, which means that some people don’t often receive the level of response that they deserve. We have officers that are pulled from different areas to support that demand on the frontline at times.”

“At the moment in Greater Manchester police every day is a busy period,” said the Tameside neighbourhood police sergeant Rob Froggatt. “Every day police officers are being run ragged.”

He said his neighbourhood officers were often pulled on to response policing when those teams needed more support in order to do their jobs safely. “It’s a fine balance,” he said, “but I’d say we deal with it quite well.”

Tameside response officer PC Daniel Bragg has been in his job for seven years, and said with the exception of perhaps New Year’s Eve, this summer had been the busiest he had ever known.

“Over the last few months, obviously with the World Cup, the sun, it’s just non-stop,” he said. “Due to the football you have more people jumping in cars after pubs, so we had a lot more crashes. When it gets warm, naturally with older people you have a lot more deaths occurring.”

Bragg said domestic incidents and mental health crises were also two big drivers of 999 calls. “It was absolutely manic again last week, non-stop,” he said, adding that senior officers were being sent out on jobs in order to meet response targets.

after newsletter promotion

Officers attended 14,991 grade 1 incidents (where there is an immediate emergency) in July, achieving an average response time of seven minutes and 54 seconds, and 10,266 grade 2 (serious incidents lacking immediate danger), with an average response time of one hour and two minutes.

In the last month, Bragg said, the team had been responding to up to 40 calls in a night shift; typically that number would lie somewhere between 10 and 20.

“You’re doubling or quadrupling that in one night,” he said. “You are out of the station from 9 o’clock when a job comes in, and then you’re coming back in at 7 o’ clock really, just going job to job.”

With more hot summers on the horizon, Bragg said: “I do think if it continues like this over the years to come, there would have to be a change just in terms of staffing. It’s kind of impossible to police what we’re policing at the minute.”

“When I look at the three-month period and compare it to the same three months last year, it’s been a really significant increase,” said the Tameside district superintendent, Arif Nawaz. “We’re looking at around an extra 572 grade 2 incidents and an extra 272 grade 1 incidents. So that effectively means my response teams have to deal with an extra seven grade 1s and 2s every single day.”

As well as the weather, Manchester’s rapid development brought more people to the city, which in turn placed additional strain on policing, Nawaz said. “The economic development around Manchester is brilliant for the region but it’s also contributing. The Co-op Arena is a new site attracting 20,000 people each event. That’s in addition to the AO Arena. So that’s just one simple example of something that’s great for the economy, but there’s a policing demand.”

The repeated heatwaves were, Nawaz said, “a very serious issue that as a society we need to consider, as a police service we need to consider”.

“The government’s looking at it as well, so who knows what the future will bring?” he added. “Clearly it is in our thinking around how we prepare ourselves for this.”

‘It was barbaric. I was crying my eyes out’: why are so many women left in agony by routine womb examinations?

The Guardian Sun, 16 Aug 2026 13:00:27 GMT

There are more than 70,000 hysteroscopies every year in England alone. The NHS calls them ‘low complexity’ – yet a shocking number of patients complain of inadequate pain relief and medical staff who refuse to take them seriously

In February this year, Beth Harris sat in the day surgery waiting room of her local hospital and tried to steady her nerves.

She was there for a hysteroscopy, in this case to remove a fibroid. A thin surgical instrument with a lens, a light, a blade and an irrigation system for pumping saline solution would be inserted through her vagina and cervix, into her womb. The saline solution would widen the womb and the fibroid would be shaved away. Her hospital had advised taking paracetamol or ibuprofen an hour before the appointment, which Harris had done. However, the appointment was for 1pm, and by 4pm, she was still waiting in her hospital gown, surrounded by other patients.

Hysteroscopies are common procedures – classed by the NHS as “high volume low complexity”. In 2021, 71,000 took place in England alone. This was Harris’s third. “I’d been shocked by how painful the first two were,” she says. They had been “diagnostic” only – examinations of the inside of the womb – because years of breast cancer medication had led her womb lining to thicken. When she learned that she had a fibroid that needed removing, Harris’s first question was: “Will it be painful?” Her gynaecologist assured her that she would be given local anaesthetic and “wouldn’t feel anything”. He compared it to “going to the dentist”.

Any doubts Harris harboured while awaiting that procedure were multiplied by the two patients treated ahead of her. “The first woman was hysterical when she came out,” she says. “The nurse had to get the consultant to talk to her. The second collapsed in the recovery room. Nobody came to her, so a little old man in his gown and slippers, a random patient, got involved and found a nurse. They took her away on a trolley.”

When Harris was finally called in, there were several people in the theatre. “There was the gynaecologist, nurses, an anaesthetist behind me, although he didn’t do anything. They were talking to each other throughout – no one was sitting with me. It was very casual.” The gynaecologist administered local anaesthetic – a small injection near the cervix – but there was no pause to see if it had worked. “There was no gap, no questions,” she says. “The injection itself was painful, but the procedure, with this spinning blade inside you, was unbelievable. The pressure, the pushing of the machine, the manipulation – it was barbaric. I’ve never experienced anything like it in my life. I felt as if I’d been assaulted. By the end, I was crying my eyes out.” A nurse led her, sobbing, to the recovery room. “There was no dignity, no privacy,” says Harris. “I said to her: ‘There must be a better way of doing this.’”

Katharine Tylko, a founder member of the campaign group Hysteroscopy Action (HA), has been saying the same thing for 16 years. HA was formed in 2010 to demand that all hysteroscopy patients are fully informed about the procedure, including the risk of severe pain, and given a full range of pain relief choices – local anaesthesia, gas and air, conscious sedation, epidural, and, for those who need it, general anaesthetic. “In short, we want parity with colonoscopy patients, half of whom are men,” says Tylko. In April, the renewed Women’s Health Strategy set out by the then health secretary Wes Streeting seemed a major breakthrough. Action 7 of the strategy called for informed consent and a choice of pain relief for hysteroscopies. “We were thrilled,” says Tylko, “but there’s been nothing since. Just silence.”

Many conditions might require a hysteroscopy. By far the most common is heavy or unexplained bleeding. In 2018, guidelines from the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence made them the primary diagnostic tool for this. A hysteroscopy’s “inside view” of the womb makes them the gold standard for ruling out any sinister pathology such as endometrial cancer. They are also used to investigate cases of unexplained infertility or recurrent miscarriage, to remove uterine fibroids, polyps or scar tissue.

Once hysteroscopies required a general anaesthetic, but this changed through the 2000s and 2010s after clinical audits and trials established that outpatient hysteroscopies were safe, much faster and more cost-effective. (Present NHS targets are that 90% of diagnostic and 50% of operative hysteroscopies take place in an outpatient setting.) Pain relief options vary wildly across the country. Too often, says Tylko, there is nothing beyond a nurse to hold your hand and supply a constant stream of “hairdresser chitchat”.

Tylko, 71, a musician and translator, required a hysteroscopy 23 years ago, because of unexplained bleeding. “It was late-stage womb cancer which took two years to be diagnosed,” she says. “By then, I was bleeding so much, I was sleeping on bath towels.” After numerous GP appointments, Tylko asked why she wasn’t being referred for investigation. “My GP told me that I would ‘freak out’ at an NHS gynae clinic,” says Tylko. The GP had reached this conclusion partly because Tylko hadn’t had a baby, so her cervical canal had not been stretched, and also because she found smear tests difficult (she now knows this was almost certainly because of undiagnosed endometriosis).

“That night was probably the worst night of my life,” says Tylko. “I thought: ‘She thinks I’ve got something – and she thinks I probably won’t be able to stand the test for it.’ I went privately and still had to jump through lots more hoops, but I finally got a hysteroscopy under general anaesthetic.”

Through her subsequent cancer treatment, Tylko met many women who had been traumatised by their hysteroscopies. “I’d been told that only 2% of women had problems with them,” she says. “I was given the message that if I was ‘normal’, if I’d had children, I wouldn’t be complaining. Then I met women who’d had children with no pain relief but who’d fainted after their hysteroscopies.” The penny finally dropped that she wasn’t the only one who struggled with gynecological procedures.

More than 13,000 women have completed HA’s online survey, which set out to learn more from women’s experiences, and its petition is nearing 70,000 signatures. The comments make harrowing reading. In 2020, a benchmark multicentre study found that mean pain scores for outpatient hysteroscopies were 5.2 (that’s “moderate” on a hospital ward and would merit codeine) and 35% of women had a “severe” pain score of seven and above.

“As a campaign, we’ve had real difficulty treading a rational path between trying to effect change but not putting women off something that can predict cancer,” says Tylko. “We’ve always put the caveat that two-thirds of women do not experience severe pain.” Equally though, outpatient hysteroscopies have a failure rate of around 10%, with pain as the predominant reason, points out Richard Harrison, lecturer and co-lead of pain research at Reading University. “That, too, can lead to a whole lack of engagement with future medical procedures, which could be lifesaving.”

Harrison worked on a recently published study that analysed data from nearly 5,000 women who had undergone hysteroscopies. For Harrison and his co-authors, the issue sits within a wider body of research on the gender pain gap – it’s already well established that women presenting in health care settings with pain are prescribed less analgesic than men, and are more likely to be given antidepressants instead. In this hysteroscopy study, they identified a “gynaecological pain gaslighting” where women were repeatedly told: “It can’t be that bad” and: “Most women tolerate this procedure well.”

Helen Garnett, 56, from North Lincolnshire, was so certain that she would be “gaslit” that she secretly recorded her outpatient hysteroscopy and later released it online (with voices altered). “I’d already had two hysteroscopies for heavy bleeding which had been so horrendous, I’d almost passed out,” she says. This time, she called her GP and clinic in advance to request pain relief – and was told her consultant would discuss it on the day. The recording is excruciating to hear. Garnett is nervous, clearly but apologetically asking for pain relief – “I’m not wimpy but this I find so painful” – but is swept through with none. Instead she was left with patronising chatter from nurses: “Do you think we should have some music in here? I could sing to you!”; “You’re doing amazing!”; “Well done you!”

“It feels as if someone is sweeping a knife around inside you,” says Garnett. “I have three daughters, I run my own business, I thought I’d be able to advocate for myself more, but I just couldn’t. It’s crazy. You lose all sense of being an adult as they treat you in such a childlike manner. I’m surprised they don’t give you sweets and a sticker on the way out. As soon as I got away, I burst into tears. I didn’t want them to see me crying like a baby.”

Some gynaecologists are determined to make changes. Dr Gail Busby, a consultant gynaecologist for 26 years, admits it has been a “learning curve”. “A long time ago, I don’t think we were aware how painful an outpatient hysteroscopy can be,” she says. “As a gynaecologist, you’re so focused on the procedure. We thought it was period-like, crampy pain, which is the case for a lot of women, but it is absolutely undeniable that some women have severe pain and they need to be listened to.”

Two incidents forced Busby to reevaluate. The first was learning through a patient about HA and its campaign. The second was her own experience of a colonoscopy. “It was with sedation, but for me, it was the most hideous, painful thing ever. Some people have no problems with them. I had tears running down my face.” Busby has had a hysteroscopy, too, with no pain relief, and for her, that was fine. “I just think people are wired differently and there’s no way you can predict if you’re going to fall into the one-in-three women who have severe pain,” she says. Busby now offers deep sedation – administered by an anaesthetist and the patient will sleep through most of the procedure – to her hysteroscopy patients at her private Spire clinic and her NHS practice at St Mary’s Hospital in Manchester. “Not everyone needs it, but the women who say they need it really need it.”

Consultant obstetrician and gynaecologist Richard Flint offers conscious sedation – a combination of analgesia and sedative via a needle in your arm – at his clinic in Chelsea and Westminster hospital. “I’ve been performing hysteroscopies for eight years now, and though many patients are fine with outpatient hysteroscopies, there is a large proportion for whom it is agonising,” he says. “From my point of view, I stop immediately and those procedures are really heart-sink moments. You feel you’ve failed the patient.”

In 2023, Flint introduced conscious sedation at C&W, one day a week. They are now expanding it to a five-day service (the only hospital currently offering it for hysteroscopies). They also offer it for other outpatient procedures such as cystoscopies (examinations of the bladder), IUD insertions and manual vacuum aspirations after miscarriage. At the same time, the clinic is trialling the Wid-easy test, a vaginal swab that checks for womb cancer in women with abnormal bleeding. It is already in routine use in Austria and Switzerland, has been introduced in Germany, and is on trial for NHS use in various clinics across the UK. “That is massively reducing the number of hysteroscopies we need to do,” Flint says. He now has data on more than 300 hysteroscopies performed under conscious sedation, which he is releasing shortly. “The pain scores are so much better. The average is two out of 10,” he says. “What has sealed it for me is seeing patients whose previous hysteroscopies had to be abandoned. They usually say: ‘Why didn’t I have this before?’”

There are other small signs of progress. The British Society for Gynaecological Endoscopy has recently appointed a female president – the first in decades – consultant gynaecologist Rebecca Mallick. This month, Mallick and Royal College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists (RCOG) president Dr Alison Wright met with members of HA. “Alison and I were shocked and have a lot of things to think about,” says Mallick. At present, RCOG guidelines state that outpatient hysteroscopy patients should be fully informed about the procedure first, and “made aware” that there are other settings and pain relief offerings, including a general anaesthetic or intravenous sedation. “We could do a deep dive into why best practice isn’t always happening,” says Mallick. “We’ve got half a million people on the gynae waiting list, so clinics want to see as many people as possible. Are we giving enough time to talk through all the options or just trying to firefight numbers? We need to look at how we can support hysteroscopists to offer all types of analgesic. We also need to advocate for more funding and resources so we can tackle the backlog and improve care.”

Tylko sees this as part of a much bigger picture. “We’re a gathering snowball made up of all sorts of gynae-women’s groups,” she says. “Endometriosis UK, Sling the Mesh, women fighting for better maternity care, better IUD fittings. We are getting together and saying: ‘This has to end.’”

For Harris, any hard-won changes will come too late. She has chosen to have a hysterectomy. “I’ve found a gynaecologist I trust and she is the only one I will let do it,” she says, “but I’m on the waiting list to see a psychologist first to help me get through it. At the moment, since that last hysteroscopy, every medical appointment makes me cry and panic.” Harris is taking this route partly so that she will never need another one. “I will not undergo any more tests, no more procedures, no more examinations. I’ve reached my red light. This is how I’ll bring it to a close.”

My lovely French husband has made the ultimate sacrifice for me – he’s now officially British

The Guardian Sun, 16 Aug 2026 13:00:26 GMT

In Leeds Civic Hall, I watched 20 new citizens pledge their allegiance to King Charles and his heirs. But it wasn’t patriotism that brought tears to my eyes

I haven’t felt great about asking my husband to become British. There was the idiotic Life in the UK test that every applicant has to pass; the cost; the faff; and the uncertainty, which still hasn’t ended. I found out his application had been accepted when he came into the kitchen in June with a face like thunder. “But that’s brilliant! You’ll never need to know how many Scottish ski resorts there are again!” I said, puzzled. He explained that, because we’re going on holiday before he can get a British passport to go with his French one, he’ll be in an immigration grey area that could mean he gets refused re-entry. He should, theoretically, be OK, but it’s confusing.

Why would he even want to come back to this place with its threadbare services, toxic waterways, obsession with “picky bits” and ridiculous politics? His Home Office email arrived just after the Makerfield byelection and that night the news showed the returning officer’s poker-faced declaration again: our future prime minister flanked by a politely clapping Binface and an oversized, blank-eyed fox. I started laughing, hysterically, guiltily. What have I done to him? “Will the world go a different colour when I’m British?” he asked on the train to the ceremony. “Yeah, reverse Wizard of Oz – everything goes grey.”

But if you are becoming British, because you really love your wife or for any other reason, Leeds Civic Hall is a good spot for it. We admired the outside, embellished with large, golden owls, from the terrace of Wetherspoons, where another set of ceremony attenders – a south Asian couple our age, smartly dressed, finishing up an appropriate full English – were taking a “before” pic. We exchanged shy congratulations, then headed inside, where there was dark wood and stained glass, a proper sense of historical gravitas and a brief panic about the travel issue.

An inadequate fan moved stifling air around feebly as the registrar explained people shouldn’t plan trips abroad before getting their British passports, to some overheated consternation. An intensive-care doctor decided to defer, unwilling to risk missing her shifts, but after some shrugging and a few fingers-crossed gestures, everyone else went ahead.

I’m so glad we did. It was kind, laid-back and gently funny in a way that almost made me feel patriotic. There was a warning from the registrar not to laminate citizenship certificates (“You do not want to give the Home Office any more money!”), plus one for my husband that she’d probably say his name, Olivier, “with a Yorkshire twang” (she did; it was lovely). At one point, the whole team decided to move the table with the draped union jack for better photos, propping King Charles, in his clip frame, against the speaker used for a single mumbled verse of the national anthem.

The business part of becoming British was very brief. Olivier had practised affirming allegiance back home (“No, you’re not pledging loyalty to his hair – its heirs”), worried about speaking solo, but it was a group effort. Everyone swore or affirmed, then pledged, then the registrar said simply they were all citizens now – and I found myself crying.

It had been such an act of love for us – I hugged him, whispered my thanks – but also it was impossible not to be moved by everyone else. The frail, stooped woman who left her walker to go up, proudly unaided, for her certificate. The radiant teen in a white minidress who was getting her A-level results the same day, adulthood unfolding in the dazzling sunshine. The tiny mother photographed by her giant, bashful teenage son in a sharp suit and blinding-white trainers. The grey-haired Chinese woman in wire-rimmed glasses, attending alone, who asked me to take her beaming picture. The guy who ducked out apologetically before group photos, saying he had to get to work. The 20 people from Spain, Bahrain, Bangladesh, China, Eritrea, France, Ghana, India, Iran, Iraq, Libya, Pakistan, Poland, Romania and South Africa, who had done something hard for love, safety or a different life.

An hour later, we were back on the train. The world hasn’t gone grey for my husband, he says – wait until he finds himself stranded in a foreign airport – and, for a moment, for me, it felt quite golden.

Emma Beddington is a Guardian columnist

‘I see the incredible promise’: on set of an AI film shoot as new studios embrace controversial tech

The Guardian Sun, 16 Aug 2026 12:00:25 GMT

Amid fears for jobs, some film-makers say AI could enable them bypass studio giants and take more creative risks

Near the collonaded entrance to Sony Pictures’ historic Culver City film studio, a tech-powered rival has sprung up this summer. The artists at Promise, a new studio feeding off the potential of AI, can glimpse the lots where Singin’ in the Rain and Men in Black were shot, but no longer do they need to get beyond the studio’s high walls to make their visions come true.

From far more modest premises, they are making movies with rapidly accelerating AI models that create backgrounds, special effects and even “synthetic performers” – using US models but also driven by market-leading Chinese AI.

Backed by Google, Silicon Valley venture capitalists and Disney, Promise is one of a rising number of AI film studios now taking root in Hollywood, with the result that traditional studios’ vast sound stages and financing are becoming less necessary.

It is a controversial trend. Leading directors including Christopher Nolan and Guillermo del Toro have criticised generative technology, actors and writers are fearing for their jobs, and the Democratic congresswoman Laura Friedman, who represents Hollywood’s actors, writers and directors, warned last month: “We can’t wait until we see tens of thousands of American workers displaced.”

But the excitement and energy about AI’s potential was palpable this week at Promise’s new base when a human actor, Tori Thomas, waited for her call amid rows of computers for early shooting on the studio’s newly announced AI-enabled horror film, Touch Grass, with a budget in the low millions of dollars.

The sound stage was little more than a corner of the office hung with white sheets. A small camera followed Thomas as she scrambled in a chase scene, then the AI did the rest. It superimposed her movement in real time on to a field of swaying grass generated by a Chinese AI model, Seedance 2.5, released this month, which looks set to dramatically slash production times.

Whole scenes – actor and backdrop – were instantly visible on the director’s handheld monitor, as if they were filming in real locations. Even the seedheads in the AI-generated meadow moved as Thomas appeared to brush past. In another take, the field was easily replaced by a nightmarish underground cavern. With a glance at the screen, Thomas could immediately see the backdrop she was acting with.

Promise is not alone in embracing the technology, which Netflix last week said it had used in 300 of its 1,000 titles in 2026. Ron Howard, the veteran director of the Da Vinci Code and A Beautiful Mind, is set to release an AI-enabled animated documentary feature about prisoners of war in Vietnam, working with another new AI studio, Obsidian. Brad Pitt said this week that while there was a lot of pushback, “AI is going to be the very thing that, if used as a tool, is going to help these mid-budget films, $40m- to $90m-budgeted films, get made.”

That chimed with predictions from a new wave of AI native film-makers, such as Kavan “the Kid” Cardoza, 37, who has set up the Phantom X studio. He predicted a creative renaissance circumventing the studio giants not seen since Quentin Tarantino and Spike Lee’s breakthroughs more than 30 years ago.

The Promise shoot involved veteran film-makers including Joel Hynek, an Oscar winner who worked on the manual special effects for Arnold Schwarzenegger’s 1987 action-horror film Predator.

“When we went from optical to digital film, we thought we’d gone to heaven,” he told the Guardian. “It’s like that again. So many things are easy to do. I am an embracer of AI. Some people are wary of it, a little afraid of it, but I see the incredible promise.”

Others, like Nolan, voice concern. “I’ve never seen a technology advancing so rapidly, so completely rejected by the public,” the Odyssey director has said. “Everybody’s suspicion of it is so extreme, particularly young people.”

There has been a backlash against an AI resurrection of the late actor Val Kilmer to star in a new feature and the emergence of the AI “actor” Tilly Norwood, with the actor Emily Blunt calling it “really, really scary” and pleading: “Please stop taking away our human connection.”

But the new AI studios are undeterred. Dave Clark, the director of Promise’s Touch Grass – who is also working on an animation, Hardcore 94, set to an early 1990s LA hip-hop soundtrack – said that with “great dialogue and backstory”, AI-generated characters could become interesting and believable.

The US actors’ union Sag-Aftra will no doubt beg to differ, but Cardoza predicted: “Next year [AI actors will] be just as good as real actors.”

George Strompolos, a co-founder and the chief executive of Promise, estimated that hybrid AI films – human actors alongside AI technology – would prove 20% to 50% cheaper than conventional production. That could free film-makers from requiring major studio investment.

“We’re at the beginning of a golden era of independent, highly empowered creative companies – call them small studios, micro studios – that will lead to more creative risk-taking,” he said.

Joanna Popper, a producer and an adviser on AI to production companies, said the positive view on AI in film and TV was that it “empowers anybody with a talent and a discipline for storytelling to be able to go make what they want to make”. But she said: “The concern is … if five tech companies suck all of the financial gain out of the industry.”

Imagine, the 41-year-old studio run by Howard and Brian Grazer, now has an AI studio, Obsidian, operating from space in its Beverly Hills HQ. It has partnered with Obsidian to make The Code, an AI-enabled, Howard-directed animated feature based on drawings made in Vietnamese captivity by US prisoners of war.

D Ryan Reeb, an executive producer at Obsidian, estimated the technology delivered a 30% to 40% cost saving. He said he had met with dozens of top production companies interested in the technology and predicted all would use it. But AI in Hollywood has drawn comparison to plastic surgery: everyone’s doing it but nobody wants to talk about it. “It’s 100% like that,” Reeb said.

An AI native film-maker such as Cardoza, who makes films in his spare bedroom in Playa Vista, has no reason to downplay his AI use. It has helped him reach 28m YouTube views for his Chronicles of Bone fantasy universe series launched online last autumn, featuring his versions of Robin Hood, Peter Pan, King Arthur and Tinkerbell and a lucrative deal with the Magnific AI platform. Cardoza believes AI film-makers are attracting audiences because, ironically, their direct authorial voice has greater authenticity than in Hollywood where “they turn writing into algorithms”.

“I’ve had meetings with studios where [they say] a horror movie has to have X amount of jump scares … Why can’t I just write the story? And if there’s two jump scares, there’s two. If there’s 10, there’s 10. Why are we hitting markers? That’s not creativity – that’s manufacture.”

He said the growth in AI-led film-making “reminds me more of the 90s era when you got Tarantino, [Robert] Rodriguez and all these guys popping off … You put on any one of their movies and you will know that it’s theirs without their name being shown because of the style and voice.” Now, he said, films in cinemas “all look the same”.

Cardoza highly rates the models made by Chinese tech companies who are “smoking everybody on everything – the image generation models, the video generation models.”

He assumes the Chinese models are so powerful because they have been “trained on everything under the sun”, in a way that US models cannot be because of intellectual property restrictions. But with Washington considering restrictions on Chinese open-source AI models, Cardoza opposes a ban on such powerful tools, which have allowed him a creative flourishing.

“I’ll move to China,” he said. “I’m not even lying.”

‘Why did it become personal?’: furore over plans to expand Kent oyster shack

The Guardian Sun, 16 Aug 2026 12:00:24 GMT

James Green’s oyster company owns a chunk of Whitstable’s shoreline but success has not brought affection from residents

The clink of glasses and the lapping of the tide was punctuated by giggling toddlers and the slurp of oysters at tables populated by people gently sizzling on a baking day on the Kent seaside.

But James Green, of the Whitstable Oyster Fishery Company, had the demeanour of a man who had found grit in his mollusc. “I don’t like to use the term but it is nimbyism,” he said. “Why did it become personal? I don’t know really. Because we’re a family business, it’s a relatively small town?”

Green, 58, is the director of the WOFC, a company he inherited from his father and whose roots can be traced back to 1793. He has become embroiled in a battle over his plans for a seafood empire.

The WOFC harvests about 2m oysters a year from Whitstable’s seabeds, half of which stay on the south coast to be sold in the company’s hotel and the four restaurants it runs on the front.

It is Green’s application to extend the seating of one of those restaurants, the Forge oyster shack, on to a patch of beach used to store boats belonging to members of the Whitstable Yacht Club, that has caused a furore and which he says highlights a national problem.

Green is battling, he says, to grow a business that employs 200 people but could take on more, and which has cemented Whitstable’s reputation as “Britain’s Oysteropolis”. The new seating for the Forge would allow visitors to enjoy “half a dozen oysters and a glass of muscadet” on the sand, he said, and offer further reason to visit the town.

In 1865, more than 100 boats in Whitstable harvested about 80m oysters for sale at the Billingsgate fish market each year. By the 1970s, overfishing, pollution and the arrival of introduced diseases with imported stock resulted in the collapse of the industry.

Green’s father, Barrie, bought the WOFC in 1976. The company had one employee and was barely functioning. It was Green’s sons, James and Richard, who started the industrial-scale farming of non-native Pacific rock oysters in 2008, helping to make Whitstable’s reputation what it is today. But the Greens had to fight a lengthy and expensive campaign nearly a decade ago for the right to maintain the thousands of metal racks off the beach on which they grow.

The company’s success – it is the owner of a considerable chunk of the town’s beach and its shoreline – has not brought affection. The planning application in June for extra seating space and a pergola for the Forge has already attracted more than 200 opposing submissions, including from the Environment Agency which is concerned about the impact on flood defences.

Some Whitstable residents called it “a carbuncle” and a “horrifying visual, physical and commercial intrusion”. “Disastrous,” said another of the intention for the cafe to serve alcohol and seafood to customers’ tables on both sides of the King Charles III coastal path that traces the outline of the coast.

Paul McNally, speaking on behalf of the Whitstable Beach Campaign, a group that was at the vanguard of the attempt to block the metal racks in 2018, said there was no justification for the Forge’s extension on to the beach.

“Our remit, for many years, has been a simple one – to protect the unspoilt nature of Whitstable beach and maintain public access to it. Both of which would be compromised by the current development proposal.”

Green, who spent £1m on his planning application for the racks, and who unsuccessfully sought a licensing application for a similar extension of the Forge five years ago, detects a “general antipathy” towards his company as well as a lack of realism about the economic challenges facing the area and the UK.

“I think this country has a problem with commercial enterprises and expansion maybe,” he said. “And people don’t like change. Maybe we are perceived as quite a big company in a small town.”

Five years ago, when asked to consider an appeal against Canterbury city council’s rejection of the company’s plans, a district judge noted that Green – an “able and determined businessman who through force of will and personality drives forward his projects to commercial success” – had “generated some public animosity towards him personally”.

Green and his company had become the “source of tension, even open hostility, with some within the local community”, the judge added.

Stuart Heaver, a Green party councillor in Whitstable who opposes the extension plans for the Forge, said it was an unfortunate side to the dispute. “People are highly protective of the beach, and it’s a maritime town,” he said. “It is a close-knit community and people get very excited when people try to alter things.

“I have met James Green a few times, a perfectly sensible and nice fellow, but there is a history in the town of a little bit of friction between the company and local residents.”

Green remains unabashed. The licensing application failed last time in part due to the scale of opposition to it, including fromWhitstable Yacht Club, which leases the beach from the WOFC to store its boats.

This time the club, after being offered a better lease in return for giving up some space, has said it has no objection. “The Whitstable economy is based on tourism, like it or lump it,” said Green. “In this day and age you have to do things that are going to make it somewhere people want to go.

“To me, it is completely bonkers that it shouldn’t be supported. I am not looking to build flats on the beach – it’s decking and a pergola, for fuck’s sake.”
