Andy Burnham has barely acknowledged the climate crisis. If only Britain’s workers had that luxury

The Guardian Sun, 16 Aug 2026 11:33:42 GMT

Nurses collapsing, builders with heatstroke, bus drivers in cabs that reach 44C. The new PM wanted to spend the summer talking about the cost of living – he should change his plans

I don’t think I have ever written before about a British strike directly related to the climate emergency. But that’s exactly what began late last week in north London, with a zeitgeisty connection to Andy Burnham’s fixation on buses: picket lines outside depots and massed walkouts, while the temperatures in the relevant parts of the capital and its suburbs hovered at about 34C (93F).

Last Friday, more than 1,500 drivers employed by the transport giant Arriva began a planned run of 26 stoppages through to October, affecting bus routes spread between London and Essex. Everything is being led by the union Unite, whose recent grievances include alleged company union-busting and assaults by the public on staff. But the fundamental basis of the dispute is at the heart of the national condition: the near-impossibility for millions of people of working through another insanely hot summer.

Most of Arriva North London’s buses, says Unite, have old-fashioned air cooling systems rather than air conditioning, which means that onboard temperatures have come down by only two or three degrees during this year’s five heatwaves. On other such vehicles, it insists, the air-con is broken. The cabs where drivers sit are essentially compact greenhouses, and can easily reach 40C or higher. And there is another grim twist: union members complain of a shortage of toilets on too many routes, meaning they refrain from drinking water. Unite has been warning about all this since the phases of intense heat that began back in May; its members, the union says, have experienced “heat exhaustion, heatstroke and dehydration”.

Arriva’s last financial figures showed a pre-tax profit of £133m. The company insists that it has “introduced short-term measures to protect drivers”, and is now also spending money on “longer-term fixes, including cab air-conditioning upgrades and our ongoing investment in new fleet”. But the root of its current problems seem clear. There is a longstanding failure, which runs across the UK’s public and private sectors – and also transcends national boundaries – to understand the mounting everyday effects of global heating, and to engage in what so many 21st-century companies and institutions remain so bad at: protective investment, with both eyes fixed not just on the searing inevitabilities of the future, but realities that are already here.

Arriva places tight restrictions on its drivers talking to the media, so Unite pointed me instead to Mo, who has worked for another London bus operator for over 15 years, and had come to a picket line to show the strikers his support. “When it’s very hot, it’s very difficult to concentrate,” he told me. “Imagine the heat you feel when you put your hand near an oven. That’s what it’s like.” What, I wondered, had happened when these problems were raised with management? “Sometimes, we don’t want to raise this stuff, because they don’t want to hear it. If you say, ‘I’ve got a hot cab, I want to come out,’ they’re like, ‘Well, we’re going to lose mileage; we’re going to get penalised by TfL [Transport for London].’ I know the mayor’s put the message out” – in June, Sadiq Khan said he was committed to improving working conditions for drivers – “but the company says, ‘He doesn’t employ you. We do.’”

There are no end of similarly unsettling reports from other occupations. The Royal College of Nursing says some of its members working in the health service have recently collapsed, while others have reported dizziness, nausea and dripping with sweat “from head to toe”, along with profound concerns about NHS patients’ most basic welfare. Recent research into the building trade from the University of Reading showed that 44% of the construction workers it contacted had experienced a heat-related illness, such as heatstroke, heat exhaustion or dehydration. Moreover, 57% said they had received no compulsory training on how to deal with heat.

Almost exactly a year ago, I wrote about the tragic story of Montse Aguilar, a 51-year-old woman who worked as a street cleaner in Barcelona, and returned home from a working day in which the city’s temperatures had reached 35C, only to collapse, hit her head and die. Soon after, people marched carrying banners that read “Extreme heat is also workplace violence”, and street cleaners demanded better summer workwear and more breaks. Much to her family’s distress, the city council has still not recognised her death as a workplace accident, and there has yet to be an autopsy.

This year, Barcelona’s authorities handed out about 1,400 bracelets for staff working outdoors – including street cleaners, park workers and refuse specialists – which measure workers’ body temperatures and go into alert mode if they sense that the wearer is at risk: as and when that happens, the person concerned has to stop working. But despite Spain’s reputation for comparatively stringent heat regulations, unions continue to draw attention to a supposed system of protection still full of gaps. Late last month, the CGT union filed official complaints with Barcelona’s labour inspectorate about what it deems deficient management of those wristbands, a lack of air-con in working vehicles and pledges from the city council being applied “late and halfway”.

Across the world, every hot season inevitably brings more victims. In the US, official figures suggest that more than 550 workers die annually from heat exposure across the country. One recent story is that of Umeshkumar Thakkar, a 58-year-old postal worker who lived in Little Elm, Texas – who, though the cause of his death has yet to be officially established, has been cited as the third such employee in three years to die in the Dallas area amid extreme heat. Amazingly, Texas has barred its cities and counties from passing local heat protections – while, to quote the New York Times, “The Trump administration is moving to rewrite Biden-era rules that would mandate breaks and access to water and shade for workers.” Hydration, it seems, is that bit too woke.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more

after newsletter promotion

The UK’s position, it is a relief to say, is not nearly as dreadful, though there is still much work to do. For people working indoors, official guidance suggests a minimum temperature of 16C, which falls to 13C for “physical work”, but there are no maximum temperatures for either indoor or outdoor labour. Things do finally seem to be moving: last month, the Department for Work and Pensions said that the Health and Safety Executive will soon launch a public consultation on improvements to safety-at-work rules that will cover levels of heat at work. There again, the official line from the prime minister’s spokesperson sounds bleak: “We have no plans to introduce a mandatory maximum workplace temperature.”

In the wake of the Green MP Hannah Spencer’s private member’s bill to establish exactly that, Unite is loudly making the case – as are the TUC and the independent advisory Climate Change Committee, which wants employers to “ensure that workplaces and working practices are safe for employees, including for those working outside”. Meanwhile, having planned for a late summer talking about the cost of living, Burnham did not mention the climate crisis until last Friday, in a country where brown fields are so starved of water they are now turning a scorched yellow, homes have been engulfed by wildfires, and far too many workers are finding the once-simple business of earning a living physically impossible. Like many people – including, I would imagine, plenty of those north London bus drivers – my guarded optimism about the new prime minister and his government endures. But the last of those issues needs as much urgent action as the others, before another boiling summer takes an even grimmer toll.

John Harris is a Guardian columnist

Burnham urged to crack down on gig economy firms to protect 4m workers

The Guardian Sun, 16 Aug 2026 11:29:41 GMT

Exclusive: Campaigners say millions are missing out on key rights including sick pay and protection against unfair dismissal

Andy Burnham is being urged to protect 4 million gig economy workers by prosecuting companies that use widespread “bogus” self-employment practices to deny people their rights.

As the prime minister fleshes out his agenda, the Fabian Society and the Joseph Rowntree Foundation have warned that millions of workers are missing out on key statutory rights including parental leave, redundancy pay and protection against unfair dismissal.

Publishing a joint report calling on Burnham to take action, the Labour-linked thinktank and the anti-poverty charity said changes were essential to make work pay amid the cost of living crisis.

The report calls on the government’s Fair Work Agency – launched in April as a powerful watchdog for workers’ rights – to use its civil proceedings powers to prosecute companies suspected of engaging in “widespread bogus self-employment”.

It also urges ministers to push ahead with changes to employment law to combat longstanding misuse of the system.

Britain’s employment laws are unusual among leading economies for including three classifications of employment status. An employee has the most rights and responsibilities, while a self-employed person has limited protections but fewer obligations. There is also an intermediate “worker”, or “limb (b)” status, with fewer rights and obligations than a full employee.

According to the report, as many as 4 million workers – including hairdressers, personal trainers, delivery workers and drivers for gig economy platforms – work in this gap. Experts say many have been hired by gig economy companies in this way to avoid granting them employment rights.

Labour had promised to create a single “worker” status for all but the genuinely self-employed, before rowing back on the plan to fend off Conservative attacks on its approach to business before the 2024 general election.

Once in power, the policy was not included in Labour’s shake-up of employment rights, and though it promised to consult on “moving towards a single status of worker”, this has not materialised.

Labour faces intense lobbying from business over its sweeping Employment Rights Act, which includes a ban on exploitative zero-hours contracts and day-one rights to statutory sick pay.

Last week, official government analysis showed the planned changes would help to support economic growth and offer workers more protections, though they would cost businesses an estimated £350m to £2.9bn.

In his first week in office, Burnham spoke to business leaders to state his determination to push ahead with the plan for the biggest shake-up of employment rights in a generation.

However, the Fabian Society and Joseph Rowntree Foundation said changes to address employment status were needed to ensure gig economy workers would benefit from these upgraded protections.

The report calls for the burden of proof for whether someone is an employee, worker or self-employed to be shifted from the worker to the employer. This would help people to avoid fighting lengthy legal battles to secure basic rights such as the minimum wage and holiday pay.

Luke Raikes, the deputy general secretary of the Fabian Society, said: “The government must ensure those who play fast and loose with employment law can’t undercut the majority of good employers who play by the rules.

“If it looks like employment then employers should be treating people as employees by default and should expect enforcement action if they aren’t complying. Insecure workers should not have to take on a company’s lawyers – sometimes all the way to the supreme court – just to establish the basic rights they are owed.”

A government spokesperson said: “Our plan to make work pay will boost secure employment, improve job security and deliver stronger, higher living standards. The Fair Work Agency is already helping workers get the rights they are entitled to. We’ve committed to consult on employment status and will consider how the Fair Work Agency can use its civil proceedings power alongside that.”

Man under threat of deportation to Jamaica wins right to rejoin his British family

The Guardian Sun, 16 Aug 2026 11:27:22 GMT

Mark Nelson released from immigration detention on bail after lawyers challenge decision to remove him

A Jamaican man who has lived more than half his life in the UK and was facing imminent deportation has been allowed to reunite with his British family after a legal challenge.

Mark Nelson, 47, came to the UK in 2000 and later set up his own car-mechanic business. He has five British children and a British partner. He faced deportation in 2022 after serving a four-year prison sentence for possession with intent to supply a class B drug, abstracting electricity and two offences of racially aggravated intentional harassment. He had not committed any further offences.

The deportation was later cancelled and instead he was tagged and told to report weekly at a Home Office centre. But last month – almost 10 years after his original conviction – Nelson was arrested, detained and told that the government again planned to deport him to Jamaica.

The Home Office gave him a ticket for a flight on 7 August, but after reading about his case in the Guardian, lawyers offered to represent him pro bono to challenge his deportation.

After they made an 11th-hour application for a judicial review the Home Office backed down on the deportation and cancelled his ticket. This week he was granted bail and can return to the home he shares with his partner, Rachel Derbyshire, in the north of England and see his children again.

Nelson said he was overjoyed to to have left the immigration detention centre near Heathrow where he had spent several weeks in hot and crowded conditions.

“I’ve spoken to my kids, my partner and my brother,” he said. “Everyone is so excited about my release. If it hadn’t been for the lawyers who got in touch after reading the Guardian article I would be back in Jamaica by now, separated from my family, not knowing when I would see them again.

“I have no family members there and believe my life would be at risk.”

Naga Kandiah of MTC Solicitors, who contacted Nelson after reading about his case, lodged the judicial review application. He has also lodged an appeal relating to his immigration case in the first-tier tribunal and a referral has been made for him to the national referral mechanism as a potential victim of modern slavery.

Kandiah said: “He committed his offences in 2017 and served his sentence. Yet nearly a decade later he continues to endure the threat of deportation, with the devastating possibility that he could be permanently torn away from his British children and partner. A prison sentence should not become a life sentence by another name.

“Vulnerable people can struggle to secure legal representation when they need it most. When a person facing removal cannot access timely legal advice, the risk is that the Home Office can remove them before their case has been properly scrutinised.”

Nelson wrote an opinion piece for the Guardian in 2022 about being under threat of deportation. He said Jamaica was a place where he no longer knew anyone after his great-grandparents, who brought him up there, died when he was 16.

A Home Office spokesperson said: “All foreign national offenders who receive a prison sentence in the UK are referred for deportation at the earliest opportunity.

“We have removed or deported almost 70,000 people who were here illegally since the last election, an increase of 41%.”

Dining across the divide: ‘At one point she said, “I don’t want to offend you, but you seem quite privileged”’

The Guardian Sun, 16 Aug 2026 11:00:24 GMT

A trainee accountant and a company director had differing views on opportunities for young people, but could they find common ground on the new prime minister? Want to meet someone from across the divide? Click here to find out how

Occupation Trainee accountant and part-time arts producer

Voting record Green in the past and is now a Labour member

Amuse bouche In 2024 she was president of the Cambridge Footlights student comedy society

Occupation Director of a healthcare services company and part-time blogger on health and urban planning

Voting record Democrat when she was in the US, Conservative in the UK

Amuse bouche She is very into the River Thames. She rows and swims in it, and regularly spots seals and egrets

Clare I was really looking forward to it. We clicked on the fact that we both love the idea of dining across the divide.

Margaret I was a bit nervous, as all I knew about her was that she was a “Kemi [Badenoch] fan”. I know Conservatives, but don’t know anyone who would say that about themselves. But I found it really interesting hearing someone voice those opinions, and we agreed on a lot.

Clare I had a watermelon carpaccio, mint and feta salad, then mussels with chips and, for dessert, a peach sorbet with chantilly. It was very nice.

Margaret I’m vegan, so my options were limited. I had a mock sushi dish made from watermelon, and some fries, then a divine blackcurrant sorbet. We shared a bottle of orange wine.

Clare I think Kemi Badenoch is very courageous, focused and honest. Her party’s been decimated and is facing some of the biggest challenges they’ve ever had. It’s brave of her to take the role and stick to her convictions.

Margaret I think Kemi Badenoch is a contrarian. When she said the UK should support the US and Israel in the conflict in Iran, I felt it was “let’s just go to the other side of what the government is saying”.

Clare She seemed genuinely excited about Andy Burnham coming into leadership. Believe it or not, I feel positive about that, too. I’m not a basher; I’m always an optimist.

Margaret I think she was more excited about Burnham than I was, which surprised me. It’s great to have someone who’s making the left and centrists so excited, but I’m always cautious when I feel myself getting excited about a political figure. I was a teenager in very left-leaning Liverpool when Jeremy Corbyn was the leader of the Labour party and it was almost a cultish fever. But I don’t know if he would have been a good leader, on reflection.

Clare Being involved with the Conservative party, I never really felt any discrimination as a woman. But you look at data and see that women earn less than men, so clearly women face discrimination.

Margaret I would have thought that someone who had Clare’s level of success, and especially someone with her political stance, might think women have an easier time, but we talked about how so many of the core features of our society were built by men, for men. Women are getting into those spaces now, and some might see that as positive discrimination – but that’s not such a bad thing.

Clare The situation young people are in, particularly with housing, is awful. She lives in a warehouse with a couple of people. She says it’s a lovely warehouse and a great setup, but I campaign actively for more housing.

Margaret For me it’s less about housing and more about opportunities for young people. At one point she said, “I don’t want to offend you, but you do seem to be quite privileged.” I wasn’t offended, but I do disagree. Being from Liverpool and ambitious, I had to work very, very hard to get down to London as it’s where all the opportunities seem to be.

Clare it’s getting harder to meet someone with a different view – especially if you’re 22 and you’ve grown up online. So my takeaway is that everybody should do this. There is common ground in everything.

Margaret Clare came from the US as a Democrat and then aligned with the Conservatives, and there can be an ingrained dismissiveness of someone like that. But I really enjoyed speaking to her. There are so many different kinds of people in the world, and most are wonderful and well-meaning when you actually get down to it.

Additional reporting: Kitty Drake

Clare and Margaret ate at The Bull and Last, London NW5

‘I don’t always go full banana!’ From the yellow man to a playful shrink, stylish people on what they wear every day – and why

The Guardian Sun, 16 Aug 2026 11:00:23 GMT

How does a rabbi choose her shoes? Why does a psychoanalyst like slogan tees? And why does a doctor avoid wearing scrubs at work? Seven striking dressers share their surprising style stories

Andrew Geldart, 65, retired engineer, Cornwall

For 30 years as a civil engineer I wore conventional grey and navy, then I retired at 55, moved down to Bude in Cornwall with my wife, Lynn, and the sun came out. Bude is a positive place, where you can be yourself. Everyone is friendly; it’s paradise.

I first started down the yellow route 10 years ago when we moved to Bude with a camper van called Primrose. People gave me yellow accessories for it and the seed was sown – I thought I might wear yellow myself. Now it’s a mainstay of my wardrobe. I wear it practically every day. I have everything from yellow caps to yellow shoes. I prefer sunflower yellow rather than mustard tones: it’s bright and cheerful.

I don’t always go “full banana”! I dress according to the situation. I wouldn’t wear yellow to a Remembrance Day parade, but I would to a funeral of a friend, as I’m known for wearing it and I would be honouring them. If I want to go under the radar, I wear beige. I’m a church leader and help run the food bank: usually people know me there and adjust their behaviour accordingly, but when they don’t recognise me because I’m not in yellow, I can blend into the background and hear what the community really want.

There are practical benefits. My grandchildren can easily spot me in a crowd. In fact, they walk past me if I’m not wearing yellow, and ask: “Where’s Pops?” But the main reason I choose to stand out is to connect with people, to show that I am friendly and approachable, even if I’m not smiling.

Someone says, “I like your glasses”, nearly every day (I have a jazzy, stripy, bright yellow summer pair and a more muted, translucent yellow winter pair), and that opens the door to a conversation. There are so many isolated people looking down at their phones, and if I can encourage someone to talk, I’m happy. I want to spread a bit of love in the world and to show that it’s safe to say how you really are, to get past just “Good morning”. A coffee and a chat can be a little glimpse of sunshine.

I have toyed with changing to red or green, and that would be a new conversation – “What happened? Why aren’t you wearing yellow?” It’s a colour that works for me, but never say never: men’s fashion is quite limited when it comes to yellow, so I may be forced to change to another bright colour one day.

Sometimes the old conventional and staid engineer part of me thinks, “Can I get away with this? Is this too much?” But I saw a picture of the late David Hockney in his yellow glasses recently and thought, “Maybe I’m not ridiculous.” I want to give people the courage to step outside the box – let’s make life enjoyable.

As told to Emily Cunningham

Anouchka Grose, 56, psychoanalyst, London

I don’t want to dress too conservatively as I don’t want to look like an authority figure, or like someone who believes that “analytic neutrality” – the idea that the therapist is a blank slate – means some kind of John Lewis cosplay. “Neutrality” can’t mean aligning with a dominant norm – psychotherapists need to be critical thinkers. But what I wear also can’t be so unusual that the client is distracted. Overall, I’m aiming for a kind of quiet surrealism – a balance between comfortable, pleasurable and characterful.

So I have a vague uniform of a genderless jumper or jacket – a strict-looking black jacket with pointy shoulders, say – with a man’s shirt or T-shirt, big trousers (I’m currently loving a stripy pair from Maison Margiela I found on eBay) and ugly shoes, usually Uggs I buy secondhand. Most things are outsized, or loose.

Very often my T-shirts will have a slogan – my favourite is “Dress for the male gays”. It references Laura Mulvey’s theory that there could be a male gaze that things are constructed around, which was one of the first ways into psychoanalysis for me. But it’s also a funny wordplay referencing the post-Freudians, who thought of homosexuality as a kind of sickness to cure. I see that T-shirt as a sort of apology for the past homophobia of psychoanalysis. Plus it makes clients laugh, which is allowed. (Freud took jokes extremely seriously.)

Subverting the expectations of how a shrink ought to dress has been a real theme for me. A patient once asked me: “Are you allowed to wear those trousers to work?” They were balloonish red and white checked ones. And sometimes when I’ve given papers at analytic conferences, the other shrinks will be, like, “Yeah, but what do you wear for work?” (It is no different from what I am wearing at the conference.)

I’ve always loved clothes and the way they transmit meaning. I love the crazy semiotics of them – communicating social signals to other people who know those signals. That seems very psychoanalytic to me.

They always say that as a psychoanalyst you get the patients you deserve. I really like that idea. There have been some people I frightened away because of how I looked, and that’s good.

Maybe that’s why I don’t spend too long worrying how people will perceive me. Psychoanalysis teaches you that associations are fractured and kaleidoscopic. So you can’t really control the meanings that other people make; any garment could mean anything to anyone.

Annastasia, 62, author, Devon

What I wear is an integral aspect of my identity. I am what I wear, and what I wear is secondhand, sometimes reproduction, clothing that dates between the 1920s and about 1966. It stops there because I think the mid‑60s is when life started to change from being a very ordered, slow society to something else. I was born in 1964, so I’ve pretty much lived in the something else period; I’ve always rejected the current timeline I live in.

Seeing The Wizard of Oz when I was four was the starting point. I was born into a poor, working-class family, and everything seemed really grey. That film, with its heightened colours, fired my imagination as to what clothing – and the world – could look like. Then, when I was about six, a friend of my mother’s dropped round a pile of what she thought were dressing-up clothes – 50s ball gowns and cocktail dresses. When I put them on, I felt completely myself, which I didn’t in the functional, ubiquitous clothes of the day. I saw then that getting dressed could become a creative thing. At 12, I began dressing like this. Now, every day the first creative choices I make are what to wear. It’s ritualistic.

My love of vintage clothing is an outward rejection of advanced capitalism and the tyranny of its desperate buy, buy, buy culture, which results in so much clothing being sent to landfill. I like colours that are more muted, which you get in vintage fabrics. The last thing I would buy as a winter coat would be a puffer jacket that makes you look like a caterpillar. It would be wool, 1950s, cinched in.

Through my clothing, I am expressing that attire can be inexpensive, ethical, well made and, to me, aesthetically pleasing. I like the values of vintage clothing: care, attention, consideration and slowness. But that isn’t to say that I’m about nostalgia or traditional values. I would hate anyone to think I was espousing tradwife values via the way I dress. Quite honestly, in my 60s, I can dress the way I want to.

I have faced criticism for what I wear. When I was working alongside women and girls in Birmingham in the 70s and 80s, feminist organisations used to be very judgmental towards me. It was as if I had to prove my credentials more than other women because I wasn’t wearing jeans and Dr Martens. By contrast, the people I visited as part of the community outreach I was doing used to say how impressed they were that I had made such an effort to dress nicely for them.

I now write time-slip fiction – where present-day characters get entangled with those from the past – under the pen name Pearl Fane. The pivotal character lives in England in the 50s. It’s so useful because I can relate to how she might have experienced the world by how clothing felt on her.

People are surprised I dress like this every day – but I wouldn’t know any other way of being.

Arielle Stein, 35, rabbi, New York

I have been figuring out my style for a long time. I started out as a visual artist; now I’m a congregational rabbi, and I’ve been working to meld the more formal with the more alternative. The result is a quirky mix of some business-casual, some downtown hipster, and then truly random things that delight me.

Style has always been a way to communicate my identity; I think of it as a form of storytelling. As a rabbi, there are definitely norms around how you should present. But I think being on the younger side, and a woman, freed me from a lot of that; no matter what, I wasn’t going to look like the traditional model. Plus, I deeply love to subvert a norm: for me it’s about adding to the mosaic of what’s possible.

I have a role in a lot of important life-cycle moments and I think it’s vital I don’t take centre stage. But people are drawn to me either on an artistic or creative level, or on a peer level. So the style element is important.

Our generation has had a lot of struggles connecting to religion and spirituality, and I think for people to meet a rabbi who looks like them definitely creates a sense of comfort. My style often functions as an invitation: I get a lot of emails that start with something about style and then get into something that person has wanted to talk about and hasn’t yet found a way that felt comfortable to them.

There are a few occasions when I have more of a uniform. At the synagogue I work at, we’re a pretty traditional Reform congregation, and so we all wear a mandated robe on Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur. But, at the same time, because we are a progressive denomination, we all select our own shoes.

Shoes in general are a nice way of bringing that alternative personal flavour. I like to coordinate mine with the 12 Hebrew months: for instance, wearing low-key Birkenstocks for the contemplative month of Tammuz; freaky jelly sandals for Adar, which is the month of Purim and the craziest time of the year; and Vibram five-toed Mary Janes for Nisan, the month of exodus and the Passover story, as they’d be perfect for getting through the desert. In fact, I wear different shoes for each night of Passover, from studded Madewell mules on night five, when I’m thinking about plagues and boils, to blood-red Tory Burch mules on night six, when I’m thinking about the Passover sacrifice.

We often get stuck in an idea that Judaism is one way or one thing only, and that’s exceedingly not true. I think we’re living in a visual culture right now, so this type of representation helps people remember that. It creates an opportunity for people to come as they are and to feel as if they can be Jewish in a way that feels authentic to them.

Key for me is showing the Jewish community and the world that multiplicity is a deep part of who we are, and caring about style doesn’t mean that you don’t have a place in the Jewish world.

Dr Bhasha Mukherjee, 30, GP, London

There aren’t really any rules for how to dress as a GP. One of my first bosses used to wear a full suit, and another would dress in a band T-shirt and jeans. I think you can take those liberties when you have been around long enough and developed a relationship with patients.

I tend to wear something that is a cross between expressing how I’m feeling and being comfortable. I exercise every day, so part of my outfit is usually sportswear, but it’s a little bit glam, a little bit sexy, and I might wear it under a blazer. I love wearing a blazer; it’s power dressing. But it’s not going to be a boring black blazer. It’s going to be patterned, maybe even fuchsia pink. I love colour – dopamine dressing is a core theme for me.

Jewellery is also important – I’ve got autism and ADHD, and I use it as a tactile, fidgeting thing. I will fidget with my necklace as I’m talking to patients because it helps me stay focused on what they’re saying.

There’s evidence for trust levels in doctors being dependent on what they wear. But it’s not always simple. I remember one day I turned up in scrubs and my boss was, like, “Don’t be looking so scruffy at work.” I think Covid changed scrubs. They were definitely a dress code during the pandemic – they became the norm – but since then they have been hijacked by non-medical people on social media, a status symbol for influencers trying to gain the public’s trust. It confuses patients. I don’t need scrubs and a stethoscope to showcase my professionalism. Plus, I like to express myself more – I feel as if that’s more welcoming to patients, anyway.

A part of me likes being a rebel. All through medical school, as a woman, I got shamed for wearing certain things at work. I would get called out by female colleagues who said my lipstick shade was too dark and unprofessional. Now I don’t feel like anybody can tell me that. I grew up consuming fashion magazines in the 00s – I do not walk out of the house without lipstick on.

One thing I won’t wear in a professional setting is Indian dress. When I dress in that way I’m very maximalist and I will wear the full outfit: the sari, the head jewellery, neck jewellery. I can’t pare it back, so I’ve never dressed that way for work.

Lorenzo Tondo, 44, international correspondent, Sicily

I can pinpoint the exact moment when my obsession with workwear began. It was the winter of 2018 and I was heading to the frozen mountains of Bosnia to cover the refugee crisis. Thousands of Syrian, Iraqi and Afghan refugees were moving along the Balkan route, hoping to reach Europe after weeks of walking through snow, mud and dense forests.

I needed clothes that were practical and forgiving. That was when I remembered a pair of old Carhartt trousers buried in a cupboard. I had worn them heavily in the late 1990s and early 2000s. Wide-cut and designed to take a beating, they were faded now, tighter than I remembered, but still comfortable. I decided to take them with me. I needed trousers I wouldn’t mourn if they ended the day soaked through, caked in mud or torn. Their approachability was a plus, too: I’ve reported on the war in Ukraine, in the occupied West Bank and in Syria for the last six years and know that a blazer, however well intentioned, can quietly reinforce distance.

Ever since then, I’ve hunted down loose-fitting vintage pieces: early-90s Carhartt jackets and at least three pairs of wide-leg trousers not unlike the ones I used to skate in as a teenager. I have worn them on the frontlines of the war in Ukraine, in cities flattened by the earthquake in Turkey, and amid the chalky dust of Idlib, in rebel-held north-west Syria. But also at home in Italy: for shopping, or heading out for a day trip with my children, or going out for dinner with friends.

This was the style I had grown up with in the 90s, in a small town on the south-western coast of Sicily. Grunge originated in the Pacific north-west of America – a place of rain and lumber towns. I might have belonged to a very different community nearly 10,000km away, but I felt a shared sense of values. In my town, people dressed in Dolce & Gabbana and Gucci on Sundays. Wearing old clothes felt like a form of quiet, necessary rebellion against the superficial aesthetics of luxury fashion.

As I got older, I started drifting towards something more conventional. Then grunge came back into fashion, along with the bands I used to listen: Pearl Jam, Nirvana and Rage Against the Machine. Call it Peter Pan syndrome if you like, but slim jeans, tidy knitwear and carefully tailored coats have never felt like home. Grunge is a style that helps me feel rooted, wherever I am. Last year, I attended a press conference that the Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, was giving in Jerusalem. Most people were in suits and ties. I was wearing baggy, faded jeans and a loose beige shirt. Being one of the only people dressed differently brought back that feeling of rebellion that had fuelled my youth. Lorenzo Tondo

Lucy Edwards, 30, disability activist, near Birmingham

What I wear has changed a lot over the years. I lost my eyesight nearly 14 years ago – the sight in my right eye at 11 and left eye at 17. I don’t wear the clothes “sighted Lucy” used to wear – I’ve come so far and if I were to dress as her that would be weird. Sighted Lucy had a lot of internalised ableism. She wore things that might have made her feel amazing because she looked in the mirror – they were a lot more skin-tight – and now blind Lucy prioritises things that are flowy and tactile. It’s been a long journey to get here.

I feel happiest when I feel the most comfy, which isn’t necessarily what looks the best, and I’m OK with that. I had this little voice in my head for so long, saying, “A sighted person has to tell you whether it looks good, whether it flatters your body”. Whereas now what I wear is just what I feel the best in, and often that is sequins, feathers, velour, silk – things that feel nice.

When I was planning my wedding, all the girls in my life came down and watched me try on dresses, but it was really important that I put the dress on alone first and asked myself, “Do I want to show this to my family? Do I want their sighted opinion, or do I just want my opinion here?” So that was a big part of me choosing. The dress I picked was so lovely that I didn’t have to have that visual affirmation – I knew in myself it was right. Although I did love their reaction when I came out in it.

I do still ask my sighted family about colour, and my sister is my mirror when I need one. She has autism, and because her world is black and white she will say directly, “No, you can’t wear that” or “Yes, you can.” That provides so much comfort. Often, if I dress in colour it tends to be the same colour top and bottom, which is why I end up wearing a lot of co-ords.

When it comes to what I wear, my voice has definitely got louder the older I’ve become. My motto is: if they’re gonna look, make them stare. So I make sure to have a glittery harness for my guide dog, Miss Molly, or a glittery cane for me. I also make sure me and Miss Molly match. I see it as part of my activism. For so long I hated being a guide-dog user. But now I’m, like, “No, Lucy, that is so much internalised ableism, absolutely effing not.”

I get dressed more for myself now than ever. I still wear heels, which surprises some people. I’m less likely to go for stilettos, but if I do I just change my cane height to match. I put on makeup and get dressed. People will ask why, given it’s so visual. But I’m seeing the non‑visual elements of it. It’s a ritual and it grounds me. What I wear has to feel happy. Getting dressed now is freeing – I can just be myself.

Destroyed crops, riverbed cyclists and a ‘Rock of Starvation’: how drought has devastated the Danube

The Guardian Sun, 16 Aug 2026 10:37:30 GMT

The Guardian travelled 100 miles along the EU’s longest river, where some residents are struggling to secure drinking water

For centuries, the rock was seen as a warning. When it began to emerge from the Danube, beneath Gellért Hill in Budapest, it meant the river had fallen so low that floating mills could no longer operate, crops were probably failing, and hunger would almost certainly follow. That is why, in the Hungarian capital, where over time the boulder became little more than a legend, it was named Ínség-szikla – the Rock of Starvation.

Today, amid record-low water levels on the Danube, the rock has not only emerged from the water, but surfaced almost in its entirety, along with the sandy riverbed on which it rests, astonishing geologists and government scientists sent to examine it. And, much as the rock was said to warn, Hungary is now facing an unprecedented energy crisis that has forced the country to shut down all but one of its Danube-cooled nuclear reactors for the first time in 44 years.

The Guardian travelled for more than 100 miles (160km) along the banks of the Danube, the EU’s longest river, which sustains the 10 countries it crosses, visiting villages and towns where residents are struggling to secure drinking water and farmers are fighting to keep their crops alive.

Last week, the Hungarian prime minister, Péter Magyar, warned that the economic damage caused by this year’s drought was expected to surpass that of the historic dry spell that devastated Hungary’s farmland in 2022.

While the full extent of the losses is still difficult to assess, István Somogyi, a 56-year-old farmer from Pócsmegyer, a village on the Danube, in Pest County, has already done his calculations.

“I’ve lost nearly 50% of my harvest this year and it could go up to 70%,” he said. “It’s gone. Everything has dried up. Since I started farming this land after the end of communist rule, I’ve never seen a catastrophe like this.”

Somogyi said the unprecedented crisis did not come out of nowhere, and that the heatwaves and droughts of previous years had already offered a warning. Scientists say that human-caused climate breakdown is making every heatwave in the world more intense and more likely to happen.

“You could see this coming,” he said. “The harvest was already poor last year. But we were lucky because the Danube stayed high. Despite the intense heat, there was still enough water in the soil. This time, there is no hope of saving our crops.”

On the near-deserted roads running alongside the river, families with children sought relief in the Danube’s shallow waters, while, not far away, military water tankers were siphoning water from rural wells, hauling vital supplies to the storage pools that feed the local grid.

Across the river from Pócsmegyer, on the opposite bank of the Danube, lies Szentendre, a town known for its community of artists. During the most intense days of the heatwave, some evening performances have been held by candlelight in an effort to reduce electricity consumption.

Here, in recent weeks, vast, desert-like islands have emerged. The exposed riverbed is cracked like a mosaic of hard, dry clay, baked by suffocating heat that has pushed temperatures in Budapest close to 42C, with overnight temperatures hitting a high of 28C. Europe is warming faster than any other continent, with intense summer heat and prolonged drought being amplified by the deepening human-caused climate crisis. Extreme conditions continue to fuel wildfires and strain water supplies.

In some stretches of the Danube near Szentendre, it is now possible to walk through it with the water barely reaching above your ankles.

“Swimming and navigation are banned here,” said László Balázs, 44, head of the local river rescue service. “But people escaping the heat still enter the water, unaware it can suddenly drop into deep pools where they risk drowning.”

At the end of June, Budapest police (BRFK) said three people had gone missing in the Danube over a single weekend. Water police later recovered one body near Iváncsa, while searches continued downstream for the other two missing swimmers.

The drought and resulting disruption to energy supplies have also left some Hungarian towns struggling with shortages of drinking water. In a room inside Szentendre’s tourist information office, thousands of bottles of water are stored ready to be distributed, particularly to elderly and vulnerable residents.

“About 4,000 to 5,000 households were left without water,” said József Gulyás, 62, Szentendre’s deputy mayor. “We distributed 25 tonnes of water and received about 100 emergency calls a day. We had never experienced anything so serious. Elderly women would hug the officers delivering water and burst into tears.”

Driving from north to south, towards the Hungarian capital, Budapest, where the level of the Danube under normal conditions reaches an average height of 2 to 3 metres, and can rise as high as 8 metres, intense summer heat and continuing drought conditions caused the river to fall to a record low of just 14-19 cm on 4 August.

The water levels have fallen so dramatically that, as the Danube has retreated, it has revealed a succession of relics long hidden beneath its waters, including the remains of a woolly mammoth, a bridge destroyed after the second world war in Budapest, a Nazi warship and an unexploded British bomb.

The water is so low in the capital that on 28 July, at about 4.30pm, Gábor Kürti, president of the Magyar Kerékpárosklub (Hungarian cyclists’ club) and owner of a cargo bike company, left his office in central Budapest, jumped on his bicycle and, in an unprecedented feat, rode for 30km along the exposed bed of the Danube, with his journey quickly going viral on social media.

“I wanted to show that if you can cycle along the bed of the Danube for 30km, it means that, because of this climate emergency, we have literally hit rock bottom,” he told the Guardian.

Riding his KTM X-Strada 20 gravel bike, Kürti set off from the mouth of the Szilas stream (Szilas-patak) and made his way across fine gravel, large pebbles, hard-packed sand and mud, eventually reaching the ferry terminal at Vác about three hours later.

“For many people it was an extraordinary adventure. For me, it was heartbreaking,” he said. “Cycling through parts of the river where, as a child, I used to swim or go kayaking, and which I could now cross on a bicycle, filled me with an indescribable sadness. It was like looking at the scene of a terrible accident. Throughout that journey, the scale of the catastrophe was unfolding before my eyes.”

Kürti took the Guardian into what, until only a few months ago, was the striking floodplain forest in Nagytétény named Kis-Háros-sziget, a protected area home to climbing plants, wild vines and several families of European beavers.

The river is reached by walking across ground that would normally lie several metres beneath the water. Here, one branch of the Danube has receded so dramatically that it came to an abrupt halt, blocked by an exposed riverbed left behind by the drought.

Its dry, clay-like surface looks like an image from a future shaped by the escalating human-caused climate crisis. Yet this is happening now. Passersby walk across what was once the river, their feet sinking into patches of mud. Kayakers struggle to make their way through the remaining shallow channels; many eventually give up, lift their kayaks on to their shoulders and walk home.

Hungarian authorities have been pumping water into large areas of the country’s nature reserves such as the one in Nagytétény, to keep marshlands from drying out as the drought intensifies.

Continuing south, the road finally reaches Paks, home to Hungary’s nuclear power plant, its towers rising above the horizon. Here, municipal workers have been working weekends to keep more than 700 threatened trees alive and water the town’s flowerbeds.

“I’ve been doing this job for 18 years,” said Szilvia Farkas, 39, who is employed by Dunakom Zrt in Paks, owned entirely by the municipality, to plant and water trees and plants. “I have never seen so much vegetation dry out in all my years doing this job, and I have never worked as hard as I have this year to try to keep it alive.”

Dunakom Zrt uses its own drilled well for water extraction. In addition, the company is able to extract water from a decantation basin. The public is not permitted to use tap water for irrigation at the moment; instead, residents collect greywater and use it to water their gardens.

In the country’s more marginalised and deprived areas, the water crisis has compounded longstanding problems for thousands of people who were already living in difficult conditions before the drought, struggling with inadequate access to running water and sewage systems.

Géza Orsós Renáta, 43, who lives with her four children in a small farmhouse on the outskirts of Paks, has never had access to running water. Orsós, who also works for Dunakom Zrt, helping to water public green spaces drying out in the heat, has long relied on water from a neighbour.

“Even in winter, we have to pump water and heat it in large bowls so we can wash,” she said. “Now a friend brings us water once a week. But it is becoming unbearable.”

Driving back from Paks, tall, swollen clouds occasionally gather on the horizon in the clear skies above Budapest, appearing to promise the return of rain, only to fade by evening, dashing the hopes of an entire country.

For now, people can do little but cling to the hope that the Rock of Starvation will disappear once more beneath the currents of the Danube, returning to the depths of the river and becoming little more than a legend again.

But Somogyi, who grew up hearing the story of the boulder passed down through generations, and who is now witnessing the consequences of the warning it was said to foretell, knows it will not.

“The drought will return next year,” he said. “That is the trend. And there isn’t much that we can do.”

Zsuzsa Borbély contributed to this report

This article was amended on 16 August 2026. An earlier version included a map which placed Croatia in Serbia’s location; this has been corrected.

A positive new report raises the question: was Reeves undermined by dodgy data?

The Guardian Sun, 16 Aug 2026 09:30:05 GMT

Assessment’s finding of a jump in UK productivity emphasises urgent need to appoint a national statistician

The keen new chancellor, John Healey, responded to last week’s better-than-expected economic news by claiming the government was “bringing hope back”. Growth did not plunge as feared after Donald Trump unleashed war on Iran – with GDP expanding at a pretty decent 0.4% in the second quarter.

But what if we should have held on to a bit more hope all along? A new assessment of the UK’s recent productivity suggests this critical measure of the country’s economic strength may have been systematically underestimated.

Instead of stagnation, it points to a “meaningful pickup” in productivity since mid-2024, with annual growth of about 1.6% – up from an average of 0.3% in the previous decade.

This has very much not been the prevailing narrative since Labour came to power. Indeed, Rachel Reeves spent months last year scrambling to respond to a downgrade in productivity projections from the Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR) – from 1.3% annual growth to 1% – with a knock-on effect for the public finances.

Other things being equal, weaker productivity means weaker growth, which broadly translates to lower tax revenues and a bigger public deficit.

The OBR rethink didn’t reflect anything Labour had done, resulting instead from the long-term failure of productivity growth to bounce back after the 2008 global financial crisis. And part of the reason it became so pivotal was because Reeves had left herself so little room for manoeuvre.

But the productivity downgrade contributed to the gloomy sense that Labour was overseeing an economy beset by intractable long-term challenges. And it increased the size of the tax grab Reeves needed to make at last year’s budget to rebuild the headroom against her fiscal rules and pay for Labour’s welfare U-turn.

The new estimates, from the Centre for Economic Performance at the London School of Economics (LSE), where former Reeves advisers John Van Reenen and Anna Valero have now returned to their desks, paint a markedly different picture.

Productivity is defined as how much output each worker produces, but the UK has been botching the job of sizing up the workforce now for several years. The beleaguered Office for National Statistics (ONS) withdrew the status of accredited official statistic from its labour force survey (LFS) in 2024 as it struggled with plunging response rates from consumers.

Instead of using the LFS, which the OBR has to rely on, the LSE co-authors, including Van Reenen and Valero, together with Niki Barbas, use estimates made by the Resolution Foundation thinktank.

Resolution’s approach relies on an alternative dataset published by the ONS, based on what companies tell the tax authorities through the PAYE system (augmented with other sources to account for the self-employed).

The differences are wide. While the LFS records a 377,000 increase in the number of employees since mid-2024, the tax-based measure shows a decline of 133,000.

Of course, depending on what’s happened to those missing workers – retirement, unemployment, sickness, childcare – this may be a different cause for concern. Reeves has been accused of depressing hiring by piling costs on to employers.

But using the smaller estimate for the number of employees suggests that far from flatlining, productivity has jumped. That raises the intriguing possibility that, with better data, the OBR downgrade, and the massive headache it created for the then chancellor, could have been avoided.

Van Reenen says that “the best current guess does suggest we are getting more out of our workers than we used to”.

He dismisses the idea that what has happened is just layoffs among low-skilled workers, pushing up average productivity. “I don’t think that’s the main story: a chunk of this appears to be real.”

It’s too early to say what may be driving an uplift in productivity, let alone whether it will be sustained – but one hypothesis is that AI is starting to bear fruit in some sectors.

“It’s certainly a possibility that we are seeing the first signs of that starting to happen,” Van Reenen says.

Not surprisingly, he points to his former boss Reeves’s policies – including a significant increase in public investment and the stripping back of planning rules – as reasons to hope the improvement could continue.

The latest official GDP figures showed business investment – widely seen as one determinant of productivity – rising strongly, though experts were quick to caution that it could be reversed as high energy prices take their toll.

Whatever the future brings, the wide discrepancy with the official figures underlines how urgent a priority it should have been to fix the gaping holes in the UK’s jobs data earlier, and more effectively.

The poorly resourced ONS has been doggedly developing a new, online version of the LFS. Instead of the cumbersome 40-45 minute phone call needed to complete the existing questionnaire, it takes about 15 minutes.

In an update last week, the ONS acknowledged that the refreshed survey design appeared to be turning up slightly different results – including, for example, lower levels of long-term sickness. It also confirmed that it would be November next year at the earliest before it could switch over to the new version.

The UK has had no national statistician, the head of the ONS, for more than a year since Ian Diamond resigned in May 2025. The vacancy hardly speaks of burning urgency in Whitehall.

Some of Labour’s worst domestic struggles over the past two years, from winter fuel to the welfare row, were self-inflicted. But as Reeves returns to the backbenches this autumn, she could be excused for feeling her challenges at No 11 were exacerbated by dodgy data.

‘I thought – if I die, I’ve had a good innings’: producer James Ford on life, death and making an album from his hospital bed

The Guardian Sun, 16 Aug 2026 09:00:21 GMT

The Arctic Monkeys, Pet Shop Boys and Pulp collaborator was at the height of his powers as Britain’s most in-demand music producer when leukaemia struck. ‘I realised life is exceptionally fragile,’ he says

There was a moment outside the door of a recording studio in rural France, staring at a half-eaten apple that he believed possessed psychedelic properties, when James Ford knew things had really got out of hand. He was stood with Klaxons; all of the band members were hypnotised by this rotting fruit which throbbed on the floor with kaleidoscopic intensity. They were convinced that its blooming mould was in fact their spiritual guru.

The band had been riding the wave of their huge, scene-defining debut album, 2007’s Myths of the Near Future – which was produced by Ford – and were now trying to record the interminably difficult follow-up, aided by daily doses of a concoction they’d taken to calling “the five-star general”.

“It was a huge bag, five drugs mixed together, probably ketamine and speed, I don’t know what else, but it was quite a psychedelic powder and they were doing it every morning and throughout the day,” says Ford. He realised he couldn’t rein things back in. “And after a two-and-a-half-week period … things got fucking weird.”

So weird, in fact, that the head of the UK record label came over on the Eurostar carrying a bell jar at the band’s request, only to find out it was to cover an apple that had been chewed up and spat out by a passing dog and was now being called Mr Tabernacle. Klaxons, it’s fair to say, had lost their minds a little bit. The album was aborted.

“We thought we were making The Dark Side of the Moon,” says Ford with a giggle, now sitting in the studio in his east London home. Instead, that “ill-fated second record” became the only project that Ford has never finished in a career that has since established him as the music industry’s go-to magic weapon.

It is quite the trajectory. Ford went from tearing up 00s dancefloors as one half, alongside Jas Shaw, of Simian Mobile Disco – musicians and DJs who elevated the electro-rave era of the decade – to becoming the most sought-after ear in music. In the last decade, with little in the way of hype, he has quietly become the pre-eminent producer of his generation.

Ford is who you call when you’re trying to make a career-defining album (Arctic Monkeys; Florence + the Machine; Jessie Ware; Fontaines DC), who you trust to realise a stunning comeback (Pulp; Blur; Gorillaz; Depeche Mode) and who you need to help translate critical buzz into commercial success (Geese; The Last Dinner Party; Black Country, New Road).

“It’s a very broad term ‘producer’,” he says, trying to explain his role. “It doesn’t really describe what happens; I’m trying to get to the bottom of someone else’s vision and pull that out there.” Be it Pet Shop Boys or Jessie Ware, artists agree that Ford doesn’t produce in a conventional sense. “I think if you try to imprint your sound, it seems a weird ego-y thing to do, to try to do a Phil Spector on everyone’s record.” And so he doesn’t impose a sound or vibe on to the room so much as mediate, and draw artists in and out of whatever creative pattern they’re in.

At home, surrounded by synths, guitars and all manner of recording equipment, Ford seems relaxed and is softly spoken, with a light touch of the Staffordshire accent he grew up with. The heyday of his hedonism may be behind him, but it’s obvious that he still loves what he does. It is this and a general sense of ease that has earned Ford a level of trust from artists at their most vulnerable. A gracious, nice guy in an industry famously short of decency, it’s easy to understand why the world’s biggest artists are knocking down his door to work with him.

Still, it’s a minor miracle we’re even meeting today. On Christmas Eve 2024 Ford was with his wife and young son at his in-laws’ in Folkestone when he got “hit like a ton of bricks”. He was laid out on the sofa, unable to get up with a fever that wouldn’t break and a flu-like illness that refused to let up. He had worked flat out all year, and in the weeks running up to December had felt unusually fatigued. He wondered whether he was heading for burnout, but this was something entirely new.

He was admitted to the local A&E; his blood tests were “all over the place”. Having travelled to India with Damon Albarn some weeks earlier, doctors initially suspected he had picked up a tropical disease. “There were a lot of red herrings,” he says. “It took ages to get any kind of diagnosis because my bloods had to get sent to London, so I spent weeks in this horrible state, and just felt I was going to die. It was awful.”

Weeks later, on a Friday night, “someone unceremoniously came in and said: ‘We’ve found leukaemia. You need to go to a cancer ward.’” And that was it. If his life had flashed before him, Ford, who had just turned 46, could admit it had been a good one. A great one, even. “I’ve got a wonderful family with my wife and little boy, I’ve got a great relationship with my parents, a good career, I’ve travelled a lot, done a lot of things with a lot of people that I’ve dreamed of working with,” he says. And he has partied hard, I joke, having borne witness to multiple Simian Mobile Disco sets and afterparties. “I’ve partied really hard,” he says. “I’ve had some great times, I’ve got a lot of good memories and I’ve made some things I’m really proud of. I think I’ve been a generally good person in the world. And so I was almost at the point where I was like, if I die, I’ve had a good innings. I wouldn’t be that scared of it.”

Ford was eventually transferred to St Barts hospital in London and pummelled with rounds of drugs. He spent the early weeks of 2025 obliterated by the illness. Then came the second round of chemotherapy, and something of a breakthrough. He asked his wife Sereen, whom he met as a student at Manchester University, to bring in his laptop, an Ikea fold-up table, some synthesisers, a microphone and a guitar to his hospital room. Supported by staff at the hospital, who could see it cheered him up and got him out of bed, Ford began making music. Nurses got used to administering their daily medical care while Ford messed with drumbeats and sang, locked in his creative flow state. In two weeks, Ford wrote and recorded his new album, Lost in Another World, which would be remarkable enough on its own – were it not for the fact that it is also stunning.

Despite being sung and recorded by Ford in a creative jag while contemplating life and death, the record feels like his signature sound – melodic, electronic, art-pop. It’s joyful where you expect it to be bleak. Over the course of nine months, Ford went through two more rounds of chemotherapy, a stem cell transplant, sepsis – three times – and a stay in intensive care. To say it has been an unremittingly traumatic year sells it short, but he – and the album – wear it lightly.

“I don’t know if nervous is the right word,” he says of Lost in Another World’s impending release. “It’s more odd because it takes me back to that moment of being ill. And I’d intentionally left it, but now I’m having to talk about it. At first, even hearing it back for the first time, I was like ‘Ugh!’” I insist we don’t have to talk about the depths of his illness.

“I always felt pretty invincible, though,” says Ford, reflecting on it. “And then suddenly, you’re like: ‘Oh, I’m not.’ And it was that thing: two or three years before this, I started running. I was going to the gym regularly. I was eating well. I’d lost weight, I’d given up drinking, given up all drugs, blah blah, the full cycle. And then I fucking get leukaemia!”

Despite the toll the cancer took, Ford still somehow managed to produce two more major albums when he was really ill. One for Gorillaz, the other for the Mercury prize-nominated War Child album, Help(2), where he was producing the likes of Olivia Rodrigo and Beth Gibbons from his hospital bed. “Remote producing a session [going on] at Abbey Road while having a blood transfusion was not on my 2025 bingo card,” he posted on Instagram at the time.

Ford was not allowed any visitors for long stretches in hospital, Sereen excepted, because his immunity was so shot. “Funnily enough, Jarvis [Cocker] came in when he wasn’t meant to. But he’s so recognised, they were bamboozled and let him in and he’d very sweetly bought me some of his favourite books and wrote little things in them of what he liked and stuff. It was wonderful but I was a bit: ‘Wow, OK!’”

Mentally at least, music saved him. “It was amazing to have something to focus on that made me feel good, to get into that zone where I shut down everything else on the outside. The lyrics [for Lost in Another World] literally just fell out. Obviously I had a bunch of stuff to process, but it was the easiest music-making process I’ve ever had.”

How is he doing now? “I’m still not fully out of it.” Ford will have his bloods closely monitored for the next few years and attend regular checkups to track whether the cancer comes back. For now, he is gearing up for a number of live shows following the album’s arrival into the world and rehearsals are under way.

“The obvious thing that has come out of all of this is that it does make you recognise what and who the important things in your life are and that life is exceptionally fragile,” he says of his renewed work-life balance. “Not to spend any time with people who aren’t worth spending time with and on projects that aren’t worth spending time on. Just being really selective and intentional about every choice you make. And that can be as simple as ‘spend more time in nature’, ‘spend more time with my family’, ‘maybe not work so hard’.”

He smiles at the last one. “None of that is particularly groundbreaking. It’s stuff you see every day on the internet, but it’s different when you live through it. I definitely had read about the value of gratitude and all of those things, but I could never really take it on board in a way that I have now.”

Lost in Another World by James Ellis Ford is out now; he plays Rough Trade East, London, 17 August; and the Horse Hospital, London, 17 September.

King Charles and Prince William face £10m energy upgrade bill for estates

The Guardian Sun, 16 Aug 2026 09:00:21 GMT

New rules could affect nine in 10 rental properties in duchies of Cornwall and Lancaster and at Sandringham

King Charles and Prince William could be forced to spend up to £10m upgrading hundreds of rental properties on their private estates to meet planned energy-efficiency rules.

The government has announced that landlords will need to ensure their properties have energy performance certificate (EPC) ratings of C or higher by 2030 – up from the current requirement of an E.

EPCs are documents that provide an energy-efficiency score for properties, in relation to their running costs.

Introduced in 2007 amid growing concern about carbon emissions, they help to estimate energy bills and environmental impact. The most energy-efficient properties are awarded an A rating, and the worst are given a G rating.

A Guardian investigation has found that almost nine in 10 domestic properties on the duchies of Cornwall and Lancaster and the Sandringham estate have had EPC ratings of D or lower.

Both Charles and William have been praised for their environmental advocacy. They are likely to be criticised if the estates fail to meet the new government standards as fears about soaring energy costs and the climate crisis intensify.

They face spending up to £10,000 to upgrade each property, and could be fined £30,000 for every home they continue to rent without carrying out the necessary work.

A government spokesperson said: “Everyone deserves to live in a warm, comfortable home. Our plans for private rental homes to be EPC C by 2030 could lift up to half a million households out of fuel poverty by 2030, cutting bills to give families across the country the breathing space they need.”

Nationally, just over half of all rental properties currently have an EPC rating below C, but the Guardian has found that properties on the three large royal estates are more poorly insulated and expensive to heat than average.

The king inherited the Sandringham estate and the Duchy of Lancaster from his mother, Queen Elizabeth II, after her death in 2022. He did not pay inheritance tax on either estate because assets passed between monarchs are exempt.

The Duchy of Lancaster was established in 1265 to provide a private income for the sovereign and its profits soared during the late queen’s reign. It spans about 18,000 hectares (44,000 acres), stretching from the north-west of England to parts of London.

The income generated by Sandringham, bought by Queen Victoria in 1862 and set over 8,000 hectares (19,000 acres) in rural Norfolk, has not been disclosed.

When Charles became king after his mother’s death, he passed the Duchy of Cornwall to William. Founded in 1337 to generate money for male heirs to the throne, it too became significantly more profitable in recent decades. It covers about 55,000 hectares (135,000 acres) and is concentrated mainly in the south-west of England.

The Guardian examined more than 700 domestic EPCs across the three estates and found that 630 would fail to meet the government’s proposed requirements.

This analysis revealed that 99% of the rental properties on the Sandringham estate had an EPC rating of D or lower. The figure was more than 90% for the Duchy of Lancaster and about 80% for the Duchy of Cornwall.

The investigation excluded properties that appear to have been converted into holiday lets or those with separate leasehold titles, as it is unclear how the new rules will apply to them.

The precise number of domestic properties across the three estates is also unclear because they do not publish lists of their landholdings, though the figure is believed to exceed 1,200.

In the past, aides working at the two duchies have gone to great lengths to obscure details of their property portfolios, withholding the information even from parliament.

However, if this sample of more than half is representative, then more than 1,000 properties could fall foul of the new rules, requiring improvement if they are to be rented out.

The renovation costs could exceed £10m, similar to the annual combined residential rental income of the duchies. The duchies pay out about £50m a year to Charles and William. They are exempt from most business taxes, which helps them maximise their profits.

The details of how landlords will be required to upgrade their properties from a minimum of an E to a C from 2030 are yet to be published by the government.

This week, the Guardian revealed that more than 100 domestic properties on royal estates have EPC ratings of F or G.

Some have exemptions from the minimum energy efficiency standards regulations, while others are outside the scope of the rules as they are farmhouses or because the tenancies pre-date the current regulations. It is unclear if these loopholes will remain in place when the rules are amended.

A Whitehall source said: “We recently consulted on reforms to the energy performance of buildings regime and will update in due course.

“Some buildings, such as historic or mixed tenure, may not be able to upgrade to the new standard and some limited exemptions are in place on this basis. About 48% of privately rented properties are already at a current EPC C standard. We will consider further guidance for mixed-use buildings, ahead of the new standards coming into force.”

The royal estates are less energy efficient than most privately rented homes because they are mainly older rural properties, often heated by oil, coal or wood.

Only the Duchy of Cornwall’s newer builds at Poundbury, in Dorset, and Nansledan, in Cornwall, consistently meet the new planned targets for efficiency. However, of more than 300 Duchy of Cornwall EPCs the Guardian examined, just 11% were rated B and 8% rated C.

The rest were D or lower, and if this is typical of the rest of the Duchy of Cornwall’s 600 or more rental properties, then the total improvement bill could reach up to £5m – or about one quarter of the estate’s annual profits.

On top of a previously announced £500m investment over the next decade, the Duchy of Cornwall said that “an additional £50m is planned for improving the condition and efficiency of our existing properties”.

The Duchy of Cornwall said it had a “unique portfolio, including many historic buildings located in isolated rural and island locations”.

“While this confers a special character, it also brings some unique challenges which we have started to address systematically through our retrofit programme,” a spokesperson said.

“We recognise that these challenges mean work does not always happen as fast as we would like, but we will continue to work closely with our tenants to identify effective and practical energy-efficiency improvements as quickly as possible.”

The duchy added that it had spent £11m on home improvements since 2022, and in the last year had delivered 150 “modern, energy-efficient homes, all of which are EPC A or B”.

However, in response to follow-up questions from the Guardian, it confirmed that only six of the new properties were duchy private rents, with most having been sold.

The Duchy of Lancaster’s annual report states that it operates more than 300 domestic rental properties, but the precise figure is not known.

The Guardian found more than 200 properties on the estate that have domestic EPCs. More than 90% of them have ratings of lower than C. Nearly half are rated E and over a quarter are rated D. The total potential bill for improvements could top £2m.

The Duchy of Lancaster said it placed “great importance” on “being a responsible landlord”.

“Any tenant with concerns is encouraged to contact us directly and can be assured we will address these issues promptly and constructively,” a spokesperson added.

“Over the last year, the Duchy of Lancaster has invested more than £3m in residential property repairs and upgrades as part of our ongoing commitment to provide well-maintained homes compliant with all legislation.

“While improving the energy efficiency of some historic buildings is challenging, we continue to work to improve their EPC ratings.”

The Guardian has seen EPCs for more than 150 properties on the Sandringham estate, understood to be about half of the total. None were rated A or B, with just one rated C. Almost all could need work to meet the new regulations, with 99% rated from D down to G.

The biggest group – 120 properties, equivalent to 75% of those analysed – are rated E, the minimum EPC rating allowed for rented properties since new rules in 2018.

This includes Marsh Farm, where Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor now lives. It has an EPC produced in 2019, which rated it as a low E, just two points above an F. If our findings reflect the wider Sandringham estate, the total bill for energy-efficiency improvements by 2030 could come to £3m.

A spokesperson said Sandringham has “a mixture of property and tenancy types, which are fully compliant with MEES regulations”.

“We continue to invest significantly in an ongoing programme of maintenance and improvement works on all properties, including those out of scope of the regulations, to upgrade energy efficiency across the estate,” she added.

“While we do not comment on individual cases, these regulations do not apply to every property on the estate, and exemptions are necessary on a small number of properties.”

Jonathan Bean, a spokesperson for campaign group Fuel Poverty Action, said: “The royal duchies should be leading the way in upgrading all their properties to a minimum EPC of C by 2030 to protect people’s health and the environment.

“Instead they are dragging their feet and looking for loopholes. If even the richest landlords are allowed to get away with it, what hope is there of getting the rest to do the right thing?

“The government must act now to close all loopholes and increase enforcement efforts.”

A duchy of Cornwall spokesperson said it was unable to confirm the accuracy of our findings as the Guardian did not provide the estate with a list of properties we had inspected, to protect the tenants who spoke to us on condition of anonymity.

Move over, Odysseus: time for the women of ancient Greece to have their moment in the sun

The Guardian Sun, 16 Aug 2026 07:00:20 GMT

The hottest ticket in theatreland will soon be Cate Blanchett in Electra/Persona. Caged female rage continues to capture audiences

It feels like a very Greek summer here in the UK. The ground is scorched, it last rained months ago, and the giant publicity machine for Christopher Nolan’s billion-dollar-grossing The Odyssey – from red-carpet frocks to professorial disapproval – is a Charybdis, swallowing all other cultural events in its gaping maw. Mere Mortals – San Francisco Ballet’s astonishing work inspired by the story of Pandora – runs in Edinburgh this month before going to Sadler’s Wells in September. And Greek tragedy continues to fill London’s theatres.

Last week, I went to see Simon Stone’s reworking of Aeschylus’s Oresteia at the Bridge theatre in south London, and it was packed. Even on a Thursday afternoon, there was a huge audience for the story of a family who turn on one another, wreaking intergenerational violence until their whole house lies in tatters and madness. Partly that is because of the excellent cast: David Morrissey and Mary-Louise Parker play Christopher and Montie – a modern Agamemnon and Clytemnestra, their marital squabbles fizzing back and forth until he cracks and she snaps. Their children are the ones who will have to try to reconcile the impossible: duty to their murdered father, respect to their murderous mother.

Partly it is because Stone has earned his audience for Greek tragedy. His version of Phaedra with Janet McTeer at London’s National Theatre in 2023 blended Euripides, Seneca and Racine. And his adaptation of Euripides’s Medea, starring Marieke Heebink at the Barbican in 2019, remains one of the best things I have ever seen. This modern-day version began with Medea leaving the asylum where she has spent the past year, after attempting to kill her ex-husband for his infidelity to her and their children. The dread piled up like bodies as the play moved to its wrenching conclusion. These very different plays posed a similar question: what do women do with their rage, if speaking it goes unheard?

The hottest Greek ticket of the year, though, is surely for Cate Blanchett in the upcoming Electra/Persona by Benedict Andrews. Electra is a fascinating choice, not least because we have three different versions of her story: Sophocles and Euripides each wrote one, and Aeschylus’s Choephoroi covers the same part of the myth. There are plenty of variations between the three, not least because Euripides takes potshots at Aeschylus’s version, mocking a recognition scene that depended on Electra identifying her long-absent brother from a lock of hair and a footprint, both of which (implausibly) resemble her own.

But the essential beats of her story are these: Agamemnon is murdered by his wife, Clytemnestra, and her lover, Aegisthus. Clytemnestra feels wholly justified in her actions, because Agamemnon had killed her older daughter 10 years earlier. She has spent the whole Trojan war waiting for the chance to take her revenge. But her surviving children – Electra and Orestes – cannot forgive her for killing their father, no matter the reason. Orestes has grown up away from home, biding his time.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion
