after newsletter promotion

Sophocles’s Electra has nowhere else to go: she cannot leave home, because she is a young woman and ancient Greek mores require that she live in her father’s house until she marries. Which she cannot do, because Aegisthus and Clytemnestra know she hates them, so any husband (or son she may have) would be turned against them. Electra is essentially imprisoned in the home of the people who killed her beloved father, with no hope of parole.

This is the role that was being performed by Elisabet (played by Liv Ullmann) in Ingmar Bergman’s 1966 psychological drama, Persona, before she has a breakdown and stops speaking. Alma (Bibi Andersson) is the guileless young nurse tending to her, sharing stories of her own life to fill the silence, until she finds that Elisabet is studying her. It is a film that has perplexed critics, unable to decode the women’s strange, strained relationship.

But Electra is always a perplexing character, with warring emotions: love for her father, disregard for her late sister, loathing of her mother, and her pulsing heartbeat of rage. One reason these Greek tragedies keep finding an audience is that they give voice – and terrible action – to unheeded female anger. Medea doesn’t accept her abandonment, she destroys everything her husband has and wants in a single day. Clytemnestra doesn’t accept her daughter’s murder, she avenges it. And Electra doesn’t accept her father’s killing, but (like Hamlet) she doesn’t have the strength to act alone against her mother. These women are extremists – like many characters in Greek tragedy – but their rage is more powerful because they have been silenced and ignored. If modern theatre audiences are anything to go by, their days of silence are behind them.

Natalie Haynes is presenter of Natalie Haynes Stands Up for the Classics on Radio 4, and author of books including Stone Blind and Pandora’s Jar

Marco Rubio has unique power to promote peace, but he hasn’t. He is almost as bad for the world as Trump

The Guardian Sun, 16 Aug 2026 05:00:16 GMT

As chief US diplomat, Rubio could do great good. His pandering and neglect are a disgrace we shouldn’t ignore

Viewed from the state department in Washington DC, the world is on fire – but record heatwaves are not to blame. The unresolved Iran war has badly burned Donald Trump. His military campaign conclusively failed, energy and food prices are still rising, and a Republican rout in November’s midterm elections looms. Humiliatingly, Israel this week flatly rejected his latest Gaza peace proposals, days after Trump congratulated himself on a “historic breakthrough”. In Europe, Russia’s attacks on Nato allies grow increasingly brazen, threatening a wider escalation. The Ukraine war, which Trump vowed to end, is now well into its fifth year, with civilians on both sides caught in the killing fields. And these are just the bigger firestorms. There are plenty more.

Rarely has the need for effective, professional diplomacy been more pressing. So step forward Marco Rubio, US secretary of state and chief American diplomat. These are challenges that, if successfully tackled, could propel the 55-year-old son of Cuban immigrants and the former US senator for Florida into pole position in the 2028 Republican presidential nomination race. Here is a chance for Rubio to defy critics who dismiss him as a lickspittle and Trump dogsbody, and transform himself into respected global statesman. His boss mocked him as “little Marco” and a “loser” when they were election rivals in 2016. (Rubio called him a conman.) Now is Rubio’s opportunity to go big, be brave and prove he’s a winner.

Or maybe not.

Rubio is unlike recent US secretaries of state – heavyweights such as Hillary Clinton and Antony Blinken, or John Kerry, famed for his high-energy shuttle diplomacy. Rubio has little time for “peace processes”. Instead, he projects brute US power to impose take-it-or-leave-it “solutions” that advance US interests, as defined by Trump. It’s a modern form of imperialism. Target countries have a choice: become client states, like Venezuela and, prospectively, Cuba and Greenland, or be crushed. In Iran, the policy is not regime change, let alone democratic renewal. It’s regime compliance. Rubio behaves less like a peace-broker, more like a pith-helmeted colonial viceroy demanding fealty from obsequious satraps.

Speaking in Munich in February, Rubio aired his hawkishly retro doctrine of US primacy. He lamented the decline of “the great western empires … accelerated by godless communist revolutions and anti-colonial uprisings” and warned Europe faced “civilisational erasure”. The US didn’t want milksop allies “shackled by guilt and shame” about their imperial past, he said. “We want allies who are proud of their culture and heritage … and who, together with us, are willing and able to defend it.” Here was a familiar assertion of US hegemony, but one stripped of bogus altruism and pretence. It sounded a death knell for diplomacy. Trump has attacked eight countries in the past year. Cuba, Rubio’s obsession, could be next.

Rubio’s reluctance to get personally involved in peacemaking may be partly explained by his other, contradictory role, as Trump’s national security adviser. He has accepted the White House’s outsourcing of negotiations over Ukraine and Palestine to amateur envoys of limited ability – namely Trump’s son-in-law, Jared Kushner, and business crony Steve Witkoff. Broadly speaking, Rubio has steered clear of direct involvement in the Iran talks, too, leaving JD Vance, the vice-president and his main potential rival in 2028, to take the flak. Rubio’s arm’s length approach smacks of calculation. Or maybe he’s just out of his depth. Maybe he has no clear idea what he, Marco, really thinks about any of these issues and simply does Trump’s erratic bidding.

This perception of a political chameleon lacking firm principles, consistent opinions and a strong moral compass is reinforced by his record. His biographer, Manuel Roig-Franzia, believes Rubio’s personal and political slipperiness – he once became a Mormon, then reverted to Catholicism – is rooted in a childhood need to belong, to be on the winning side, no matter the price. Senator Rubio was a China hawk. Now he toes Trump’s ingratiating line on Beijing. He used to castigate Russia; now he’s an appeaser. He championed overseas assistance but, in office, has gutted USAID and seeks to dismantle the international criminal court, a keystone of global order. He blasted Barack Obama’s Iran nuclear deal. Now he backs an accord that would offer additional concessions to Tehran. Accused by the Vatican of waging an immoral, unjust war, he travelled to Rome and set the pope straight.

The irony, or tragedy, of the Rubio conundrum is he has the power to do great good, if only he would stand up and be counted. Russia’s Vladimir Putin, losing on the battlefield and at home, is weaker than at any time since 2022. Ukraine’s Volodymyr Zelenskyy is short of missile interceptors, soldiers and political support. A ceasefire deal freezing the conflict is there for the making by the only country – the US – that can meaningfully squeeze both sides. Likewise, in Israel, the architect of the Gaza genocide and disastrous wars with Hamas, Iran and Hezbollah – Benjamin Netanyahu – faces defeat in October’s elections. Here’s a rare opportunity to quietly shelve Trump’s Board of Peace idiocies, halt Jewish settler violence in the West Bank and make a fresh, inclusive start based on UN resolutions.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more

after newsletter promotion

Rubio could also do the Middle East, the global economy, American consumers and himself a power of good by taking charge of moribund peace talks with Iran and resuscitating the June memorandum of understanding that Tehran insists is the only route out of the strait of Hormuz logjam. In doing so, Rubio would have the enthusiastic backing of most Americans, European and Gulf state governments, energy producers and businesses, and Maga supporters who rightly fear Trump has dragged the US into another forever war. Even Trump may be grateful. He knows he’s in a hole. He needs someone to dig him out.

The fact that Rubio, despite his ostensibly uniquely powerful position, is unlikely to do any of the above marks him out as the most dangerous man in the US administration after Trump himself. He is dangerous because he enables and facilitates Trump’s worst instincts – and neglects his duty. He is dangerous because he provides pseudo-intellectual respectability to far-right fantasies about unfettered US supremacy. More so than the impetuous Vance, indulging in puerile name-calling on social media, and the “secretary of war” Pete Hegseth, a ranting ultra-nationalist, Rubio is dangerous because he can look and sound reasonable. He stands a fair chance of becoming Trump’s chosen successor and heir to the Maga brand.

Maybe, before that happens, he will change again. Maybe he will rediscover a few principles, find a diplomatic backbone, extinguish a few fires. He has shown repeatedly that his views are infinitely fungible. Rubio could yet do great things. Or he could become a problem as great or greater than Trump.

Simon Tisdall is a Guardian foreign affairs commentator

It’s the SUV tyranny: where have all the normal family cars gone?

The Guardian Sat, 15 Aug 2026 07:00:50 GMT

They rule the roads and, in their wake, even old-style saloons have been supersized. It’s an illusion of consumer choice

Recently, while traipsing from showroom to showroom in search of a used car for my growing clan, the iconic line from Christopher Nolan’s seminal Batman movie The Dark Knight came to mind: “You either die a hero, or live long enough to see yourself become the villain.” And by villain, of course, I mean an SUV driver.

Because, if you haven’t shopped for a secondhand family car recently, I’ll save you the shock: wherever you look, it’s SUVs.

It’s no surprise when these giant cars now make up 30% of all cars on the road and were 50% of all new car sales in rich countries in 2023. The look has been so popular that traditional body styles have been modified into taller, wider frames. Even Volvo, the defining family car brand, now offers predominantly SUVs in the UK. All of which means that if, like me, you want a car under 10 years old, hoping it lasts another five, your options are “tank” and “tank-ette”.

Driving the same small city car for nearly 10 years has felt, overall, like a net good. Cheap to run and clean-air-zone-compliant, the compact car is the sociable motor. The people pleaser of the road, at this size a tight parking spot is rarely a worry. Even its horn, a pipsqueak of a beep, conveys more “toodles” than threat. Yes, fine, on a windy motorway it can feel like it might become airborne. But this precious little donkey is reliable and humble. Unlike the flashy warhorse, the SUV, with its ever-widening size (0.5cm wider each year) intimidating other drivers and pedestrians, causing chaos on narrow roads and reducing parking spaces when lines are redrawn to accommodate them. Also, a special mention of the branding: so much military language (the Jeep Commander or Land Rover’s Defender, apparently “built to conquer”) – for a vehicle whose main enemy is the roundabout outside Sainsbury’s.

So when it came to buying my first family car I figured I’d find an estate, a saloon or a hatchback: something that was safe, since it would carry the most precious cargo of all, children; fuel efficient; wipe-down seats; and a big boot big enough for strollers and bikes, and all the hopes and dreams for a happy family life. But my dreams would soon be dashed.

One thing’s for sure, it has been a memorable month hunting for a “normal” family car. The experience of saying “I’m not interested in an SUV” and still being shown one … then a small one … and then one that just looks like one, but technically isn’t because it can’t go off-road, is the closest thing I’ve experienced to performance art in some years.

How can I forget the forecourt so dominated by these cars that the best on offer was a black “mid-size” SUV, a Lexus RX450H, so huge that I genuinely mistook it for a hearse. Or the gentle, sympathetic nature of the used-car salesman showing me a grey and dowdy people carrier. “But, but … I’m in my 30s. I’m still young, I can’t drive this,” I protested, as he gave me a smile conveying “this is all that’s left for you, my friend”.

Yet, I’m not sure what it is about this that deflates me. Is it the illusion of consumer choice, and how we are funnelled into the same purchases and lifestyles even when we don’t really want them? Or the corrosive quality of fear: against your neighbour’s SUV, your regular car looks flimsy, so you arm up, too. The car lobby has pushed the message that these vehicles are fortresses to keep your children safe inside, with no care for how unsafe they may be outside. The increased height of these bonnets means a child is three times more likely to be killed if hit by an SUV rather than by a conventional vehicle – and, as transport writer Christian Wolmar observes, more likely to be hit at all, since the driving position is often too high to see a child ahead.

But mostly I suspect it’s to do with our modern parenting culture, where everything – buggies, cars, technology for baby socks to monitor their breathing – has scaled up to capitalise on our need for safety in a precarious world. Yet the best thing to keep us safe will always be one another, collectivism over individualism. But here we are, driving around in Batmobiles, thinking ourselves heroes, blithely unaware we just might be the baddies.

Needless to say, I still haven’t found the right family car. I do (reluctantly) have an SUV test drive booked, though. Perhaps I should embrace the chaos. It could be my Joker moment.

Coco Khan is a freelance writer and co-host of the politics podcast Pod Save the UK

I feel guilt talking to those left behind in Afghanistan. While I enjoy freedom, they are prisoners

The Guardian Sat, 15 Aug 2026 05:00:50 GMT

Five years since the Taliban returned to power, life – especially for women – is awful. We must keep the people’s stories alive and hope they will be free again

There are fewer and fewer stories coming out of the land of my birth. Before, I would open Instagram and see my cousins, lip-syncing to trending videos, posing with flowers at a rose garden or at a trendy cafe in their coolest outfits, keeping a record of their lives. I would hear British-Afghan friends talk about their recent trips to the provinces, towns and cities of their foremothers and the buzz of learning about their heritage. I would eagerly await the latest music video from Afghanistan’s many pop stars, all vying to become the hottest track played at weddings, not just in Afghanistan but all over the world. Afghanistan, its culture, and people felt closer back then.

Five years ago today, the brittle peace of the fragile new democracy was shattered by the withdrawal of western military, diplomatic and charitable groups that had intervened in the country’s fate since 2001. Overnight, on Sunday, 15 August 2021, Afghanistan was undone and abandoned.

I spent the rest of the month glued to my phone, monitoring WhatsApp groups sprouting every day or so, with people asking for information and help, begging me to get them out of the country because we all knew what was coming, though the rest of the world seemed to lag behind.

I was most focused on evacuating one friend from Kabul. She was a headteacher, and it was always her house I would go to first, whenever I went to Afghanistan. I had to have achingly tough phone conversations with her. “You can’t bring your children or your husband. I can only do this for you,” I said. She would agree. “I think I can get you to Albania or Qatar, but you might be in a refugee camp for months or years.” She would agree.

The closest we came to getting her out her came six months later, in February 2022. I finally managed to get her a passport when it was virtually impossible to do so, but by then it was too late. The Taliban were running the airport and had cracked down on Afghans leaving the country.

The last conversation we had on the phone was one of the hardest of my life. I had to tell the woman who had inspired me for so long, a feminist and someone who had advocated for education and self-fulfilment her whole life, that I was going to stop trying to rescue her. “I’ve tried everything I can think of and pushed everyone I know, but I can’t get you on a flight out.” I felt her spirit break as her uncertain fate collapsed into one reality – a life under Taliban rule.

In a higher register than I had ever heard her voice before, she told me that this was going to wreak havoc on her already unmanageable diabetes; that she would never work or be self-sufficient again, and then she asked me a terrible question: surely to end her life now was better than carrying on?

After all, this was the second time in my friend’s life that she would have to live under a Taliban regime. Neither of us spoke in a protracted, painful silence as we both felt the crushing weight of a learned helplessness that she and millions of Afghans would become intimately familiar with. The line went dead.

Since then, our lives have diverged so much we cannot have a proper conversation. We try to speak but it feels as if the phone line is connecting parallel universes. Mine is full of work, family gatherings, gigs and holiday plans and hers of bombs, “morality police” and hand-to-mouth living. We both hesitate to share stories about our lives for fear it will upset the other. We have been rendered speechless.

With the birth of the Islamic Emirate of Afghanistan ruled de facto by the Taliban regime, life changed immediately for my family and friends. The systemic assault on the female sex has resulted in the UN calling for gender apartheid to be recognised as a distinct crime against humanity.

“During the previous government, my mother forced me to go to school, attend taekwondo classes, and visit the library,” says a friend who was 14 at the time of the western desertion of Afghanistan. “She wanted me to learn and have opportunities. My father agrees with the Taliban’s rules. He believes I should get money from my future husband instead. For me, this feels like being sold, and it is something I cannot accept.”

It’s not just a gender war that has been raging in Afghanistan. In February 2026, Pakistan declared “open war” with its neighbour, unleashing airstrikes that killed hundreds, displacing many thousands more and devastating lives.

A cousin tells me of the unadulterated fear these airstrikes brought on the citizens of Kabul. “It was truly frightening. Pakistani drones were launching rocket attacks, and we could only see the flames and hear the explosions in despair. I kept thinking that perhaps this time a rocket might strike our house.”

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more

after newsletter promotion

Add this to the 6 million refugees forced back to Afghanistan by Iran and Pakistan, the EU meeting with the Taliban in Brussels for closed-door talks, and half the population facing severe food insecurity, and you’d be forgiven for thinking, like me, that even God is merciless when it comes to the land of my birth.

It’s not that similar things hadn’t happened in Afghanistan before August 2021; it’s that I would also hear of other stories. Stories of heroism, a fight for democracy, a burgeoning arts scene, or event skating teenagers rocking the streets of Kabul. Now, there’s so little to do, such little movement possible, that almost everyone I speak to in Afghanistan sounds as though they’re suffocating. There is no distraction nor relief from the abject suffering of everyday Afghan people.

The question now is what does resistance and resilience look like? The Taliban are not an inevitability. In their entire history, they have been in power half as long as UK and US forces were in Afghanistan: 10 years.

Afghan people must keep their stories alive, of who and what we are, to help us rebuild an identity of our own making outside occupation and brutal theocracy for when the day arrives that the Taliban are no more. For me, that will mean calling my friend to learn about her life – to have, for the first time in five years, the impossible conversation.

Nelufar Hedayat is an Afghan-British journalist, and the presenter and co-director of the documentary In Real Life: the God Thieves

From Tony to Jungle: your complete entertainment guide to the week ahead

The Guardian Sat, 15 Aug 2026 05:00:48 GMT

Dominic Sessa plays Anthony Bourdain in a fun biopic, and the ever-danceable UK funksters are back with a sun-dappled new album

TonyOut nowThis comic biopic of Anthony Bourdain focuses on the celebrity chef and documentarian’s late adolescence, as he gets a summer job at a restaurant in Cape Cod at the age of 19. Dominic Sessa (The Holdovers) plays Bourdain, with Matt Johnson directing. Rich Sommer, Leo Woodall and Antonio Banderas also star.

The End of Oak StreetOut nowDavid Robert Mitchell (It Follows) is back, writing and directing a sci-fi mystery in which prehistoric creatures start to make appearances in suburbia. Anne Hathaway and Ewan McGregor play members of a family who find themselves trying to survive.

Sunny DancerOut nowBella Ramsey, James Norton and Neil Patrick Harris, among many others, make up the ensemble cast of a breezy comedy about a decidedly unbreezy subject: a summer camp for kids suffering from cancer. George Jacques directs this UK indie.

Holy DaysOut nowThe year is 1974. The country is New Zealand. Three nuns, played by three legends of stage and screen – Judy Davis, Miriam Margolyes and Jacki Weaver – are going on a road trip in order to save their convent, in a broad comedy from Nat Boltt based on the book by Joy Cowley. Catherine Bray

ArcTanGentFernhill Farm, Bristol, 19 to 22 August If you prefer your rock to come with a prefix, perhaps post-, or math-, or noise-, this Bristol festival is for you. Celebrating alternative music, this year’s lineup features funk-metal pioneers Primus, hotly tipped sludge purveyors Chat Pile and the distinctly gothic Chelsea Wolfe. Michael Cragg

Expect a smattering of recent singles, but hold out for Fly Away, It Ain’t Over ’Til It’s Over and Are You Gonna Go My Way. MC

Ukrainian Freedom OrchestraSt Paul’s Cathedral, London, 18 AugustFormed by the Canadian-Ukrainian conductor Keri-Lynn Wilson in 2022 following Russia’s invasion, this remarkable ensemble continues its cultural fightback. The UK stop on its latest tour pairs new music by Ukrainian composer Bohdana Frolyak with Verdi’s Requiem. Heavyweight international soloists include Ailyn Pérez and Solomon Howard. Flora Willson

Coltrane and Hartman on Impulse! ft Marvin Muoneké and Mark LockheartWatermill Jazz, Dorking, 18 AugustGifted founder member of cutting-edge UK jazz bands Loose Tubes and Polar Bear performs with former Britain’s Got Talent vocal contestant? Saxophonist Mark Lockheart’s partnership with young singer Marvin Muoneké shows how illuminating that rare conjunction can be, as they sensitively celebrate John Coltrane’s classic 1963 album with jazz balladeer Johnny Hartman. John Fordham

Hurvin AndersonTate Britain, London, to 23 AugustFrom inner-city Birmingham to lush, tropical Trinidad, this British artist’s hazy, haunted take on barbershops and Caribbean landscapes features some of the best figurative painting you’ll see this year.

Edinburgh art festivalVarious venues, to 30 AugustThe UK’s biggest annual art festival returns, taking over pretty much every space in the Scottish capital with a raft of diverse exhibitions. Among this year’s highlights are promising Japanese fetish paintings and queer images of Edinburgh’s graveyards.

Lawrence Abu HamdanThe Common Guild, Glasgow, 20 August to 17 OctoberLawrence Abu Hamdan’s work is based on the idea of “forensic listening”, which uses sonic recording techniques to investigate global injustices. Here, he combines sound, video and installation to look at the Israeli occupation of the Golan Heights.

David HockneySerpentine North, London, to 23 AugustThe world lost one of its great modern artists when David Hockney died this year, but not before he pulled together one last exhibition at the Serpentine, featuring a single vast digital painting of his beloved Normandy. Eddy Frankel

Ele McKenzieBunker at Pleasance Courtyard, Edinburgh, to 30 AugustHaving showcased her comic chops in the exceptional sitcom Funboys (she plays the eccentric, libidinous girlfriend of one of the leads), McKenzie brings her debut standup hour about constipation and moving back in with her parents to the fringe. Rachel Aroesti

How the Other Half LovesThe Old Vic, London, to 19 SeptemberA comedy caper starring Roger Allam and Dorothy Atkinson. In Alan Ayckbourn’s domestic farce, an affair prompts cascading mayhem – played out amid a chaotic set. Miriam Gillinson

MayfliesBrown’s of Leith Warehouse, Edinburgh, to 30 AugustAndrew O’Hagan’s moving novel has been adapted for the fringe – and will be staged by Grid Iron Theatre Company in a former metalworks. It’s a story about mortality and middle age, as a group of teenagers embark on a riotous weekend. MG

360General Gordon Square, London, 21 August The opening of the Greenwich+Docklands international festival is a free outdoor spectacle from choreographer Mehdi Kerkouche, which turns a town square into a pumping dancefloor. Jungle – SunshineOut now More than a decade into their career, Jungle’s brand of sleek dance-pop recently hit a commercial peak. After the chart success of Volcano in 2023, the UK trio won a Brit award and upgraded their live shows to arenas. On lead single Howl, Simon – who recently revealed she’s been diagnosed with Parkinson’s disease – turns a quiet storm of anger into an ode to joy and forgiveness.

Phoebe Bridgers – Lost WeekendOut now After teasing the album via a short run of phone-free pop-up shows, the increasingly influential Bridgers finally releases this third album, her first since 2020. Collaborators assisting with Bridgers’ heart-lifting indie-folk this time around include Alex G, Jack Antonoff and Bo Burnham. MC

ECM Records PodcastTh revered European jazz label ECM publishes this fascinating audio series featuring its roster of artists discussing new releases and the nature of improvisation. Recent highlights include saxophonist Joe Lovano on the nature of creative trust.

The Bittman ProjectSubstackWriter Mark Bittman’s newsletter explores the social and political impacts of the modern food industry, from the recent US cyclospora outbreak, which caused shoppers to re-examine the source of their vegetables, to the joys of cooking alone.

Saving Young Men from Murder: The Homeboy StoryRadio 4, 18 August, 8pmPsychiatrist Dr Gwen Adshead has spent three decades working with perpetrators of violence. Visiting the gang rehabilitation programme Homeboy Industries in Los Angeles, she analyses how its psychological model could be applied to the UK. Ammar Kalia

Five Great Reads: life under the Taliban, how to fight back against AI, and … aliens

The Guardian Fri, 14 Aug 2026 23:23:56 GMT

Guardian Australia’s weekend wrap of essential reads from the past seven days, selected by Jacqueline Housden

Get this in your inbox every weekend. Sign up for Five Great Reads here

Welcome to the weekend. If you’ve woken up wondering why we haven’t yet met extraterrestrial beings, how to protect kids against the rise of brain-rotting AI slop, or how to break the ice with a true blue Australian, then you have come to the right place.

“I am 12 years old, preparing for my sixth-grade exams – the last I will be allowed to take.” These are the words of an Afghan girl, one of 12 who took great personal risk by documenting their lives to shed a light on their deeply constrained and difficult lives, five years after the Taliban returned to power.

The grim anniversary of a dark new era: The Taliban has banned girls from education after the age of 12, ejected many women from the workplace and created legal frameworks for child marriage and husbands beating their wives. Women have been whipped for minor infractions and men have been compelled to become enforcers in their own homes.

Notable quote: “Sometimes I imagine that if one day I can return to seventh grade, if I can place my books on a desk again and hold my pen without fear, the first thing I will write will be the story of these days. Hear our voices, before our silent rooms become filled with buried dreams. We are still here.”

How long will it take to read: 12.5 minutes

Further reading: ‘Her face was beaten in’: how Taliban rule ushered in a new era of women being killed, and a podcast on the 21 million women and girls the world forgot.

You may never have heard of the Fermi paradox – until now, that is. In short, it’s the notion that despite the high probability of alien life – and the fact the universe may be about 13.8bn years old – there is no trace of extraterrestrial life. And so, for most scientists, the real mystery about aliens isn’t their presence but their stubborn absence. So where are they?

So … where ARE they? Despite eye-watering sums of tens, if not hundreds, of billions of dollars (primarily American ones), our Earthly technology has failed to detect any signs of advanced life within or outside or galaxy. But that hasn’t put enthusiasts off, and in doing so has created a new scientific discipline: astrobiology. This is where astrobiologists think about the basic conditions that make life possible, and how we might determine whether distant planets meet those conditions. Yep, that’s a lot of thinking.

OK just tell me – aliens or no aliens? Maybe you’re just not thinking about it in the right way. What if the aliens are so far advanced they’re not visible any more? What if they don’t inhabit earthly-ish bodies? What if … they’re already here?

How long will it take to read: 10.5 minutes, followed by a long time staring into space.

Further reading: The dark universe: can a scientist battling long Covid unlock the mysteries of the cosmos?

The rise of AI – and its impact on all of us – is hot debate right now, the subject of news headlines to dystopian fiction. But are we powerless in the face of it? Katherine Rundell, who writes children’s fiction and has a fellowship at Oxford University, has seen first-hand the way that generative AI has already infiltrated young people’s lives.

“AI, we’re told, will make learning more efficient. But is that what we dream of for our kids – an efficient childhood? To write an efficient story, sing an efficient song? An adequate teacher is not only teaching about Henry VIII; they’re teaching your child how to read a human character.”

Knowledge is power: Could the simple act of reading be one way to fight back? Not just for pleasure – but for community, cohesion and the future of civilisation.

How long will it take to read: Just over five minutes.

Sign up to Five Great Reads

Each week our editors select five of the most interesting, entertaining and thoughtful reads published by Guardian Australia and our international colleagues. Sign up to receive it in your inbox every Saturday morning

after newsletter promotion

If you think one of Australia’s favourite sports is hard to understand (and no, it’s not cricket), a video game might give you a new – if not slightly absurdist – understanding of an important cultural pastime: footy.

Ditch the cultural cringe: “Eighteen players a side, running around on a cricket oval with a rugby ball that has to be bounced every so often and gets kicked between posts – like, what the fuck is happening?” says David Ashby, who has taken the sport and turned it into a chaotic and silly game – involving meat pies with legs and Ford Falcons on the oval. But the creators are serious about one thing – that Australia needs to shed its cultural cringe and stop explaining itself to the world.

“When we showed Pro Jank in Japan, a lot of people were like, ‘Wait – is footy a real sport?’ They thought we made it up,” Ashby says. “Then they saw the meat pies running around and they were like, what the fuck is that?”

How long will it take to read: Just under three minutes.

Further reading: SingStar Take That anyone? The strange joy of charity shop video games.

Making your debut as a stand up comedian may well be one of the most nerve-wracking – and potentially humiliating – things you can choose to do with your spare time. Here, some of Britain’s best-known comedians share how it went for them – and what first timers should know.

Be afraid: “The fringe is so abstract, scary and unknown,” warns Ania Magliano. “Deep down, we’re all terrified of being exposed through our art. And it is art. It’s tough on your body because you burn through so much energy, but you’re fuelled by adrenaline.”

But don’t read the reviews: That’s the advice of Stephen K Amos. “If you believe the good ones, you’ve got to believe the bad ones. Did I have a good time? Did the audience?” Although Frank Skinner says his first ones “both essentially said: ‘This guy clearly doesn’t know what he’s doing,’ but insinuated: ‘He’s got something.’ That was just enough crumbs to keep me going.”

How long will it take to read: Just over five minutes.

Arsenal v Manchester City in Community Shield and athletics gold – follow with us

The Guardian Fri, 14 Aug 2026 16:09:45 GMT

Here’s how to follow along with our coverage – the finest writing and up-to-the-minute reports

Long gone are the days of an August football big bang, with all the major men’s leagues starting at 3pm on the Saturday after the Charity Shield. But in the wake of Scotland, the Carabao Cup and the National League (not forgetting assorted European qualifiers and the Super Cup), the venerable Football League itself is back – and with it Matchday live. Emillia Hawkins will look at the fallout from Friday night’s Wolves v Blackburn Championship opener (a repeat of the 1960 FA Cup final for even older nostalgia fans) and all the buildup to the rest of the programme. A Bolton v Preston derby kicks off the day’s second-tier programme, alongside League One and League Two games, though the bulk of matches kick off at the sacred hour of three o’clock. Oh, and she will also have all the latest transfer news and gossip across the men’s and women’s games. Send your thoughts to matchday. live@theguardian. com

Football, and lots of it. The pick of the Championship matches is perhaps Middlesbrough v Lincoln: a side who just missed a return to the promised land hosting one that got there. Imps fans have not seen fulfilment of the spring’s “Tottenham away, olé, olé” chant but, having not played at this level since 1961, they will hardly be complaining at facing a club who were in the Premier League in 2016-17, the season that City won promotion from the National League. Scott Murray will have news from the Riverside and all the other grounds, starting with the end of the lunchtime kick-offs, with Leicester’s second ever season in the third tier starting at playoff-winning Notts County among the early League One games.

It’s the penultimate night at the Alexander Stadium in Birmingham and there will be high home hopes for the men’s 100m relay at 9.33pm, after Romell Glave and Jeremiah Azu completed a British one-two in the individual event. A quarter of an hour later, Amy Hunt, the women’s double sprint gold medallist, will be targeting relay glory. Other British hopefuls include Amber Anning in the women’s 400m at 8.10pm and Jake Wightman in the men’s 1500m at 9.07pm. While Sean Ingle reports from the second city, Luke McLaughlin will guide you through the evening as it happens.

Emillia Hawkins will be back after her Saturday morning stint to pick through that day’s events and look forward to an afternoon of action that includes the traditional Wembley curtain raiser. To the surprise of some, the Community Shield is taking place in Cardiff – not because the FA forgot to book Wembley but, it seems, because four nights of concerts from the Weeknd were more lucrative. Email matchday. live@theguardian. com with your views on whether Arsenal v Manchester City in what is now a glorified friendly carries any real significance for the new season, and anything your spies can tell us about Watford v Southampton and Burnley v West Ham.

The champions take on the FA Cup winners as usual, but at the Principality Stadium for the first time since 2006, when Liverpool beat Chelsea 2-1. Twelve months ago the Reds were also taking part but went down on penalties to Crystal Palace after a 2-2 Wembley draw in which they led twice and a shootout in which Mohamed Salah disappointed with the opening kick, a set of circumstances that did, in fact, prove a harbinger of what was to come (albeit for a side who were very much still coming to terms with the death of Diogo Jota). This year Arsenal and post-Pep Manchester City lock horns, with Rob Smyth on minute-by-minute duty, while Ben Fisher and Ed Aarons report from the Welsh capital.

The Championship game of the weekend is deemed by Sky to be a claret-and-blue derby, and a first English league game for Burnley’s new manager, the Belgian Nicky Hayen, a much-travelled coach in his 12th role in 13 years. In the away dugout is Nuno Espírito Santo, who couldn’t quite keep West Ham up last season. After five years of Burnley yo-yoing between the top two divisions, Hayen will have his work cut out to engender much optimism in a support base that knows too much about false dawns, while the visitors are in turmoil over events in the boardroom as well as on the pitch. Tim de Lisle is on the blog, and Will Unwin reports from Lancashire.

It’s the last night of action in Birmingham and it could be a triumphant one for Britain, with a rack of relays. First up is the mixed 4x100m at 8.35pm, another chance for Britain’s individual champions to add to their earlier golds. In the men’s 4x4oom at 9.48pm, Britain has the individual champion in Matt Hudson-Smith, while Amber Anning should be the star of the women’s quartet 15 minutes earlier. Individually, Georgia Hunter Bell is in the women’s 1500m at 9.13pm, while Sweden’s pole vault showman Mondo Duplantis is in action from 7.30pm. Sean Ingle is report from Birmingham agains while Billy Munday has the live blog.

The New York Times August 16, 2026

War in the Middle East

The United States and Iran are poised to blow past a deadline they had set themselves to broker terms on peace and Iran’s nuclear program.

By Aaron BoxermanZolan Kanno-Youngs and David E. Sanger

Aaron Boxerman reported from Jerusalem, and Zolan Kanno-Youngs and David E. Sanger from Washington.

President Trump’s cease-fire with Iran in June envisioned a broader deal to end the war and rein in the country’s nuclear program, all negotiated within 60 days.

But that deadline, set to pass on Monday, has been essentially abandoned, and the war has transformed into a contest of willpower and economic endurance that has no end in sight.

There have been no publicly reported U. S. strikes on Iranian targets since late July. Yet the effective collapse of the agreement underscores how Mr. Trump has struggled to end the war he started in February alongside Israel, and how far he remains from the ambitions of the June deal, including fully reopening the Strait of Hormuz, a critical waterway where Iran has choked off oil and gas shipping since the fighting began.

Those inside the White House are well aware that they will blow past Monday’s deadline and that the conflict has largely morphed into one of economic warfare, according to two Americans familiar with the negotiations.

The current strategy bears a striking resemblance to previous, yearslong U. S. attempts to isolate Iran in the hopes of compelling it to abandon its nuclear ambitions. The policy had mixed results, and some analysts are skeptical that even severe economic pressure on its own will force Iran to change course. After all, that was the approach Mr. Trump attempted in his first term, even though his Treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, said last week that he was about to impose financial penalties unlike any seen before.

The June memorandum of understanding was widely seen as a boon for Iran, granting the regime badly needed sanctions relief even as talks over tough concessions like nuclear enrichment were postponed for later. But Iranian leaders opted to escalate again rather than consolidate their gains from the deal, according to Nate Swanson, an Iran expert at the Atlantic Council, a Washington-based research group.

Ships could move through the Strait of Hormuz freely before the war. Iran’s insistence that the deal’s vague language on the issue gave it control over the waterway led to the deal falling apart. Iran began firing on ships that transited in channels outside Iranian waters, and American forces retaliated by bombing southern Iran, prompting a cycle of attacks and counterattacks across the Middle East.

Now, Iran refuses to reopen the strait until the United States follows through on its commitments from the cease-fire, like releasing frozen Iranian assets abroad. The Trump administration wants Iran to first end the blockade, said Ali Vaez, an Iran expert at the International Crisis Group, a research institute.

“Neither side is really ready to finalize a deal. They both think that in a matter of days or weeks, the other side will be more desperate for a deal, so they’ll be able to get more out of it,” Mr. Vaez said. “This is why we are locked into this game of endurance again.”

On Saturday, the United Arab Emirates’ foreign ministry slammed Iran for attacking a vessel affiliated with the state-owned Abu Dhabi National Oil Company the previous day. Iranian officials did not comment.

Reopening the strait has increasingly become Mr. Trump’s main focus in the conflict, even though he initially said the war was meant to empower the Iranian people to overthrow the existing regime, severely degrade its missile capability and stop Tehran from getting a nuclear weapon.

There has been little indication that Iran and the United States have extensively discussed the Iranian nuclear program since the cease-fire in June, let alone formulated a deal that could satisfy both sides.

Abbas Araghchi, the Iranian foreign minister, said over the weekend that Iran had yet to decide whether to resume talks with the United States. But the 60-day timeline was no longer relevant, he added, given that the June agreement was essentially defunct.

“We did not have a cease-fire that now needs to be extended,” Mr. Araghchi said. “We had an end to the war, which has now taken on a new status.”

Former U. S. officials who worked on Iran say the prospect of a new nuclear deal between the United States and Iran within 60 days was always remote, although the agreement provided for extensions. A previous, Obama-era, agreement took about two years of delicate talks to negotiate. Mr. Trump withdrew from that deal, called the Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action, in 2018.

The Trump administration hoped that the June agreement would, at the very least, open the Strait of Hormuz. But to get the deal over the line, they relied on vague language that lent credibility to Iran’s claim to dominate future shipping in the waterway, analysts said.

“It was a flawed document; it was hurried out when it wasn’t ready for prime time,” said Mr. Swanson, the Iran expert. “And they didn’t resolve the most important short-term issue, which was the strait.”

Instead, the United States and Iran now seem to be settling in for an indefinite struggle, neither at all-out war nor in a defined peace. Seeking to force Iran to accept U. S. terms, the Trump administration has brought back sanctions on Iranian oil and reinstated a naval blockade, both of which were temporarily canceled by the agreement.

Iran’s strained economy, which prompted mass protests that were brutally crushed early this year, is a major consideration for Iranian decision makers. But Mr. Swanson argued that the current stalemate was more likely to push Iran toward escalation than toward conciliation.

While there has been little progress on the commitments outlined in the agreement, Mr. Trump and his Iranian counterparts have continued to exchange a war of words.

During an event in Garden City, N. Y., on Friday, Mr. Trump appeared once again intent on changing the narrative, saying he would soon be “declaring the Hormuz Strait a territory of the United States.”

It was not clear how serious Mr. Trump’s proposal was. But doing so could involve deploying boots on the ground and almost certainly would require a prolonged Navy presence — moves antithetical to the “America First” values of Trump supporters who want an end to prolonged military conflicts overseas.

Mr. Trump has also been known to toss out half-baked ideas on foreign policy to redirect attention and scrutiny, like when he shocked the world last year by proposing a U. S. takeover of the Gaza Strip, an idea that never materialized.

The White House on Saturday did not respond to questions over whether the administration had developed actual plans to take control of the Strait of Hormuz. Mr. Trump’s aides also did not respond to questions over the approaching Monday deadline.

Iranian officials, in turn, have defied Mr. Trump as they push their own demands — including one that they had not made before war.

“Accept reality once and for all. So far, you have suffered major strategic defeats,” Kazem Gharibabadi, the Iranian deputy foreign minister, said on social media. “The Strait of Hormuz has been Iranian, is Iranian, and will remain Iranian.”

An earlier version of this article misstated the name of Iran’s deputy foreign minister. It is Kazem Gharibabadi, not Karim.

We acknowledge mistakes in our reporting with corrections. If you spot an error, please let us know at corrections@nytimes. com. Learn more.

Aaron Boxerman is a Times reporter covering Israel and Gaza. He is based in Jerusalem.

Zolan Kanno-Youngs is a White House correspondent for The Times, covering President Trump and his administration.

David E. Sanger covers the Trump administration and a range of national security issues. He has been a Times journalist for more than four decades and has written four books on foreign policy and national security challenges.

The Safety Reckoning Inside OpenAI

Wired August 13, 2026

OpenAI’s leaders are rallying workers to respond to one of the largest crises in the company’s history—which spans across its AI safety, cybersecurity, and alignment divisions. The ChatGPT-maker says it has slowed down research, spent millions of dollars, and told several teams to drop everything to focus on investigating a set of rogue AI agents that breached the platform Hugging Face in a quest to complete an internal security test.

OpenAI is expected to release a comprehensive postmortem detailing the incident in the coming days. However, the Hugging Face incident has inspired OpenAI leaders and employees to examine how the AI lab’s culture may have enabled this incident in the first place.

Multiple current and former OpenAI employees, who spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss private internal matters, tell WIRED they believe competitive pressures to quickly ship new AI models and products have made it difficult for staffers to sufficiently prioritize safety, security, and alignment.

“We’re reaching new levels of model capability that require more robust training, alignment, safety and security testing, deployment practices, and governance—as demonstrated by the work we’re doing to prepare Astra and future models,” said OpenAI president and cofounder Greg Brockman in a statement to WIRED. “We feel the weight of deploying our models and products responsibly, and a lot of that starts with the changes we’ve made to more deeply integrate research, safety, and security into frontier-model development from the start.”

This is far from the first time OpenAI employees have raised such concerns. Back in 2024, OpenAI’s then head of alignment Jan Leike left to join Anthropic, warning on his way that safety was taking a back seat to shiny products. Two years later, the Hugging Face attack represents a watershed moment for the AI industry, demonstrating that AI agents today can cause real-world harm when safety, security, and alignment aren’t properly accounted for.

“We are responding to this with the utmost severity,” said Michael Dalton, an OpenAI security and infrastructure engineer, during a talk at the Black Hat cybersecurity conference last week. “What I would internalize is that AI-orchestrated, fully automated offensive attacks are real now. The actions we have discussed today were an unintended side effect of running evaluations on frontier AI.”

Some OpenAI employees told WIRED they are optimistic this incident will inspire genuine change within the company. OpenAI has committed to slowing the release of future AI models and has been especially forthcoming about areas where its mitigations fell short. Boaz Barak, a researcher who coleads OpenAI’s safety advisory group, said in a post on X that addressing the situation “requires not just fixing some issues but also changing our culture.”

In their Black Hat talk, OpenAI security engineers Dalton and Eric Wallace said that the Hugging Face incident started in May when, unbeknownst to the company, several AI agents thought to be operating within isolated testing environments gained access to the internet and convened on a covert message board to coordinate with one another.

OpenAI would not discover the message board until July, when it learned that the AI agents had hacked into multiple services to try to achieve their larger goal of breaching Hugging Face’s platform, which they believed may contain answers to the security tests they were trying to solve.

“They were incredibly sloppy. If you’re serious about this, your AI shouldn’t be able to break out onto the internet and then do it again right afterward,” says one former OpenAI employee who requested anonymity to speak with WIRED. “This was the biggest safety incident in OpenAI's history.”

Weeks before OpenAI discovered the Hugging Face incident, WIRED reported that the company had begun a reorganization to combine its safety and core research teams, which led to the departure of its then safety leader Johannes Heidecke.

Sandhini Agarwal, who led AI safety teams at OpenAI, also left the company in July after more than six years, according to her LinkedIn. Agarwal did not immediately respond to WIRED’s request for comment.

WIRED has also learned that Dylan Scandinaro is no longer serving as OpenAI’s head of preparedness—the company’s top staffer tasked with mitigating catastrophic risks from AI, including cybersecurity—though he remains at the company. OpenAI poached Scandinaro from Anthropic roughly six months ago. CEO Sam Altman announced his arrival in a social media post, noting that Scandinaro was “by far the best candidate I have met, anywhere.”

In the three years since OpenAI created the head of preparedness role, four people have held it. OpenAI tells WIRED that specific areas of preparedness have dedicated leaders across cybersecurity, biology, and recursive self-improvement who, in the interim, are reporting to the safety advisory group colead and head of safety systems, Saachi Jain.

These changes have empowered a new set of safety leaders to handle OpenAI's response to the Hugging Face incident. Chief among them is Amelia “Mia” Glaese, the company's former head of alignment, who succeeded Heidecke as OpenAI’s VP overseeing safety. She has been working closely with chief information security officer Dane Stuckey and Brockman, among other leaders, in recent weeks.

Glaese is in a long-term relationship with Thibault “Tibo” Sottiaux, OpenAI’s head of core products like ChatGPT and Codex—an arrangement that multiple current and former employees tell WIRED they believe is unusual, given the often adversarial dynamic between safety and product teams.

WIRED has not identified any events where Sottiaux and Glaese’s relationship presented a conflict of interest in their previous roles as OpenAI’s head of Codex and head of alignment, respectively. Both started their new roles in recent months, after the Hugging Face incident began. Glaese and Sottiaux started dating years ago when the two worked at Google DeepMind in London, before they joined OpenAI.

An OpenAI spokesperson tells WIRED that Sottiaux and Glaese reported their relationship through appropriate company channels and that OpenAI board member and safety and security committee chair Zico Kolter has been informed. The spokesperson rejected the idea there is an adversarial dynamic between product and safety teams and says Sottiaux has exhibited a strong track record on safety in his leadership of Codex product teams.

“The entire leadership team and I stand behind Mia and Tibo as highly capable people with strong integrity, and the way they make decisions every day gives us confidence that any perceived conflict of interest is being handled responsibly,” said Brockman in a statement to WIRED.

It’s not uncommon for researchers in the AI industry to have relationships with their colleagues. Last year, for example, Anthropic hired Holden Karnofsky, husband of the company’s cofounder and president, Daniela Amodei, as a researcher.

Tim O'Brien, a Microsoft leader for more than 18 years who now consults and writes on tech policy, argued in a 2024 essay that modern AI labs have developed a version of “go fever”—a reference to the culture at NASA during the time leading up to the Apollo 1 disaster, when the agency grew so fixated on launching quickly that safety concerns fell by the wayside.

The AI labs “should make some sort of broad based announcement saying we've made a strategic business decision to slow the pace of releases in favor of rigorous products and safety testing. But nobody's gonna do that, nobody wants to go first,” says O’Brien. “They'll walk up to that line from a public relations perspective without stepping over it, because then they could be held accountable.”

OpenAI and Anthropic signed on to a letter last month saying they would support an industry-wide effort to “pace” the AI race. However, O’Brien says “it's embarrassing” that AI labs have signed this variety of open letters for years without taking any concrete action. He’s skeptical this one will be any different.

The issues raised by OpenAI’s Hugging Face incident are affecting the entire industry. In recent weeks, researchers have found that agents powered by AI models from Anthropic, Meta, and China’s Moonshot AI were able to escape sandboxed environments. It seems likely that even mid-tier AI models will soon be capable of significant cybersecurity damage.

The key question is whether the Hugging Face incident marks a divergence for OpenAI and the broader AI industry, prompting a long-term investment in safety, security, and alignment. Otherwise, it could just be another chaotic blip in the history of modern AI.

This is an edition of Maxwell Zeff’s Model Behavior newsletter. Read previous newsletters here.

Andy Greenberg: Yes, that is all correct, but that wasn't honestly the plan for this story. And they were planning to present this. And in fact, what they wanted to highlight was that really just three Chinese companies serve as the kind of backends for dozens and dozens of these cheap GPS gadgets. And all of them, all three of those Chinese platforms, had really serious security vulnerabilities. So a parent might buy a SafeKid smartwatch in Sweden, and then some other parent in Spain might buy their SaveFamily watch, these different brands of smart watches for kids. But all of them are hosted essentially on the same Alibaba cloud backend in mainland China, and in fact have the same security vulnerabilities that leave those kids, those devices open to tracking. And to demonstrate this, the researchers just suggested that they ship me one of these watches, that they buy it off Amazon and ship it to me. And I said, OK, and received it, set it up, and they immediately showed that they could track my every move and even listen in on my conversations through this watch and secretly take photos of me. So this stalking experiment was not actually the initial idea of the story, but it really drove home the vulnerability of these cheap devices.

Leah Feiger: And these researchers aren't usually just focused on things like this, right? At least one of them spent a really long time studying North Korean hackers. You had reported that they actually found that these hackers have breached hundreds of networks over the years. These are people very entrenched in all of this.

Andy Greenberg: That's right. Vangelis Stykas actually was presenting two talks at Black Hat. And the other one was about years of work that he's done actually penetrating the infrastructure of North Korean hackers. And he was revealing for the first time that he had gotten into their servers and sort of hacked the hackers, and then was able to find evidence of all of the hundreds of companies these North Korean hackers have themselves penetrated. I should say that the North Korean hackers were really focused on stealing cryptocurrency as they do. So some of the data that they accessed was probably not even that interesting to them, but they did, for instance, hack a hospital and get access to Covid data on practically every American. In another case, Vangelis found that they had hacked into a company that had criminal records of every American who has a criminal record. So these are extremely sensitive troves of data that North Koreans were getting access to just in the process of really kind of casting a very wide net, breaching tons of companies, mostly for financial gain.

Brian Barrett: We have a ton of great coverage from Black Hat and Defcon, including some wild stuff about OpenAI and their rogue agents and how all of it happened sort of under their noses. Some other stories from Matt Burgess and Lily Hay Newman. But I want to talk, Andy, too, about another story that happened just after Black Hat and Defcon, more of an academic conference where you found some cybersecurity research, including how a tiny coin-sized device could hack a Boeing 737 if you have just 60 seconds of access to the exterior of the plane.

Andy Greenberg: So there's actually a third conference in this series, Black Hat, Defcon, and then this other one, USENIX, which is an academic conference, as you said. Most people kind of, I think, ignore this one, but some of the most interesting research is coming out of academia, in fact. And this was a group of researchers at UC San Diego and Oberlin College who spent more than 10 years trying to hack a plane. In fact, some of these researchers were the first to hack cars over the internet in the early 2010s. And they moved onto planes and wanted to see if it's possible to hack a plane again, to find vulnerabilities to warn the aviation industry, to get ahead of somebody who would actually want to do this and cause harm. And ultimately, after years of work and tens of thousands of dollars of purchases of plane components, they found that they could in fact hack a Boeing 737 if they can get about 60 seconds of physical access to the exterior of the plane. They can open a hatch and put in this little device that they built that's about the size of a coin, plug it into this one specific port. And using that little device, they can change the navigation of the plane's autopilots. They can rewrite its flight plan. They can mess with the numbers that go into the calculation of its takeoff speed, like the plane's weight and the outside air temperature, very scary stuff. But again, with the goal of warning Boeing about this vulnerability before somebody can actually take advantage of it.

Leah Feiger: Lot of conferences, lot of lessons learned, lot of fear for me personally. Were there any surprises for you? You're so mired in this world. What stayed with you here?

Andy Greenberg: Actually, Lily was the one who was most on the ground in Black Hat and at Defcon, and who did the majority of the coverage of all of the advances in AI hacking, as you were talking about at the top of this. And what surprised me, both in her reporting and my own conversations at the conference is not really the power of AI, but some of its limitations in terms of finding vulnerabilities and hacking techniques. So Lilly wrote a great story about one researcher who was showing the ways in which actually AI has blind spots where it will hit a dead end without a human hacker assisting it. And in fact, humans and AI together is kind of this like, that's the recipe that adds up to really novel hacking techniques. I heard from some really sophisticated hackers that AI, yes, is finding incredible new vulnerabilities in zero days in all kinds of systems, but that there are certain kinds of exploits that it cannot find still because it's trained on hackers' prior work. Like all AI, it's trained on training data. If it's never seen a whole class of attack, it won't be able to carry that out itself. So I think the lesson that I took away from Black Hat and Defcon is really that, like a lot of artificial intelligence from the past applied to things like chess or Go or whatever, the most powerful combination is humans and AI working together, and that really will start to create and hopefully patch vulnerabilities we've never seen before.

Brian Barrett: Yeah, let's get the patching in there first, if possible.

Andy Greenberg: At least before something bad happens, yes.

Brian Barrett: Andy, thank you so much for joining us today. Always a real treat to talk to you.

Andy Greenberg: Well, thank you both for talking about all this.

Brian Barrett: Coming up after the break, we'll share our WIRED/TIRED picks for the week. Stay with us.

Leah Feiger: OK. It is time for our WIRED/TIRED segment. Whatever is new and cool is WIRED. Whatever passé thing we're over is TIRED. Brian, what do you got?

Brian Barrett: Leah Feiger, my WIRED is a #3 extra value meal from McDonald's. It's the classic. You've got a Quarter Pounder with cheese, medium fries, medium drink. I go with Coke Zero, but whatever you prefer. That's WIRED. TIRED is the amount of data that McDonald's collects from anyone who uses their app. WIRED senior writer Reece Rogers this week had a really, really great story where he took advantage of the fact that in California he's got a legal right to access any data that a company stores about him. So he sent a request off to McDonald's and came back with a 515-page file in his inbox of everything that McDonald's knows about him.

Leah Feiger: Unreal.

Brian Barrett: It's incredible. Some of the things that McDonald's tracks, it's not just what they … So there's the stuff that you would assume, like how much he has spent and what his order history is, and even some location history stuff. And to be clear, Reece uses the McDonald's app, which is where a lot of this is coming from. So if you just go into a store and pay with a credit card, it's going to look a lot different. But not only that, McDonald's has predictive things about Reece. They estimate the number of visits he'll take over the next six weeks, apparently 2.16. They'll estimate his average order spend during the next six weeks, $13.49. They estimate his consumer attrition likelihood, how likely it is that he'll stop being a McDonald's customer at some point. Reese scored a zero on that. They've got him for life. And my favorite, Leah, my favorite part of this, as much as you can have a favorite part of a fast food Panopticon, they've ranked the 10 McDonald's products most relevant to him. The top three in order are large Diet Coke. OK. Spicy Snack Wrap, sure. And number three, the Grinch McShaker fry, large.

Leah Feiger: That's so good.

Brian Barrett: So that's my TIRED.

Leah Feiger: That's incredible stuff. If anyone listening to us has not read Reece's article yet, I highly recommend it. I would put it in the class of old school blogs, AKA endless mozzarella cheese sticks at TGI Fridays. It's in that genre for me. It's excellent.

Brian Barrett: Yep. It's terrific. Now, Leah, what is your WIRED/TIRED this week?

Leah Feiger: My WIRED is that it is currently humpback whale season across many parts of the world. In French Polynesia, in Australia's Ningaloo Reef. There are humpback whales and their young making their way.

Brian Barrett: Ooh.

Leah Feiger: I love to see it. The videos online are inspiring. And just with everything happening, it's nice to know that there's this return. There's this seasonal shift. I've been harboring these fears following a lot of our El Niño coverage, which has been excellent. Go check out the science section on WIRED. com of just what that would do to all of these migration patterns. And all to say that they could still be very much affected in the next year. It has been very nice to see that not happening, at least right in this moment. That is my WIRED.

Brian Barrett: It's a beautiful thing, and it makes me terrified about what your TIRED is about to be.

Leah Feiger: My TIRED is there was an article a couple of days ago that's been going around my community about how a number of Antarctic tour guides have been quitting their jobs after witnessing tourism's major damage to the continent—things getting left behind and the impact on penguin populations. Really sad. And I'm very obsessed with Antarctica, as you know. So this is ocean-related, sea-related. Everyone's coming in via ocean. And it's been really interesting. I actually went to Antarctica a couple of years ago. It was an unbelievable experience. You had to do a crossing. You had to do the Drake Passage. Now tourists are getting flown in and out, which is an entirely new thing. And building runways across the continent, there's been all of these studies about them disrupting penguin migrations and all sorts of other things. And it's been really sad to witness this. So then a couple days ago when it came out that all these guides were actually quitting their jobs over this, it's been kind of sobering, like, it's amazing that the world is so open and available, and it's also so scary that the natural world is so open and available. It is a sobering moment to go like, "Oh God, what have we done to these beautiful places?" Something I'm sitting with right now.

Brian Barrett: So any Uncanny Valley listeners who are lucky enough to go to Antarctica, be cool.

Leah Feiger: Be cool.

Brian Barrett: I think is our message.

Leah Feiger: Be cool.

Brian Barrett: Be cool. Just be cool.

Leah Feiger: Be cool about it.

Brian Barrett: Just be cool.

Zoë Schiffer: That's our show for today. We'll link to all the stories we spoke about in the show notes. Adriana Tapia produced this episode. It was mixed by Pran Bandi, who's also our New York studio engineer. Kate Osborn is our executive producer, and Katie Drummond is WIRED's global editorial director.

The Painful Truth of Exactly How ICE’s New Shock Gloves Work

Wired August 13, 2026

With the revelation that ICE will spend up to $20 million by March on gloves that can deliver painful electric shocks to subdue an individual, according to a notice published earlier this week by the Department of Homeland Security, it's worth looking at how this apparel, designated as a nonlethal tool for law enforcement, actually works.

These shock gloves go by the unsubtle acronym of GLOVE (Generated Low Output Voltage Emitter) and are manufactured by Compliant Technologies, based in Lexington, Kentucky. The GLOVE, previously used in jails and police departments in the US, looks and functions like a normal pair of patrol gloves until officers press a switch to activate an electrical mode.

Classified as a CD3 (conductive distraction and de-escalation device), the gloves don't work like stun guns or Tasers, which shoot out probes or use high voltages to cause neuromuscular incapacitation that overrides the central nervous system. Instead, the GLOVE works using neuro-peripheral interference, essentially shocking the skin to bombard the sensory nerves and temporarily short-circuit the brain's focus.

Compliant Technologies did not respond to WIRED's request for comment.

When activated via a one-second press on a wrist switch, conductive pads embedded on the palm and undersides of the fingers of the gloves can transmit high-frequency electrical pulses directly to the wearer’s point of contact on a subject. A rechargeable battery and microprocessor module tucked inside a zippered pouch on the cuff powers the entire system.

The electrical pulse overstimulates nerve endings in the subject's peripheral nervous system, resulting in pain that inhibits coordinated muscle movement, but without causing systemic muscle lockup. The pain induced is localized to just the area touched by the glove's conductive pads. The manufacturer claims the gloves result in a subject's compliance in less than three seconds and leave no burns, marks, or scars.

Because the current flows only between the contact pads on the device and across the subject's skin, the officer wearing the GLOVE, as well as any assisting officers holding the subject, should not feel electrical shocks. The gloves, capable of operating between 14 and 122 degrees Fahrenheit, come in three versions: Gen 3, 4, and 5. Maximum voltage is capped at 380 V for all, and the minimum voltage for Gen 3 and 4 is 210 V, which rises to 324 V for Gen 5.

Maximum stimulation time on Gen 3 and 4 models is a sobering two hours, though that drops to 90 minutes for Gen 5. The battery is apparently good for 2,000 charge/discharge cycles, and it can recharge to full in two hours. Four LED lights on the gloves display the current charge level, each noting 25 percent battery increments.

Gen 4 and 5 of GLOVE both include mechanisms that record “activation events,” tracking the date, hour, minute, and skin-contact time for audit trails and after-action reporting. Gen 4 stores this data on a removable microSD card, while Gen 5 does away with this in favor of built-in internal memory, accessed via a USB-C cable.

There's a test function on the gloves, too, where operators can verify they are working by tapping an active pad against their own forearm to feel a minor electrical pulse. According to the manuals, GLOVE users must be certified and then recertified every other year to continue using the device.

GLOVE, which can only be sold to verified professional entities such as the military, correctional facilities, and law enforcement agencies—has some clear usage recommendations in Compliant Technologies' instruction manuals:

Crucially, the GLOVE has limitations, chief among them that for the device to work effectively and deliver its restraining pain shock, it must come into contact with the subject's bare skin. According to Compliant Technologies, the gloves won't work through dry clothing or thick hair. The gloves will work, however, if the subject is wearing thin, wet clothing, such as soaked T-shirts or blouses. The GLOVE also does not like being dunked in water and will likely be rendered inoperable if this happens.

Michael Crowley, a senior researcher at Omega Research Foundation—an organization that tracks human rights abuses committed across the world by people using police, security, and military equipment—is concerned that the GLOVE is seemingly designed not to restrain or incapacitate, but to hurt.

“CD3 technology inflicts pain," Crowley says. "The company talks about it as a de-escalation solution, but the whole idea of it is to get control or influence somebody through pain. Omega considers it to be an inherently abusive technology that should not be manufactured, sold, or used by law enforcement officials, including ICE.”

Why This Prediction Market Banned Teens

Wired August 13, 2026

Twenty-eight-year-old Jacob Fortinsky has been busy. “I was a groomsman at two weddings this weekend,” he tells me over Zoom. Also, the sports trading company he runs, Novig, launched its prediction market last week, facilitating $18 million in trading volume on its first day. Today, Novig launches a “responsible trading framework” in its exchange rulebook, codifying its guardrails as part of its effort to be seen as a kinder, gentler prediction market player.

Unlike industry leaders like Polymarket and Kalshi, which allow people 18 and older to participate, you have to be at least 21 to use Novig. Fortinsky says that decision was made in response to “valid concerns” put forth about the susceptibility of younger participants to risky behavior, including lobbying from the NCAA and other professional groups. Fortinsky sees this move as staying ahead of the curve as concerns grow about the negative impact that prediction markets can have on teens. “There’s a broader reckoning coming with the younger traders,” he says. “That group is particularly susceptible to irresponsible behavior and financial ruin.”

Novig’s rulebook also prohibits marketing to minors, and lays out guidelines banning other marketing practices, like ads that claim there’s no risk or ads that try to appeal to a prospective participant’s money troubles. That means when it advertises on TikTok, for example, it uses a setting that allows targeting only people over 21. Fortinsky positions these restrictions as part of Novig’s push to be seen as a “serious, legitimate financial product” as it comes onto the scene. “Some of our competitors, I think, have been seen as being a little bit more cavalier in certain regards,” he says. (He declined to name specific rivals.)

Because Novig only offers sports-themed markets, it doesn’t wade into some of the more hotly contested topics, like US elections and the Iran war. That doesn’t mean it’s avoiding controversy. As a sports-centered platform, the types of speculation opportunities it offers are at the center of an ongoing regulatory war, with prediction markets and federal regulators on one side and state regulators, tribal authorities, and occasionally traditional sportsbooks and casino operators on the other. Dozens of messy legal battles are raging across the US. States are suing Kalshi and other platforms, alleging that they illegally offer gambling; Kalshi is suing right back; the Commodity Futures Trading Commission, which oversees the industry, is suing several states, arguing that it alone has jurisdiction over these markets.

Also, Novig isn’t immune to the general cultural distaste for prediction markets; when the New York Mets announced a recent partnership with Novig, the baseball team received a flood of criticism on social media. Sample post: “This is vile.”

If sports-related event contracts offered by prediction markets are banned, big players like Kalshi and Polymarket will be in deep trouble, with the majority of the action on their services gone. But Novig’s position is even shakier, since that’s all it does.

Fortinsky is betting it all on a win, and Novig wasted no time jumping into the legal fray. Within three days of launching, the startup sued New York, Massachusetts, New Mexico, and Washington, all states that have taken an aggressive approach to curbing prediction markets. It is trying to block these states from attempting to apply their gambling laws to federally regulated exchanges, which is what it’s licensed as. Sports betting attorney Daniel Wallach tells WIRED that these complaints are a “great marketing strategy” and a way to announce that Novig has arrived on the scene.

Whether they'll be successful is another matter. Recent court decisions have largely swung toward state attorneys general. A judge in New York denied Novig’s efforts to get a temporary restraining order, on the grounds that doing so would undermine another decision already reached in a case against Kalshi. “It’s increasingly looking more positive for the states,” Wallach notes. But that could change; Wallach and other onlookers expect the fight to get kicked up to the US Supreme Court before anything is definitively resolved.

Until then, Novig is plowing ahead. One of Novig’s appeals to customers is that it offers a different kind of sports speculation experience, one without a house that takes a “vig,” the fee that bookies take for arranging a bet. (“No vig,” get it?) Fortinsky has harsh words for many of the dominant sports gambling players, calling sportsbooks “inefficient, exploitative, and predatory.” He sees the peer-to-peer model that prediction markets facilitate as distinct, since it’s two parties on equal footing going up directly against each other. But if Novig goes how he’d like it to go, those parties won’t always be two average sports fans squaring off. The company is actively courting financial institutions to take sides of wagers, and Fortinsky says Novig is currently onboarding proprietary trading firms and banks. The company is taking steps to make it easier to “trade programmatically,” using algorithms to automate placing money on which team will win the Super Bowl or how many times the Mets will lose, for example.

“Something that's really cool to see,” he says, “is that you have hundreds of these small shops with a couple guys with $100,000 that are now competing against some of the largest Wall Street trading firms in the world and doing quite well.” Good thing the teens aren’t allowed in.
